/atv-side-by-side-accident-lawyers/atv-p.title: ATV Product Defect Lawyers
/atv-side-by-side-accident-lawyers/atv-p.excerpt: Injured by a defective ATV or side-by-side in Georgia or South Carolina? Our product liability attorneys hold manufacturers accountable for dangerous design defects, mechanical failures, and recalled components.

_roden_faqs.question: How do I know if a defect caused my ATV accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Signs of a product defect include unexpected mechanical failures (throttle sticking, brakes failing, steering locking), post-crash fire, structural failures (frame cracks, suspension collapse), and any situation where the ATV behaved unexpectedly. An engineering expert can inspect the vehicle to determine if a defect was involved.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the ATV manufacturer even if I was partially at fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia allows recovery if you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina allows recovery if you are less than 51% at fault. Even if operator error contributed to the crash, a product defect may bear significant responsibility.

_roden_faqs.question: Does a CPSC recall help my product liability case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. A recall is strong evidence that the manufacturer acknowledged a safety defect. However, you do not need a recall to pursue a defect claim — many defective products have never been recalled. An experienced attorney can evaluate your case regardless.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the deadline to file an ATV product defect lawsuit?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia allows 2 years for personal injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) with a 10-year statute of repose from the product's first sale. South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Contact an attorney promptly to preserve your rights.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do with the ATV after a crash involving a suspected defect?
_roden_faqs.answer: Do not repair, modify, or dispose of the ATV. Photograph it from all angles, document the failed component, and contact an attorney immediately. We will issue a preservation letter and arrange for independent engineering inspection of the vehicle.

/atv-side-by-side-accident-lawyers/atv-r.title: ATV Rental and Tour Accident Lawyers
/atv-side-by-side-accident-lawyers/atv-r.excerpt: Injured during an ATV rental or guided tour in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys hold tour operators and rental companies accountable for unsafe equipment, inadequate training, and dangerous trail conditions.

_roden_faqs.question: Does the liability waiver I signed prevent me from suing the ATV rental company?
_roden_faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Georgia and South Carolina courts do not enforce waivers that attempt to absolve a business of gross negligence, willful misconduct, or violations of safety statutes. An attorney can evaluate whether the waiver is enforceable in your specific case.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if I am injured during an ATV tour?
_roden_faqs.answer: Seek immediate medical attention, photograph the ATV and the scene, get contact information for the tour guide and other participants, save a copy of any waiver you signed, do not give recorded statements to the company's insurance, and contact an attorney promptly.

_roden_faqs.question: Is the rental company liable if the ATV they provided was poorly maintained?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Rental companies have a duty to maintain their vehicles in safe operating condition. Renting an ATV with worn brakes, steering defects, or other mechanical problems constitutes negligence that can make the company liable for injuries caused by the equipment failure.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue if the tour guide led us through dangerous terrain?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Tour operators have a duty to select appropriate trails for the group's skill level, provide adequate warnings about hazards, and supervise riders throughout the tour. Leading inexperienced riders through advanced terrain without proper warnings is negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for an ATV rental accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia allows 2 years from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), and South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Contact an attorney promptly to ensure your claim is filed within the applicable deadline.

/atv-side-by-side-accident-lawyers/atv-r.title: ATV Road Collision Lawyers
/atv-side-by-side-accident-lawyers/atv-r.excerpt: Injured in an ATV or UTV collision on a public road in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys handle complex liability cases involving off-highway vehicles struck by motor vehicles on roadways.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I recover compensation if my ATV was on the road illegally when I was hit?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Even if the ATV was on the road in violation of Georgia or South Carolina law, the motor vehicle driver still owed a duty of care. Under comparative fault rules, you can recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault in Georgia or less than 51% in South Carolina.

_roden_faqs.question: Is it legal to ride an ATV on public roads in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Generally no. Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 40-7-120) prohibits ATV operation on public roads with limited exceptions for agricultural use, road crossings, and certain designated areas. Some counties may have additional local regulations.

_roden_faqs.question: Who is at fault when a car hits an ATV on a road?
_roden_faqs.answer: Fault depends on the specific circumstances — including whether the ATV was legally on the road, whether the car driver was speeding or distracted, and whether both parties had adequate lighting and visibility. Both drivers may share fault under comparative negligence rules.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if I am hit by a car while riding my ATV?
_roden_faqs.answer: Call 911 immediately, do not move if you suspect spinal injuries, photograph the scene and both vehicles, get the driver's insurance information, obtain witness contact details, seek medical attention, and contact an ATV accident attorney before speaking with any insurance company.

_roden_faqs.question: What damages are available in an ATV road collision case?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may recover medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, permanent disability, property damage, and in fatal cases, wrongful death damages. Punitive damages may be available if the motor vehicle driver was impaired or engaged in reckless conduct.

/atv-side-by-side-accident-lawyers/atv-r.title: ATV Rollover Accident Lawyers
/atv-side-by-side-accident-lawyers/atv-r.excerpt: Injured in an ATV rollover accident in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys pursue maximum compensation for victims of ATV rollovers caused by defective design, unsafe terrain, and operator negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: Why are ATVs so prone to rollovers?
_roden_faqs.answer: ATVs have a high center of gravity relative to their narrow wheelbase, making them inherently unstable — especially on slopes, during turns, and when carrying passengers or heavy loads. Unlike side-by-side UTVs, most ATVs also lack roll cages to protect riders during a rollover.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the ATV manufacturer if the vehicle rolled over due to a design defect?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11) and South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 15-73-10), manufacturers are strictly liable for design defects that make their products unreasonably dangerous. An ATV with inadequate stability margins may be considered defectively designed.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after an ATV rollover accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Seek immediate medical attention, do not move the ATV from the crash site if possible, photograph the scene and the ATV from multiple angles, preserve the ATV for expert inspection, get witness information, and contact an ATV accident attorney before speaking with insurance adjusters.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for an ATV rollover claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of injury to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Product liability claims may have additional time limitations, so prompt legal consultation is important.

_roden_faqs.question: Are property owners liable for ATV rollover accidents on their land?
_roden_faqs.answer: Property owners who invite or permit ATV riding on their land may be liable if they fail to warn of known hazards such as steep grades, hidden drop-offs, or unstable terrain. Georgia and South Carolina premises liability laws require property owners to maintain reasonably safe conditions for invited users.

/atv-side-by-side-accident-lawyers/child.excerpt: Child injured or killed in an ATV accident in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys hold negligent adults, property owners, and manufacturers accountable for preventable child ATV injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: What age is too young to ride an ATV in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: The CPSC recommends no ATV use for children under 6 years old. Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 40-7-120) restricts children under 16 from operating ATVs on public land without a safety course and prohibits age-inappropriate engine sizes. The AAP recommends no child under 16 operate any ATV.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue if another adult let my child ride an ATV and they were injured?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. An adult who provides an ATV to a child — or permits a child to ride without proper supervision, training, or age-appropriate equipment — can be held liable under negligent entrustment and negligent supervision theories in both Georgia and South Carolina.

_roden_faqs.question: Are ATV manufacturers liable for child injuries?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potentially yes. Manufacturers who market ATVs to children, fail to include adequate age-restriction warnings, or design vehicles without appropriate speed limiters for youth models may face product liability claims for resulting injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a child ATV injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia allows 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), but special tolling rules may extend these deadlines for minor children. Consult an attorney to understand the specific deadlines in your case.

_roden_faqs.question: Can we file a wrongful death claim if our child was killed in an ATV accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-51-10) both allow parents to file wrongful death claims for the loss of a child. These claims seek compensation for the full value of the child's life, including future companionship and society.

_roden_faqs.question: Are side-by-side vehicles safer than ATVs?
_roden_faqs.answer: Side-by-sides offer some safety advantages over ATVs, including roll cages, seatbelts, and a wider wheelbase. However, they are still prone to rollovers, especially at high speeds and on uneven terrain. Their higher speeds and greater weight can also lead to more severe crash outcomes.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue Polaris if my RZR caught fire or rolled over due to a defect?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Polaris has been the subject of multiple CPSC recalls for fire hazards and mechanical defects. Under Georgia and South Carolina product liability law, you can pursue strict liability, negligence, and breach of warranty claims against the manufacturer.

_roden_faqs.question: Is it legal to drive a side-by-side on public roads in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Generally no. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 40-7-120) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 56-15-10) restrict side-by-side operation on public roads, with limited exceptions. Operating illegally on a road can affect liability determinations in an accident case.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after a UTV accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Call 911, do not move the vehicle unless necessary for safety, photograph the scene and the UTV, preserve the vehicle for expert inspection, seek medical attention, and contact an attorney before accepting any insurance settlement or signing any documents.

_roden_faqs.question: What compensation is available for a side-by-side accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may recover medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, permanent disability, disfigurement, and emotional distress. In product defect cases, punitive damages may also be available. Fatal accidents give rise to wrongful death claims by surviving family members.

/bicycle-accident-lawyers/bicycle-vs-tru.title: Bicycle vs. Truck Accident Lawyers
/bicycle-accident-lawyers/bicycle-vs-tru.excerpt: Bicycle vs. truck accidents are among the most catastrophic crashes on the road. Massive blind spots, wide turns, and the sheer size of commercial trucks make these collisions almost always fatal or life-altering.

_roden_faqs.question: Why are bicycle vs. truck accidents so dangerous?
_roden_faqs.answer: The sheer size disparity — an 80,000-pound truck vs. a 200-pound cyclist — makes these crashes almost always catastrophic. Trucks also have massive blind spots on all sides, require much longer stopping distances, and their trailers track inward during right turns, potentially crushing a cyclist positioned at the curb.

_roden_faqs.question: Who is liable in a bicycle vs. truck accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Multiple parties may be liable: the truck driver, the trucking company (for negligent hiring, training, or hours-of-service violations), the vehicle owner, and the manufacturer (for defective brakes or mirrors). Trucking companies are vicariously liable for their drivers' negligence under federal motor carrier regulations.

_roden_faqs.question: What federal regulations apply to truck-bicycle crashes?
_roden_faqs.answer: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs) govern hours of service, driver qualifications, vehicle maintenance, and mirror requirements. Violations of these regulations — such as driving beyond allowed hours, failing to maintain brakes, or improperly adjusting mirrors — are strong evidence of negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the right-turn squeeze in a truck-bicycle accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: The right-turn squeeze occurs when a truck makes a right turn and the trailer tracks inward, crushing a cyclist positioned between the truck and the curb or sidewalk. This is one of the most common and deadly truck-bicycle crash patterns. Cyclists should never position themselves between a turning truck and the curb.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a bicycle vs. truck accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia allows 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). However, trucking companies are known to quickly repair or replace vehicles and delete electronic logging data. Contact an attorney immediately so a preservation letter can be sent to the trucking company.

_roden_faqs.question: Is texting while driving illegal in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia's Hands-Free Act (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-241.2) prohibits holding, supporting, or using a wireless device while driving. Drivers may not text, email, browse the internet, or use social media while operating a vehicle. Violation is a misdemeanor with fines and license points.

_roden_faqs.question: How do you prove a driver was distracted when they hit a cyclist?
_roden_faqs.answer: We subpoena cell phone records (call logs, text timestamps, data usage), app usage data, vehicle black box data showing no pre-crash braking, witness testimony, and any available camera footage. A driver who was texting at the time of the crash leaves a clear digital trail.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I get punitive damages if a distracted driver hit me on my bicycle?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potentially, yes. Because distracted driving — particularly texting — is a conscious, voluntary choice, courts may award punitive damages to punish the driver and deter others. Georgia allows punitive damages for willful misconduct (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), and South Carolina permits them for reckless or willful conduct.

_roden_faqs.question: Are hands-free phone calls safe while driving near cyclists?
_roden_faqs.answer: Research shows that even hands-free phone conversations create significant cognitive distraction — the driver's mental focus is diverted from driving. While hands-free use is legal in Georgia and South Carolina, it still impairs a driver's ability to see and react to cyclists, and can support a negligence claim if it contributes to a crash.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a distracted driver bicycle accident?

/bicycle-accident-lawyers/dooring-accide.excerpt: Struck by a car door while cycling? Dooring accidents cause devastating injuries to cyclists. Drivers and passengers have a legal duty to check for cyclists before opening doors. Our attorneys fight for maximum compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: What is a dooring accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: A dooring accident occurs when a driver or passenger opens a car door into the path of an approaching cyclist, causing the cyclist to collide with the door or swerve into traffic. These crashes happen most often in urban areas with on-street parking adjacent to bike lanes.

_roden_faqs.question: Is it illegal to open a car door into a cyclist in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-243) prohibits opening a vehicle door on the traffic side unless it is reasonably safe and will not interfere with traffic. Violating this law is negligence per se, meaning the door-opener is legally presumed to be at fault for any resulting collision.

_roden_faqs.question: Who is at fault in a dooring accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: The person who opened the door is almost always at fault. Vehicle occupants have a legal duty to check for approaching traffic — including cyclists — before opening a door on the traffic side. The cyclist has the right to use the roadway and should not be expected to anticipate a suddenly opened door.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after a dooring accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Call 911 and request a police report. Seek medical attention immediately. Photograph the scene, including the vehicle, open door, bike lane, and your injuries. Get the driver's insurance information and contact details for any witnesses. Preserve your damaged bicycle and helmet as evidence.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a dooring accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia allows 2 years from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Act quickly to preserve evidence — surveillance footage from nearby businesses may be overwritten within days.

South Carolina has similar provisions. If a bar overserved the driver who hit you, both the driver and the bar may be liable.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence is used to prove the driver was drunk?
_roden_faqs.answer: Key evidence includes the police report, breathalyzer and blood test results, field sobriety test results, officer observations, bar and restaurant receipts, witness testimony about the driver's behavior and consumption, and any criminal conviction. _roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a hit-and-run bicycle accident claim?

_roden_faqs.question: What is a right-hook bicycle accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: A right-hook occurs when a motor vehicle turns right and cuts across the path of a cyclist traveling straight. The driver either did not see the cyclist or misjudged the cyclist's speed and position. It is one of the most common types of car-vs-bicycle collisions.

_roden_faqs.question: What is a left-cross bicycle accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: A left-cross occurs when an oncoming vehicle turns left across a cyclist's path, similar to how a car turns left in front of an oncoming car. These crashes are particularly dangerous because the angle of impact is often head-on or near-head-on, and drivers frequently fail to see or properly judge the speed of approaching cyclists.

_roden_faqs.question: Is the driver always at fault in a right-hook or left-cross crash?
_roden_faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. The driver has a duty to yield to through-traffic — including cyclists — before turning. However, Georgia and South Carolina use comparative fault, so if the cyclist contributed to the crash (running a red light, for example), their recovery may be reduced. The driver is still liable if they failed to yield.

_roden_faqs.question: Do cyclists have the same rights as cars on the road?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-294) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 56-5-3435) grant cyclists the same rights and duties as motor vehicle drivers. Cyclists are entitled to use the roadway and have the right of way when traveling straight through an intersection.

/bicycle-accident-lawyers/road-hazard-bi.excerpt: Crashed your bicycle due to a pothole, debris, railroad tracks, or other road hazard? Government entities and property owners may be liable for dangerous road conditions that cause bicycle accidents.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the government for a pothole that caused my bicycle crash?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Government entities are responsible for maintaining roads in safe condition. If they knew or should have known about the pothole and failed to repair it, they can be held liable. However, claims against government entities have special notice requirements — in Georgia, you must provide ante-litem notice within 12 months.

_roden_faqs.question: Are there special procedures for suing a government entity in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia's Tort Claims Act (O.C.G.A. § 50-21-20 et seq.) requires ante-litem notice before filing suit against the state or local government. You must provide written notice within 12 months of the incident. Failure to comply with these requirements can bar your claim entirely.

_roden_faqs.question: What road hazards are most dangerous for cyclists?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potholes, railroad tracks crossing the road at acute angles, drainage grates with parallel slots, pavement edge drop-offs, loose gravel, steel plates in construction zones, and raised utility covers are among the most dangerous road hazards for cyclists. Any of these can cause a sudden loss of control.

_roden_faqs.question: Can a construction company be liable for a bicycle crash in a work zone?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Construction companies have a duty to maintain safe conditions for all road users, including cyclists. Steel plates, loose gravel, missing lane markings, and uneven pavement transitions in construction zones can all create dangerous conditions that the contractor is liable for.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a road hazard bicycle crash?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia allows 2 years for personal injury claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Claims against government entities may have shorter notice deadlines — Georgia requires ante-litem notice within 12 months. Contact an attorney immediately.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after a bicycle accident in Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: After a bicycle accident in Savannah, your first priority is getting medical attention — even if you feel fine, many injuries like concussions and internal bleeding do not show symptoms immediately. Call 911 and file a police report with Chatham County Superior Court jurisdiction. Document the scene with photos of your bicycle, any vehicle involved, road conditions, and your injuries. Get the driver's insurance information and contact details for any witnesses. Do not give a recorded statement to the driver's insurance company before speaking with an attorney. Contact Roden Law at (912) 303-5850 for a free consultation — we handle all bicycle accident cases on a contingency fee basis, so you pay nothing unless we win your case.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a driver who hit me while I was cycling in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. In Georgia, bicyclists have the same rights to the road as motor vehicle drivers. If a driver's negligence caused your bicycle accident — whether through distracted driving, failure to yield, dooring, or running a red light — you can file a personal injury claim against them. Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule, meaning you can recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). Even if the driver claims you were partially responsible, an experienced bicycle accident attorney can help demonstrate the full extent of their negligence. Our Savannah attorneys have recovered over $300 million for injured clients across Georgia and South Carolina.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a bicycle accident lawsuit in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations for personal injury claims, including bicycle accidents, is 2 years from the date of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). If you miss this deadline, you will almost certainly lose your right to pursue compensation. While 2 years may seem like enough time, evidence disappears, witnesses forget details, and insurance companies use delays against you. We recommend consulting a bicycle accident attorney as soon as possible after your accident. Call our Savannah office at (912) 303-5850 for a free case evaluation.

_roden_faqs.question: What compensation can I receive for a bicycle accident in Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: Bicycle accident victims in Savannah may be entitled to compensation for medical bills (emergency care, surgery, rehabilitation, and future treatment), lost wages and reduced earning capacity, pain and suffering, property damage to your bicycle and equipment, scarring and disfigurement, and loss of enjoyment of life. Because cyclists have no protective barrier like a vehicle occupant, bicycle accident injuries tend to be severe — traumatic brain injuries, broken bones, spinal injuries, and road rash are common. The value of your case depends on the severity of your injuries, the impact on your daily life, and the strength of the evidence. At Roden Law, we fight to recover the full value of your claim, not a lowball insurance settlement. Call (912) 303-5850 for a free consultation.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer for a bicycle accident claim in Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: While you are not legally required to hire an attorney, bicycle accident claims present unique challenges that benefit from experienced legal representation. Insurance companies routinely blame cyclists for accidents, minimize injuries by claiming pre-existing conditions, and offer settlements far below the true value of the case. An experienced bicycle accident lawyer can investigate the accident (including obtaining traffic camera footage and accident reconstruction), handle all insurance company communications, calculate the full value of your current and future damages, and negotiate or litigate for maximum compensation. At Roden Law, we handle bicycle accident cases on a contingency fee basis — you pay nothing upfront and owe no fees unless we win. Call our Savannah office at (912) 303-5850.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the driver who hit me on my bicycle left the scene in Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: Hit-and-run bicycle accidents are unfortunately common, but you still have options for recovering compensation. If you have uninsured motorist (UM) coverage on your auto insurance policy, it may cover your bicycle accident injuries even though you were not driving a car at the time. You should immediately report the hit-and-run to the Savannah police and file a report. Document everything you remember about the vehicle (color, make, model, license plate, direction of travel). Check for nearby surveillance cameras that may have captured the accident. An experienced attorney can help track down the driver and maximize your recovery through all available insurance sources. Contact Roden Law at (912) 303-5850 — we have handled numerous hit-and-run bicycle cases across Georgia.

_roden_faqs.question: Why do I need a lawyer for a truck accident instead of handling it myself?
_roden_faqs.answer: Truck accident cases involve complex federal regulations, multiple liable parties, and aggressive insurance defense teams. _roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a truck accident lawsuit in Georgia or South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: Who can be held liable in a truck accident besides the driver?
_roden_faqs.answer: Multiple parties may be liable, including the trucking company for negligent hiring or maintenance failures, the cargo loading company for improper securement, the truck or parts manufacturer for defective components, maintenance contractors, and even government entities for dangerous road conditions.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence is important in a truck accident case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Critical evidence includes electronic logging device (ELD) data, event data recorder (black box) information, driver qualification files, vehicle maintenance records, GPS and route data, dashcam footage, and drug and alcohol test results. An attorney sends preservation letters to prevent this evidence from being destroyed.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if I was partially at fault for the truck accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia allows recovery if you are less than 50% at fault under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, and South Carolina allows recovery if you are less than 51% at fault. Your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault.

_roden_faqs.question: How much does it cost to hire a truck accident attorney?
_roden_faqs.answer: At Roden Law, we handle all truck accident cases on a contingency fee basis. You pay no upfront costs and no attorney fees unless we recover compensation for you. There is no financial risk to hiring an experienced truck accident lawyer.

/blog/5-most-common-types-of-medical-mal.title: 5 Most Common Types of Medical Malpractice in Georgia and South Carolina

_roden_faqs.question: What are the most common types of medical malpractice?
_roden_faqs.answer: The five most common types are misdiagnosis or delayed diagnosis, surgical errors, medication errors, birth injuries, and anesthesia errors. Diagnostic errors represent the largest category of paid malpractice claims in the United States.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for medical malpractice in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must file a medical malpractice lawsuit within 2 years of the date the injury occurred or was discovered (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71). There is also a 5-year statute of repose, meaning no claim can be filed more than 5 years after the negligent act regardless of when the injury was discovered.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for medical malpractice in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In South Carolina, the statute of limitations for medical malpractice is 3 years from the date of injury or discovery (S.C. Code § 15-3-545). South Carolina has a 6-year statute of repose. Additionally, South Carolina requires mandatory pre-suit mediation before filing a lawsuit.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need an expert witness for a medical malpractice case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia requires an expert affidavit from a qualified medical professional to be filed with the complaint (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1). South Carolina requires expert testimony at trial to establish the standard of care and how it was breached. Without expert support, your case will likely be dismissed.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on medical malpractice damages in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has no cap on medical malpractice damages — its damages cap was struck down in 2010. South Carolina caps non-economic damages at $350,000 per defendant and $1.05 million total for all defendants (S.C. Code § 15-32-220), adjusted for inflation.

_roden_faqs.question: How much does it cost to hire a medical malpractice lawyer?
_roden_faqs.answer: Most medical malpractice attorneys, including those at Roden Law, work on a contingency fee basis. This means you pay no upfront fees and owe nothing unless the attorney recovers compensation for you. The fee is typically a percentage of the settlement or verdict.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: The five most common types of medical malpractice are misdiagnosis, surgical errors, medication errors, birth injuries, and anesthesia errors — contributing to over 250,000 deaths annually in the U.S. Georgia requires an expert affidavit with the complaint and has a 2-year statute of limitations with a 5-year repose period (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71). South Carolina requires mandatory mediation, allows 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-545), and caps non-economic damages at $350,000 per defendant.

/blog/7-mistakes-to-avoid-after-a-motorc.title: 7 Post-Accident Mistakes That Can Destroy Your Motorcycle Claim

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do immediately after a motorcycle accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Call 911, seek emergency medical care even if injuries seem minor, document the scene with photos and video, collect the other driver's insurance information, do not admit fault, and contact a motorcycle accident attorney as soon as possible. Early action protects both your health and your legal claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I give a recorded statement to the insurance company after a motorcycle crash?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. You are not legally required to give a recorded statement to the at-fault driver's insurance company. Adjusters are trained to ask questions designed to minimize your claim or shift blame to you. Politely decline and direct all inquiries to your attorney.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a motorcycle accident claim in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has a two-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). You must file a lawsuit within two years of the accident date, or your claim is permanently barred. However, contacting an attorney immediately is important because evidence degrades quickly.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a motorcycle accident claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina allows three years to file a personal injury lawsuit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). While this provides more time than Georgia, you should still act quickly to preserve evidence, secure witness statements, and protect dashcam or surveillance footage before it is destroyed.

_roden_faqs.question: Is Georgia a helmet state for motorcycle riders?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia requires all motorcycle riders and passengers to wear helmets (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-315). Failure to wear a helmet can be used as evidence of comparative fault for head injuries, potentially reducing your compensation. South Carolina only requires helmets for riders under 21.

_roden_faqs.question: Why should I not accept the first settlement offer after a motorcycle accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: First settlement offers are almost always far below the true value of your claim. Insurers make early offers before you understand the full extent of your injuries and future treatment needs. Once you accept and sign a release, you cannot seek additional compensation — even if your injuries worsen significantly.

/blog/accident-claims-with-an-expired-li.title: Can You File a Claim With an Expired License?

_roden_faqs.question: Can I file an accident claim if my license was expired?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, an expired license does not prevent you from filing a personal injury claim. Your right to compensation depends on who caused the accident, not whether your license was current. An expired license is an administrative issue that does not cause accidents.

_roden_faqs.question: Will the insurance company deny my claim because of an expired license?
_roden_faqs.answer: Insurance companies may try to deny your claim or reduce your settlement based on an expired license, but this is generally not legally supported. An expired license does not establish causation for the accident. Having an attorney handle insurance communications prevents them from exploiting this issue.

_roden_faqs.question: Is an expired license the same as a suspended license for injury claims?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. An expired license is an administrative oversight with minimal impact on fault analysis. A suspended or revoked license — which was taken away due to violations like DUI — carries much more legal weight because it suggests a pattern of unsafe driving behavior.

_roden_faqs.question: Can an expired license be used against me in court?
_roden_faqs.answer: While driving with an expired license violates Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-20) and South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 56-1-20), courts require that the violation be the proximate cause of the accident for it to affect fault. Since an expired license does not cause accidents, it typically fails the causation test.

_roden_faqs.question: What are the penalties for driving with an expired license?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, it is a misdemeanor with fines up to $1,000 and up to 12 months in jail (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-20). In South Carolina, penalties include fines up to $300 and up to 30 days in jail for a first offense (S.C. Code § 56-1-460). The criminal case is separate from your civil injury claim.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for filing an accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, you have 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Do not let concerns about your expired license delay filing — the deadline applies regardless of your license status.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: An expired driver's license does not bar personal injury claims in Georgia or South Carolina. Courts distinguish between administrative violations and accident causation — an expired license does not cause collisions. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and South Carolina use modified comparative fault, reducing damages by fault percentage. /blog/am-i-eligible-for-workers-compensa.title: Am I Eligible for Workers' Compensation in Georgia or South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: What are the basic requirements for workers' comp eligibility?
_roden_faqs.answer: You must meet four requirements: (1) you must be classified as an employee (not an independent contractor), (2) your injury must be work-related, (3) your employer must be required to carry workers' comp insurance, and (4) you must report the injury and file your claim within the required deadlines. Workers' comp is a no-fault system — you do not need to prove employer negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: How many employees must an employer have to be required to carry workers' comp?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, employers with 3 or more employees must carry workers' compensation insurance (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-2). In South Carolina, the threshold is 4 or more employees (S.C. Code § 42-1-360). Certain categories like agricultural workers, domestic workers, and railroad employees have different rules.

_roden_faqs.question: How quickly must I report a work injury in Georgia vs. South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must report to your employer within 30 days of the injury (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80). South Carolina gives you 90 days (S.C. Code § 42-15-20). However, you should report immediately — delayed reporting is one of the most common reasons claims are denied. Formal claims must be filed within 1 year in Georgia or 2 years in South Carolina.

_roden_faqs.question: Can independent contractors get workers' compensation?
_roden_faqs.answer: Independent contractors are generally not covered by workers' comp. However, many workers are misclassified as independent contractors when they are actually employees. Both Georgia and South Carolina look at the actual working relationship — not just the label. If your employer controls how, when, and where you work, you may be an employee entitled to coverage despite being called a contractor.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I get workers' comp if the injury was my fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Workers' compensation is a no-fault system — you are eligible even if the injury was caused by your own mistake or carelessness. The only exceptions are injuries caused by intoxication (which both Georgia and South Carolina recognize as grounds for denial) or intentional self-harm.

_roden_faqs.question: Are part-time workers and undocumented workers eligible for workers' comp?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes to both. Part-time employees are covered the same as full-time workers in both Georgia and South Carolina. Undocumented workers are also eligible for workers' comp — immigration status does not affect coverage. The law focuses on the employment relationship and the work-related injury, not the worker's documentation status.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Workers' comp eligibility requires employee status, a work-related injury, employer insurance coverage, and timely reporting. Georgia requires employers with 3+ employees to carry coverage (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-2) with a 30-day reporting deadline (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80). South Carolina's threshold is 4+ employees (S.C. Code § 42-1-360) with 90 days to report (S.C. Code § 42-15-20). Workers' comp is no-fault — eligibility does not depend on proving employer negligence. Part-time and undocumented workers are covered.

/blog/animal-accident-insurance-coverage.title: Does Car Insurance Cover an Accident with an Animal in Georgia or South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: Does comprehensive insurance cover hitting a deer?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Directly striking an animal is typically covered under comprehensive insurance, not collision. You will pay your comprehensive deductible, and this type of claim generally does not increase your insurance premiums.

_roden_faqs.question: What happens if I swerve to avoid an animal and hit another car?
_roden_faqs.answer: If you swerve to avoid an animal and hit another vehicle or object, the damage falls under collision coverage, not comprehensive. You may be found partially at fault for the swerve, which could increase your insurance rates.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a livestock owner if their animal caused my accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3) and South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 47-7-120), livestock owners have a duty to keep their animals properly fenced. If they fail to do so and their animal causes a car accident, they can be held liable for injuries and damages.

_roden_faqs.question: Does liability-only insurance cover animal accident damage to my car?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. If you carry only the minimum liability insurance required by Georgia or South Carolina law, you have no coverage for damage to your own vehicle from an animal strike. Only comprehensive coverage protects against animal collision damage.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after hitting a deer in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Pull over safely, call 911, do not approach the animal, photograph the damage and scene, check for injuries, and file a comprehensive insurance claim promptly. A police report strengthens your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: When is deer strike season in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Deer-vehicle collisions peak during October through December — the deer mating season (rut). During this period, deer are more active and more likely to cross roadways, especially at dawn and dusk.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Hitting an animal directly is covered by comprehensive insurance, while swerving into another object falls under collision coverage. Livestock owners can be liable under O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3 (Georgia) and S.C. Code § 47-7-120 (South Carolina). Georgia allows 2 years for injury claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Minimum liability-only insurance does not cover animal strike damage to your vehicle.

/blog/answering-insurance-questions-afte.title: How to Answer Insurance Company Questions After a Car Accident in Georgia or South Carolina

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to talk to the other driver's insurance company after an accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. You have no legal obligation to speak with the at-fault driver's insurance company in Georgia or South Carolina. You can politely decline and refer them to your attorney. You do have a contractual duty to cooperate with your own insurer.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I give a recorded statement to an insurance adjuster?
_roden_faqs.answer: You should not give a recorded statement to the at-fault driver's insurer without consulting an attorney first. There is no law requiring it, and recorded statements can be selectively quoted to minimize or deny your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I say when an insurance adjuster calls after my accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Provide only basic information: your name, contact details, and the date and location of the accident. Do not discuss fault, your injuries in detail, or say you are fine. State that you are still receiving medical treatment and prefer to have your attorney handle further communications.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a car accident claim in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia's statute of limitations is 2 years from the accident date (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Missing these deadlines typically bars your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: What is a lowball settlement offer and should I accept it?
_roden_faqs.answer: A lowball offer is an initial settlement amount far below the true value of your claim, often made within days of the accident before you understand your full injuries. You should not accept any settlement without consulting an attorney, as signing a release permanently closes your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Can my social media posts hurt my insurance claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Insurance companies routinely monitor claimants' social media accounts. Photos of physical activities, check-ins at events, or posts about your daily life can be used to argue your injuries are not as severe as claimed. Limit social media activity during your claim.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: After a car accident in Georgia or South Carolina, you have no obligation to speak with the at-fault driver's insurer. Never give recorded statements without legal counsel. Georgia uses modified comparative fault under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33 (less than 50%), South Carolina allows recovery at 51% or less. Filing deadlines: 2 years in GA (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), 3 years in SC (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Avoid admitting fault or saying you feel fine.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if I was partially at fault?

_roden_faqs.question: What if I was the aggressor in a workplace fight?
_roden_faqs.answer: If you initiated the physical confrontation, your workers' comp claim will likely be denied in both Georgia and South Carolina. _roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a charter boat company if I was injured on a Charleston charter?

_roden_faqs.question: What is the penalty for boating under the influence (BUI) in South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a boating accident claim in South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after a boating accident in Charleston?

/blog/calculating-compensation-for-whipl.title: Calculating Compensation for Whiplash Injuries in Georgia and South Carolina

_roden_faqs.question: How much is a whiplash injury claim worth?
_roden_faqs.answer: The value of a whiplash claim depends on the severity of your injury, the duration of your recovery, your medical expenses, and your lost income. Mild whiplash that resolves within weeks may result in settlements of $2,500 to $10,000, while severe whiplash with chronic symptoms can be worth $50,000 to $150,000 or more. An experienced attorney can evaluate the specific facts of your case and provide a realistic estimate.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a whiplash injury claim in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years from the date of injury (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Missing these deadlines means losing the right to pursue compensation entirely, so it is important to consult an attorney as soon as possible after your accident.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if I was partially at fault for the accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule that allows you to recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). South Carolina allows recovery if you are less than 51% at fault. In both states, your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are 20% at fault and your damages total $50,000, you would receive $40,000.

_roden_faqs.question: Why are my whiplash symptoms delayed after the accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: It is very common for whiplash symptoms to appear days or even weeks after an accident. The adrenaline and stress hormones released during a collision can mask pain signals, and inflammation in the soft tissues of the neck may take time to develop fully. This is why medical professionals recommend seeking an evaluation immediately after any accident, even if you feel fine at the scene.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence do I need to prove a whiplash injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Key evidence includes medical records documenting your diagnosis, treatment plan, and the progression of your symptoms; photographs of the accident scene and vehicle damage; the police report; a personal pain journal describing your daily symptoms and limitations; records of all medical expenses and lost wages; and witness statements. The stronger your documentation, the more difficult it becomes for the insurance company to undervalue your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I accept the insurance company's first settlement offer for my whiplash injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: In most cases, no. Initial settlement offers from insurance companies are almost always lower than the true value of a whiplash claim. Insurers make early offers hoping you will accept before you fully understand the extent of your injury and future treatment needs. An attorney can review any offer, calculate the full value of your damages including future medical costs, and negotiate for a fair settlement on your behalf.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Whiplash injuries range from Grade 0 (no symptoms) to Grade IV (fractures or dislocations), and compensation covers medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering, and diminished quality of life. Georgia's modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. SS 51-12-33) bars recovery at 50% or more fault, while South Carolina bars recovery at 51% or more. Filing deadlines are two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. SS 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code SS 15-3-530). Thorough medical documentation and consistent treatment records are critical to maximizing a whiplash claim.

/blog/can-an-insurance-company-go-agains.title: Can an Insurance Company Go Against a Police Report in Georgia or South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: Is an insurance company required to accept the police report?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Insurance companies are not legally bound by a police officer's fault determination. The police report is one piece of evidence, not a binding legal ruling. Insurers conduct their own investigations and can reach different conclusions about who was at fault.

_roden_faqs.question: Can a police report be used as evidence at trial in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: The police report itself is generally considered hearsay and may not be directly admissible as proof of fault. However, the officer who wrote the report can testify in person about what they observed at the scene, and any traffic citations issued are admissible as evidence of negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if the police report contains errors?
_roden_faqs.answer: Request a copy of the report as soon as possible and review it for inaccuracies. You can contact the responding law enforcement agency to request corrections to factual errors. Your attorney can also submit a supplemental statement and gather independent evidence such as dashcam footage, photographs, and witness statements to contradict errors in the report.

_roden_faqs.question: How does comparative fault affect my claim if the police report is in my favor?
_roden_faqs.answer: Even with a favorable police report, the insurance company may argue you share some fault. In Georgia, you can recover as long as you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). In South Carolina, you can recover as long as you are less than 51% at fault. Your award is reduced by your percentage of responsibility.

_roden_faqs.question: Why would an insurance company dispute a police report?
_roden_faqs.answer: Common reasons include: the officer did not witness the accident and relied on statements, the insurer found conflicting evidence such as dashcam or surveillance footage, the insurer located new witnesses, the insurer hired an accident reconstruction expert who reached different conclusions, or the report contains factual errors that undermine its reliability.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I get a lawyer if the insurance company is ignoring the police report?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. When an insurance company disputes a police report that supports your claim, an experienced personal injury attorney can subpoena the officer to testify, use traffic citations as evidence of negligence, gather independent evidence to corroborate the report, and challenge the insurer's denial as potentially being made in bad faith.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Insurance companies can and frequently do dispute police report findings in Georgia and South Carolina, using their own investigators and adjusters to challenge the officer's fault determination. Police reports are generally not admissible as evidence at trial in either state, though the responding officer can testify about observations. If a police report contains errors, you can request corrections through the issuing agency. Strengthening your claim with independent evidence such as dashcam footage, witness statements, medical records, and accident reconstruction reports is essential when an insurer disputes the official report.

_roden_faqs.question: Can someone sue me personally after a car accident if I have insurance?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Having insurance does not prevent someone from filing a lawsuit against you. You face personal financial exposure only when the claimed damages exceed your coverage limits, your insurer denies coverage, or punitive damages are awarded.

_roden_faqs.question: What happens if the damages exceed my car insurance policy limits?
_roden_faqs.answer: If the injured person's damages exceed your liability coverage, they can pursue a judgment against you personally for the difference. This means your savings, home equity, investments, and future wages could be at risk. Both Georgia and South Carolina require only $25,000 per person in minimum liability coverage, which is often insufficient for serious injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: How long does someone have to sue me after a car accident in Georgia or South Carolina?

In South Carolina, the deadline is three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Exceptions exist for minors and individuals with mental incapacity, which can extend these deadlines.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I be sued if the other driver was also partially at fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, but the other driver's share of fault reduces your financial exposure. Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) where the plaintiff is barred from recovery if they are 50% or more at fault. In South Carolina, the threshold is 51%. If the other driver contributed to the crash, your liability is reduced proportionally.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if I receive a lawsuit summons after a car accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Do not ignore it — failing to respond within 30 days results in a default judgment against you. Contact your auto insurance company immediately so they can assign a defense attorney. Do not contact the plaintiff or post about the accident on social media. If the claimed damages may exceed your policy limits, consult your own attorney to protect your personal assets.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I countersue if I was also injured in the accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Even if you were partially at fault, you may have a valid counterclaim for your own injuries under Georgia or South Carolina's comparative fault rules. You can recover compensation as long as your share of fault is below the threshold — less than 50% in Georgia, less than 51% in South Carolina. An attorney can evaluate whether a counterclaim is viable.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the minimum car insurance required in Georgia?

_roden_faqs.question: What is the minimum car insurance required in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina requires the same 25/50/25 minimum liability limits as Georgia. However, South Carolina also mandates uninsured motorist (UM) coverage at the same limits as liability under S.C. Code § 38-77-150. UIM coverage must be offered but can be declined.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between UM and UIM coverage?
_roden_faqs.answer: Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage pays when the at-fault driver has no insurance at all. Underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage kicks in when the at-fault driver's insurance is not enough to cover your damages.

_roden_faqs.question: What is MedPay and how does it help after an accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Medical Payments coverage (MedPay) pays for your medical bills after an accident regardless of who was at fault. It covers hospital visits, surgery, X-rays, ambulance rides, and other medical expenses up to your policy limit. MedPay pays quickly without waiting for the liability claim to settle.

_roden_faqs.question: Does Georgia or South Carolina require MedPay coverage?
_roden_faqs.answer: Neither state requires MedPay, but both states require insurers to offer it. Given that neither state offers PIP coverage, MedPay is the closest equivalent and is highly recommended for covering immediate medical costs.

_roden_faqs.question: How does having the right insurance affect my personal injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Having UM/UIM and MedPay coverage can dramatically increase your total recovery. If the at-fault driver is uninsured or underinsured, your UM/UIM policy fills the gap. _roden_faqs.question: What is maximum medical improvement (MMI)?
_roden_faqs.answer: MMI is the point at which your condition has stabilized and further treatment is unlikely to produce significant improvement. It does not mean you are fully healed — it means you have recovered as much as medical science can achieve for your injury.

_roden_faqs.answer: Medical malpractice occurs when a healthcare provider fails to provide care that meets the accepted standard of care in their specialty, and that failure causes injury to the patient. A bad outcome alone does not prove malpractice.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need an expert witness for a medical malpractice case in South Carolina?

The expert must be licensed, must practice or have recently practiced in the same specialty as the defendant, and must have practiced within the past five years.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: The statute of limitations is three years from the date of injury or discovery (S.C. Code section 15-3-545). _roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on damages in South Carolina medical malpractice cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina does not cap economic damages in medical malpractice cases, but non-economic damages are capped by S.C. Code § 15-32-220 — a base of $350,000 against a single provider and $1.05 million where more than one is liable, adjusted annually for inflation, so the limit that applies today is higher than the base. Punitive damages are capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (S.C. Code section 15-32-530), with exceptions for certain egregious conduct.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue both the hospital and the doctor in Charleston?

Complex cases may involve the surgeon, anesthesiologist, nursing staff, the hospital, and the physician's medical group as separate defendants.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the Notice of Intent requirement in South Carolina medical malpractice cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: Before filing a medical malpractice lawsuit in South Carolina, you must serve a Notice of Intent to File Suit on each defendant at least 90 days before filing the complaint. The notice must include an expert affidavit from a qualified medical professional who has reviewed the records and identified at least one negligent act and the resulting damages. _roden_faqs.question: Can I still file a personal injury claim if the at-fault driver died in the accident?

_roden_faqs.question: Do I sue the deceased driver's family members?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. You sue the deceased driver's estate, not the family members personally. The estate is a legal entity managed by a personal representative (executor) appointed by the probate court. The deceased driver's liability insurance typically defends the case and pays any judgment up to policy limits. Family members' personal assets are generally not at risk.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the deceased driver had no insurance or not enough coverage?
_roden_faqs.answer: If the deceased driver was uninsured or underinsured, you may file a claim through your own uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage. You may also pursue a claim against the estate's assets through probate court. An attorney can identify all available sources of recovery to maximize your compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a claim against a deceased at-fault driver?
_roden_faqs.answer: The standard statutes of limitations apply — two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). However, probate creditor deadlines may impose additional requirements, particularly in South Carolina where claims against the estate must be filed within one year of death. Consult an attorney promptly to avoid missing any deadlines.

_roden_faqs.question: Is it wrong to pursue a claim when the other driver has died?
_roden_faqs.answer: Your claim is primarily against the insurance company, not the deceased driver's family. Auto insurance exists for this exact purpose — the at-fault driver paid premiums so their insurer would cover damages from their negligence. Your medical bills, lost wages, and suffering are real regardless of the other driver's fate, and not pursuing the claim only leaves you bearing the full financial burden.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence challenges arise when the at-fault driver is deceased?
_roden_faqs.answer: The deceased driver cannot testify, which means the insurance company may try to shift blame onto you without contradiction. This makes objective evidence critical: police reports, witness statements, dashcam footage, accident reconstruction analysis, cell phone records, and toxicology reports from the autopsy can all help establish fault in the absence of the other driver's testimony.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between lost wages and lost earning capacity?
_roden_faqs.answer: Lost wages are income you already missed while recovering from your injuries. Lost earning capacity is a forward-looking claim for future income you will never earn because your injuries permanently reduced your ability to work. Both are recoverable in Georgia and South Carolina personal injury cases, but they require different types of proof and expert analysis.

_roden_faqs.question: How do I prove lost wages in a personal injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: You will need documentation from your employer confirming your pay rate, hours missed, and reason for absence. Self-employed workers can use tax returns, profit-and-loss statements, contracts, and client communications.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I recover lost wages if I used sick days or vacation time?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, you can recover compensation for paid time off you were forced to use because of your accident injuries. Those sick days and vacation days have monetary value, and you should not have to deplete your benefits because of someone else's negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a lost wage claim in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia's statute of limitations for personal injury claims, including lost wages, is 2 years from the date of injury under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. If you miss this deadline, you lose the right to recover any compensation. Lost earning capacity claims follow the same 2-year deadline.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a lost wage claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina gives you 3 years from the date of injury to file a personal injury claim under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. This applies to all damages including lost wages and lost earning capacity. Filing promptly is still advisable because evidence fades and witnesses become harder to locate over time.

_roden_faqs.question: How does comparative fault affect my lost wage recovery?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, your lost wage award is reduced by your percentage of fault, and you recover nothing if you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). In South Carolina, the threshold is 51% — you can recover as long as your fault does not equal or exceed 51%. Both states reduce your total award proportionally to your share of blame.

Violations of these regulations are strong evidence of negligence in a truck accident lawsuit.

_roden_faqs.question: How much insurance are trucking companies required to carry?
_roden_faqs.answer: Federal law (49 CFR § 387) requires commercial trucking companies to carry significantly more insurance than passenger vehicle drivers. Many carriers purchase coverage well above these minimums because catastrophic truck accident injuries routinely generate claims that exceed minimum policy limits.

_roden_faqs.answer: Critical evidence in a truck accident case includes electronic logging device (ELD) data showing hours-of-service compliance, event data recorder (black box) data capturing speed and braking in the seconds before the crash, the driver's qualification file with employment history and drug test results, vehicle maintenance and inspection records, dispatch and communication records, dashcam and surveillance footage, and accident reconstruction expert analysis. _roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for filing a truck accident lawsuit in Georgia and South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between compensatory and punitive damages?
_roden_faqs.answer: Compensatory damages reimburse the injured person for actual losses such as medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering. Punitive damages are a separate award meant to punish the defendant for especially reckless or intentional conduct and deter similar behavior in the future.

_roden_faqs.question: Are punitive damages available in every personal injury case?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Punitive damages are only awarded when the defendant's conduct goes beyond ordinary negligence — such as drunk driving, intentional harm, or knowingly selling a dangerous product. They must be proven by clear and convincing evidence, a higher standard than what is required for compensatory damages.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on punitive damages in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1, Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most personal injury cases. However, the cap does not apply when the defendant acted with specific intent to cause harm, was driving under the influence, or in certain product liability cases.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the punitive damages cap in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Under S.C. Code § 15-32-530, South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times the compensatory damages or $500,000. The cap does not apply if the defendant was under the influence of alcohol or drugs or if the defendant's conduct resulted in a felony conviction.

_roden_faqs.question: How does comparative fault affect my damage award in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Both states follow modified comparative fault rules. In Georgia, you can recover as long as you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). In South Carolina, you can recover as long as you are less than 51% at fault. Your total award is reduced by your percentage of responsibility.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to pay anything upfront to hire a personal injury lawyer?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Roden Law handles personal injury cases on a contingency fee basis, which means you pay no attorney fees unless we recover compensation for you. Your initial consultation is free.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Compensatory damages reimburse injury victims for medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering, while punitive damages punish extreme misconduct like drunk driving or fraud. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 unless specific exceptions apply (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), and South Carolina has no statutory cap but requires clear and convincing evidence. Both damage types require thorough documentation and expert testimony to maximize recovery.

/blog/construction-worker-injuries-charl.title: Construction Worker Injuries in Charleston: Your Rights on the Fastest-Growing Job Sites in SC

_roden_faqs.question: What are my rights if I am injured on a construction site in Charleston?
_roden_faqs.answer: If you are an employee, you are generally entitled to South Carolina workers' compensation benefits (S.C. Code section 42-1-10 et seq.) regardless of fault. Additionally, you may have a third-party personal injury claim against parties other than your direct employer — such as the general contractor, other subcontractors, equipment manufacturers, or the property owner — who were negligent in causing your injury. Third-party claims allow recovery of full damages including pain and suffering.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue my employer if I was hurt on a construction site?
_roden_faqs.answer: Generally, no. Workers' compensation is your exclusive remedy against your direct employer in South Carolina. However, you can sue third parties whose negligence caused your injury, including the general contractor, other subcontractors, equipment manufacturers, and property owners. If you were misclassified as an independent contractor, you may not be bound by the workers' comp exclusivity bar and could potentially sue the hiring company directly.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between a workers' comp claim and a third-party claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Workers' comp provides no-fault benefits including medical treatment and partial wage replacement, but does not cover pain and suffering and caps benefits. A third-party personal injury claim requires proving negligence but allows recovery of full damages including medical bills, all lost wages, pain and suffering, and potentially punitive damages. Both claims can be pursued simultaneously.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a construction injury claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: For workers' compensation, you must report the injury to your employer within 90 days and file a formal claim within two years (S.C. Code section 42-15-40). For a third-party personal injury lawsuit, the statute of limitations is three years (S.C. Code section 15-3-530). In Georgia, the deadlines are shorter: 30 days to report for workers' comp and two years for personal injury claims.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I was classified as an independent contractor on the construction site?
_roden_faqs.answer: Many construction workers are misclassified as independent contractors when they actually meet the legal definition of an employee. If you were misclassified, you may still be entitled to workers' comp benefits. Additionally, independent contractors are not barred from suing the hiring company for negligence, potentially giving you broader lawsuit rights than an employee would have. An attorney can evaluate your actual working relationship to determine your classification.

_roden_faqs.question: What types of construction accidents are most common in Charleston?
_roden_faqs.answer: The most common serious construction accidents fall into OSHA's Fatal Four categories: falls (from roofs, scaffolding, ladders, and elevated platforms), struck-by accidents (falling objects, vehicles, swinging loads), caught-in/between incidents (machinery, trench collapses, structural components), and electrocution. Charleston's high heat and humidity also make heat-related illness a significant hazard for outdoor construction workers.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Charleston's construction boom has increased workplace injuries including falls, electrocutions, struck-by incidents, and caught-between accidents — OSHA's "Fatal Four" hazards. Injured workers may collect South Carolina workers' compensation benefits regardless of fault, and may also pursue third-party claims against negligent subcontractors, equipment manufacturers, or property owners for additional damages. Independent contractors face different rules than employees. South Carolina's three-year filing deadline (S.C. Code SS 15-3-530) applies to third-party claims, while workers' comp has separate deadlines.

/blog/contingency-fee-system/.title: How the Contingency Fee System Works: No Upfront Costs for Georgia and South Carolina Injury Claims

_roden_faqs.question: What is a contingency fee?
_roden_faqs.answer: A contingency fee is a payment arrangement where the attorney's fee is a percentage of the compensation recovered in your case. You pay nothing upfront, and if the case is unsuccessful, you owe nothing for legal representation.

_roden_faqs.question: What percentage do personal injury lawyers charge?
_roden_faqs.answer: Most personal injury attorneys charge between 33.3% (one-third) and 40% of the recovery. The percentage may increase if the case goes to trial because the attorney's investment of time and resources increases at each stage.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between attorney fees and case expenses?
_roden_faqs.answer: Attorney fees are the percentage of recovery that compensates the lawyer for legal work. Case expenses are out-of-pocket costs like filing fees, expert witnesses, medical records, and depositions. Most firms advance expenses and deduct them from the settlement.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to pay anything if my case is unsuccessful?
_roden_faqs.answer: Under the contingency fee model, you owe nothing for the attorney's time if the case does not result in a settlement or verdict. Many firms also absorb advanced case expenses, though this varies — always clarify in your fee agreement.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for personal injury claims in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has a 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina has a 3-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Missing these deadlines means losing your right to file, so consult an attorney promptly.

_roden_faqs.question: What questions should I ask before signing a contingency fee agreement?
_roden_faqs.answer: Key questions include: What is the fee percentage at each stage? Are expenses deducted before or after the attorney fee? What happens to expenses if the case fails? Can I terminate the agreement? How will settlement funds be handled?

meta._roden_key_takeaways: The contingency fee system allows injury victims to hire experienced attorneys with no upfront costs — the lawyer's fee is a percentage of the recovery, typically 33-40%. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) both require written fee agreements. Case expenses like expert witnesses and filing fees are advanced by the firm and deducted from the settlement.

/blog/continuing-post-accident-medical-t.title: Why Continuing Medical Treatment After an Accident Matters for Your Claim

_roden_faqs.question: Why is it important to see a doctor immediately after an accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Prompt medical attention creates a documented link between the accident and your injuries. Insurance companies look for gaps between the accident date and first medical visit to argue injuries were not accident-related.

_roden_faqs.question: How do gaps in treatment hurt my claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Insurance adjusters use gaps to argue injuries healed, were not serious, or were caused by something else. Even a few weeks between appointments gives insurers ammunition to reduce your settlement.

_roden_faqs.question: What is maximum medical improvement (MMI)?
_roden_faqs.answer: MMI is when your doctor determines your condition has stabilized and further treatment will not produce significant improvement. Reaching MMI allows accurate calculation of permanent impairment, future medical needs, and lost earning capacity.

_roden_faqs.question: How can I pay for treatment while my case is pending?
_roden_faqs.answer: Options include health insurance, MedPay on your auto policy, letters of protection arranged by your attorney, and Medicaid or Medicare if eligible.

_roden_faqs.question: What medical evidence strengthens my claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: ER records, diagnostic imaging (MRIs, CT scans, X-rays), surgical records, physical therapy notes, prescription records, and your doctor's prognosis. Consistent records showing ongoing symptoms create a strong narrative.

_roden_faqs.question: Can the insurance company use my medical records against me?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. They look for pre-existing conditions, prior injuries, and notes suggesting improvement. Never sign a blanket medical records release — let your attorney control what is disclosed.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Consistent medical treatment is essential for both health and your personal injury claim. Insurance companies use treatment gaps to argue injuries are not serious. Georgia requires expert testimony under O.C.G.A. § 24-7-702. South Carolina follows S.C.R.E. 702. Reaching MMI allows accurate damage calculation. Payment options include health insurance, MedPay, and letters of protection.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury claim after a crash on I-95 in Georgia?
