_roden_faqs.question: What is comparative fault in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: SC follows a modified comparative fault rule (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). You can recover damages if your fault is less than 51 percent. Your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are 20 percent at fault and damages are 100,000 dollars, you recover 80,000 dollars.

_roden_faqs.question: How is SC comparative fault different from Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia bars recovery if you are 50 percent or more at fault (O.C.G.A. section 51-12-33). SC bars recovery at 51 percent or more. This one percent difference matters in close cases.

_roden_faqs.question: How do insurance companies use comparative fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: Insurers routinely argue the injured person was partially at fault to reduce the payout. Common arguments include following too closely, distracted driving, not wearing a seatbelt, or crossing outside a crosswalk.

_roden_faqs.question: Does wearing a seatbelt affect my claim in SC?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Under S.C. Code § 56-5-6540(C), a seatbelt violation is not negligence per se or contributory negligence and is not admissible as evidence in a civil action. South Carolina does not reduce your recovery by any set percentage for seatbelt non-use, and an insurer cannot put that evidence before a jury. If an adjuster raises it, that is not a basis South Carolina law recognizes.

_roden_faqs.question: How is fault determined?
_roden_faqs.answer: Fault is determined by the jury based on evidence including police reports, witness testimony, traffic camera footage, accident reconstruction, and expert opinions.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still recover if I was mostly at fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: In SC, yes, as long as your fault is less than 51 percent. In GA, you must be less than 50 percent at fault. Even at 49 percent fault in SC, you would recover 51 percent of your damages.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the comparative fault rule for pedestrian accidents in South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a pedestrian accident lawsuit in South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a driver who hit me even if I was jaywalking in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potentially, yes. Under S.C. Code § 56-5-3150, drivers must exercise due care to avoid colliding with any pedestrian on any roadway, regardless of who has the right of way. _roden_faqs.question: What extra duties do South Carolina drivers have around children and incapacitated pedestrians?
_roden_faqs.answer: S.C. Code § 56-5-3150 requires drivers to exercise proper precaution upon observing any child or any confused or incapacitated person on a roadway. _roden_faqs.question: Can I choose my own doctor for a workers' comp injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must select from your employer's posted panel of at least six physicians (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-201). If no valid panel is posted, you can choose your own doctor. _roden_faqs.question: What benefits am I entitled to under workers' compensation?
_roden_faqs.answer: Workers' comp benefits include medical treatment (no copays or deductibles), temporary total disability (two-thirds of average weekly wage), temporary partial disability, permanent partial or total disability benefits, vocational rehabilitation, and death benefits for dependents.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if my workers' comp claim is denied?
_roden_faqs.answer: Do not give up. In Georgia, request a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge at the State Board of Workers' Compensation. In South Carolina, disputed claims are heard by the Workers' Compensation Commission. An attorney can represent you through the appeals process.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a workers' compensation claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia the deadline is 1 year from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82), and it shifts in two ways that are not interchangeable: if your employer furnished remedial treatment you have one year from the last treatment, and if you were paid weekly income benefits you have two years from the last payment. _roden_faqs.question: Can I sue my employer if I was hurt at work?
_roden_faqs.answer: Generally no. Workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer in both Georgia and South Carolina, meaning you cannot sue for negligence. However, you may have a third-party claim against another responsible party, such as a product manufacturer or subcontractor.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do immediately after a bicycle hit and run?
_roden_faqs.answer: Move to safety, call 911, try to remember the vehicle (color, make, partial plate), look for witnesses and security cameras, do not move your bicycle, and photograph everything — your injuries, the scene, debris, and any paint transfer on your bike or clothing. Time is critical for evidence preservation.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I recover compensation if the hit-and-run driver is never found?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes — through your own uninsured motorist (UM) coverage. UM coverage pays for your injuries as if the hit-and-run driver had insurance. In Georgia, UM is offered but can be rejected (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11). In South Carolina it cannot be rejected at all: S.C. Code § 38-77-150 requires every auto policy issued in the state to carry UM, so a South Carolina policyholder has it whether or not they remember choosing it. You do not need to have been driving a car — UM covers bicycle accidents too.

_roden_faqs.question: Is leaving the scene of a bicycle accident a crime in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Hit and run involving injury is a felony in both states. In Georgia, penalties include 1-5 years imprisonment (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-270). In South Carolina, penalties can reach up to 25 years for serious injury or death (S.C. Code § 56-5-1210). Drivers have a legal duty to stop and render aid.

_roden_faqs.question: Does the 3-foot passing law apply to my bicycle accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-56) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 56-5-3435) require drivers to maintain at least 3 feet of clearance when passing a cyclist. If the hit-and-run driver violated this law, it supports your negligence claim once they are identified.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a claim after a bicycle hit and run?
_roden_faqs.answer: The personal injury statute of limitations is 2 years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and 3 years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). This applies whether the driver is identified or not. For UM claims, check your policy for any additional notice requirements.

_roden_faqs.question: What compensation can I recover after a bicycle hit and run?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may recover medical expenses (emergency care, surgery, rehabilitation), lost wages, pain and suffering, property damage (bicycle and gear replacement), loss of enjoyment of life, and scarring or disfigurement. These damages are available through a UM claim or a lawsuit against the identified driver.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: After a bicycle hit and run, call 911, document everything, and seek medical treatment immediately. _roden_faqs.question: Can I fire my personal injury lawyer in the middle of my case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, you have the right to terminate your attorney at any time and for any reason. This right is protected under each state's Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.16). Your lawyer cannot hold your case hostage, and they must return your file and cooperate with the transition to your new attorney.

_roden_faqs.question: Will I owe my first lawyer money if I switch?
_roden_faqs.answer: Possibly. If your first lawyer worked on a contingency fee basis, they may be entitled to a portion of the fee based on work already completed. In Georgia, attorneys can assert a lien under O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14. In South Carolina, fee disputes are governed by the reasonableness standard under S.C. Code § 37-5-108 and the Rules of Professional Conduct. Your new attorney can help negotiate or dispute any unreasonable lien.

_roden_faqs.question: When is it too late to switch personal injury lawyers?
_roden_faqs.answer: While you always have the right to fire your attorney, switching becomes more difficult once a case is close to trial. A judge may deny a continuance request if changing lawyers would significantly delay proceedings. Switching is easiest during the investigation, treatment, or pre-litigation negotiation phases.

_roden_faqs.question: What are the warning signs I should switch lawyers?
_roden_faqs.answer: Common red flags include unreturned phone calls or emails for weeks at a time, no case updates, pressure to accept a low settlement, lack of experience with your case type, your case being handed off to junior associates without notice, and missed deadlines or filing errors. Trust your instincts — if you feel your case is not being prioritized, it may be time for a change.

_roden_faqs.question: How do I transfer my case to a new lawyer?
_roden_faqs.answer: First, consult with a new attorney to confirm they will take your case. Then send written notice to your current attorney terminating the relationship. Request your complete case file in writing. Your former attorney must comply and transfer your file. Your new lawyer will handle the transition, review the file, and continue your case from where it left off.

_roden_faqs.question: Will switching lawyers hurt my case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Not if done properly and promptly. A better attorney who is responsive, experienced, and aggressive will almost always improve your outcome compared to staying with one who is neglecting your case. The key is to switch early enough that your new lawyer has time to build the strongest possible case before any deadlines or trial dates.

_roden_faqs.question: Is my personal injury settlement taxable in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Most personal injury settlement proceeds are not taxable in Georgia. Compensation for medical expenses, pain and suffering, and property damage is excluded from federal and Georgia state income tax under IRC § 104(a)(2). However, lost wages, punitive damages, and interest on the award are typically taxable.

_roden_faqs.question: Are personal injury settlements taxable in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina follows federal tax treatment, so compensation for physical injuries is generally tax-free. Taxable components include lost wages, punitive damages (capped at three times compensatory damages or $500,000 under S.C. Code § 15-32-530), and pre-judgment interest.

_roden_faqs.question: Are punitive damages from a car accident taxable?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Punitive damages are always taxable as ordinary income regardless of the underlying claim type. They must be reported as Other Income on your federal tax return. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), and South Carolina caps them at three times compensatory or $500,000.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I pay taxes on pain and suffering from an accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Pain and suffering compensation arising from a physical injury is excluded from federal income tax under IRC § 104(a)(2). This applies in both Georgia and South Carolina and covers both economic and non-economic damages directly tied to your physical injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: Are lost wages from a settlement taxable?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Lost wages received as part of a personal injury settlement are generally taxable as ordinary income because the wages would have been taxed if you had earned them normally. Your attorney can help structure the settlement agreement to properly allocate and minimize the tax impact.

_roden_faqs.question: Can a structured settlement reduce my taxes?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. A structured settlement pays compensation over time through an annuity, and the investment income earned within the annuity is tax-free — unlike a lump sum that you invest independently. This is particularly beneficial for large settlements involving lifetime care needs from brain injuries or spinal cord injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence should I gather at the motorcycle accident scene?
_roden_faqs.answer: Photograph vehicle positions, damage from multiple angles, road conditions, skid marks, traffic signs, weather conditions, and your visible injuries. Collect witness names and contact information, and write down everything you remember about the accident as soon as possible while details are fresh.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a motorcycle accident claim in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has a 2-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. South Carolina allows 3 years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. However, evidence can be lost quickly, so you should contact an attorney as soon as possible after the accident.

_roden_faqs.question: Can not wearing a helmet affect my motorcycle accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia requires all motorcycle riders to wear helmets under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-315, while South Carolina only requires helmets for riders under 21. In either state, the defense may argue that not wearing a helmet contributed to your injuries, which could reduce your compensation under comparative fault rules.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the other driver's insurance company says the motorcycle accident was my fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: Strong evidence is your best defense. Georgia allows recovery if you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina allows recovery if you are less than 51% at fault. Scene photos, witness statements, police reports, and electronic evidence can prove the other driver's negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: What types of electronic evidence can help my motorcycle accident case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Surveillance camera footage, dashcam or helmet camera recordings, the other driver's cell phone records, vehicle event data recorder (black box) data, GPS and navigation records, and social media posts can all provide critical evidence. An attorney can issue preservation letters to prevent this evidence from being destroyed.

/blog/the-most-common-causes-of-truck-ac.title: The Most Common Causes of Truck Accidents in Georgia and South Carolina

_roden_faqs.question: What is the most common cause of truck accidents?
_roden_faqs.answer: Driver fatigue is one of the leading causes of truck accidents nationwide. The FMCSA's Large Truck Crash Causation Study found fatigue was a factor in approximately 13% of all large truck crashes. Other top causes include distracted driving, speeding due to tight delivery schedules, impaired driving, brake failures, and improper cargo loading. Most truck accidents result from a combination of factors rather than a single cause, which is why thorough investigation is critical to identifying all responsible parties.

_roden_faqs.question: Who can be held liable for a truck accident in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Multiple parties may be liable in a truck accident, including the truck driver (for negligent driving), the trucking company (under respondeat superior for employee acts or for its own negligent hiring, training, or maintenance practices), the cargo loading company (for improperly secured loads), maintenance contractors (for faulty repairs), and the truck or parts manufacturer (for defective equipment under product liability law). Georgia and South Carolina both follow modified comparative fault rules — under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, Georgia bars recovery at 50% or more fault, while South Carolina bars recovery at 51% or more fault. Identifying all liable parties is essential to maximizing compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a truck accident lawsuit in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations for personal injury claims is 2 years from the date of the accident under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. In South Carolina, you have 3 years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. However, you should not wait — federal regulations only require trucking companies to preserve electronic logging device (ELD) data for six months, and event data recorder (black box) evidence can be overwritten even sooner. An attorney should send a spoliation letter immediately to preserve critical evidence.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence is important in a truck accident case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Key evidence in truck accident cases includes electronic logging device (ELD) data showing hours-of-service compliance, the truck's event data recorder (black box) data capturing speed and braking before the crash, the driver's qualification file and drug test results, vehicle maintenance and inspection records, dispatch communications that may reveal pressure to violate safety rules, cargo loading documents and weight tickets, and accident reconstruction analysis. Because some of this evidence can be destroyed or overwritten quickly, it is critical to involve a truck accident attorney immediately to send preservation demands.

_roden_faqs.question: How is a truck accident case different from a regular car accident case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Truck accident cases are substantially more complex than car accident claims. They involve federal FMCSA regulations (hours of service, drug testing, vehicle maintenance, cargo securement) that do not apply to passenger vehicles. Multiple parties are often liable — not just the driver but also the trucking company, cargo shippers, maintenance contractors, and manufacturers. Trucking companies have aggressive legal teams and larger insurance policies (typically $1 million or more). Critical electronic evidence like ELD data and black box recordings must be preserved quickly. The injuries are also typically far more severe due to the massive size and weight differential between commercial trucks and passenger vehicles.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after being hit by a commercial truck in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Call 911 and seek immediate medical attention, even if you feel okay — truck accident injuries can be severe and symptoms may be delayed. If possible, document the scene with photos, including the truck's DOT number and company markings. Get contact information from witnesses. Do not give a recorded statement to the trucking company's insurance adjuster. Contact a truck accident attorney as soon as possible — critical evidence like ELD data, black box recordings, and driver logbooks can be destroyed or overwritten within weeks if not preserved through a spoliation letter. At Roden Law, we offer free consultations and handle all truck accident cases on a contingency fee basis.

/blog/the-role-of-vocational-rehabilitat.title: The Role of Vocational Rehabilitation in Workers' Compensation Cases in Georgia and South Carolina

_roden_faqs.question: What is vocational rehabilitation in workers' compensation?
_roden_faqs.answer: Vocational rehabilitation is a set of services that help injured workers who cannot return to their previous job develop new skills, training, or education to find suitable alternative employment. It focuses on restoring the worker's earning capacity after reaching maximum medical improvement.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I qualify for vocational rehabilitation after a work injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: You generally qualify if you sustained a compensable workplace injury, have reached maximum medical improvement with permanent restrictions, cannot return to your former position, and your employer cannot offer suitable alternative work within your limitations.

_roden_faqs.question: How does vocational rehabilitation differ between Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia's system is administered by the State Board of Workers' Compensation with a Rehabilitation Division, and Georgia recognizes a catastrophic injury designation under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1 that provides lifetime benefits. South Carolina's system is administered by the Workers' Compensation Commission under Title 42 of the S.C. Code.

_roden_faqs.question: What types of vocational rehabilitation services are available?
_roden_faqs.answer: Services include transferable skills analysis, job placement assistance, on-the-job training, formal education and certification programs, self-employment assistance, and assistive technology or workplace accommodations — all tailored to your specific needs and restrictions.

_roden_faqs.question: Can my workers' comp benefits be reduced if I refuse vocational rehabilitation?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under both Georgia and South Carolina law, failure to cooperate with reasonable rehabilitation services can result in suspension or reduction of benefits. However, you are not required to accept employment that exceeds your physical restrictions or pays significantly less than your pre-injury wages.

_roden_faqs.question: Will I still receive disability payments during vocational rehabilitation?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Injured workers generally continue to receive workers' compensation benefits, including temporary total or temporary partial disability payments, while participating in vocational rehabilitation services.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Vocational rehabilitation helps injured workers who cannot return to their pre-injury jobs through skills training, education, and job placement. Georgia administers benefits through the State Board of Workers' Compensation under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1, while South Carolina uses the Workers' Compensation Commission under Title 42. Workers' comp is no-fault in both states. Claim deadlines are one year in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82) and two years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-15-40).

_roden_faqs.question: Should I hire a lawyer who has trial experience?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Insurance companies track which lawyers actually go to trial. Attorneys with courtroom experience get significantly better settlement offers because insurers know the threat of trial is real. A lawyer who has never tried a case has less leverage in negotiations.

_roden_faqs.question: How much does a car accident lawyer cost in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Most car accident lawyers work on a contingency fee basis — you pay nothing upfront and owe nothing unless your case results in compensation. The fee is typically one-third of the recovery. If a lawyer asks for money upfront for an accident case, look elsewhere.

_roden_faqs.question: What are red flags when choosing a personal injury lawyer?
_roden_faqs.answer: Red flags include: guaranteeing a specific outcome, pressuring you to sign immediately, asking for upfront payment, being difficult to reach or unresponsive, lacking experience with your specific type of case, and having disciplinary actions on their bar record.

_roden_faqs.question: Does it matter if my lawyer is local to Georgia or South Carolina?

A local attorney understands the courts, judges, and jury tendencies in your jurisdiction, which directly affects case strategy and outcomes.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I switch lawyers if I am unhappy with my current attorney?

/blog/traffic-tickets-and-car-accident-c.title: Do Traffic Tickets Determine Fault in a Car Accident?

_roden_faqs.question: Does a traffic ticket automatically determine fault in a car accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. A traffic ticket is strong evidence of fault but is not conclusive. Fault in a civil injury claim is determined by the legal system based on all available evidence, not solely by a police citation. The officer may not have witnessed the accident and could have incomplete information.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still file a claim if I received a traffic ticket?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under comparative fault rules in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and South Carolina, you can recover damages even if you share some fault. If you were 20% at fault due to a traffic violation, you can still recover 80% of your damages. Only reaching the state threshold (50% in GA, 51% in SC) bars recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: What is negligence per se and how does it relate to traffic tickets?
_roden_faqs.answer: Negligence per se is a legal doctrine where violating a safety statute — such as a traffic law — is automatically considered negligent. For it to apply, the violation must have been the proximate cause of the accident. A citation for running a red light that caused a collision supports negligence per se; a broken taillight citation in a head-on collision does not.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I fight a traffic ticket after a car accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Often yes. Pleading guilty to a traffic violation can be used as evidence of fault in your civil injury case. A dismissal removes that evidence. Consult your personal injury attorney before making any decisions in traffic court, as the two cases are strategically linked.

_roden_faqs.question: What happens if no ticket was issued at the accident scene?
_roden_faqs.answer: The absence of a traffic citation does not mean no one was at fault. Your claim can rely on other evidence including witness statements, surveillance footage, accident reconstruction analysis, cell phone records, and vehicle black box data to establish the other driver's negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a car accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of the accident to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, you have 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Do not delay filing because of uncertainty about traffic tickets — consult an attorney promptly.

_roden_faqs.question: Who is most commonly liable for a truck accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: While the truck driver is often at fault, the trucking company frequently shares liability through vicarious liability (respondeat superior) and direct negligence such as negligent hiring, poor maintenance, or pressuring drivers to violate hours-of-service rules.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the trucking company if the driver was an independent contractor?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Courts in both Georgia and South Carolina look beyond the contractual label and examine the actual level of control the company exercises over the driver. Federal regulations also hold the motor carrier responsible for safety compliance regardless of employment classification.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a truck accident lawsuit in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has a 2-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. Because critical evidence like ELD data can be overwritten quickly, it is essential to contact an attorney immediately after the accident.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a truck accident lawsuit in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina allows 3 years to file a personal injury lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. However, trucking evidence is time-sensitive — an attorney should send a preservation letter as soon as possible.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence is important in a truck accident case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Critical evidence includes electronic logging device (ELD) data, event data recorder (black box) data, driver qualification files, vehicle maintenance records, dispatch communications, drug test results, and dashcam or surveillance footage.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I file claims against multiple parties after a truck accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Truck accident claims frequently involve multiple defendants — the driver, trucking company, cargo loader, maintenance provider, and manufacturer. Filing against all liable parties gives you access to multiple insurance policies and maximizes potential recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: What is truck accident reconstruction?
_roden_faqs.answer: Truck accident reconstruction is a forensic discipline that uses physics, engineering, and digital data analysis to scientifically recreate how a collision occurred. Certified specialists examine physical evidence, electronic data recorders, ELD logs, and vehicle damage to determine vehicle speeds, driver actions, and the sequence of events leading to the crash.

_roden_faqs.question: Why is accident reconstruction important in truck accident cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: Commercial truck accidents involve complex liability questions with multiple potential defendants. Reconstruction provides objective, scientific evidence of negligence — such as speeding, brake failure, driver fatigue from hours-of-service violations, or improper cargo loading — that strengthens your claim and helps identify all responsible parties.

_roden_faqs.question: What is a spoliation letter in a truck accident case?
_roden_faqs.answer: A spoliation letter is a formal legal demand sent to the trucking company requiring them to preserve all evidence related to the accident. This includes the truck's event data recorder (black box), ELD logs, dashcam footage, maintenance records, and driver qualification files. Without this demand, critical evidence may be destroyed during routine business operations.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a truck accident lawsuit in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia allows 2 years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). However, you should contact an attorney immediately to send a spoliation letter and begin evidence preservation, as critical electronic data like EDR recordings and dashcam footage can be overwritten within days.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a truck accident lawsuit in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina provides 3 years to file a personal injury lawsuit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). While this is longer than Georgia's deadline, prompt action is still essential to preserve electronic evidence from the truck's data systems before it is overwritten or destroyed.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I recover damages if I was partially at fault for a truck accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, in both states under modified comparative fault rules. Georgia allows recovery if you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina allows recovery if you are less than 51% at fault. Your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault. Reconstruction evidence establishing the truck driver's greater share of fault is essential.

_roden_faqs.question: Does Georgia require uninsured motorist coverage?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11, every auto liability policy in Georgia must include UM/UIM coverage unless the named insured affirmatively rejects it in writing. If you did not sign a written rejection, you likely have UM/UIM coverage on your policy.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between UM and UIM coverage?
_roden_faqs.answer: Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage applies when the at-fault driver has no insurance at all, including hit-and-run scenarios. Underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage applies when the at-fault driver has insurance but their limits are insufficient to cover your damages.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I stack UM/UIM coverage in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina allows stacking of UM/UIM coverage across multiple vehicles on the same policy unless you signed a valid anti-stacking waiver under S.C. Code § 38-77-160. If the waiver was improperly obtained, it may be challengeable in court.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between add-on and offset UIM?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia uses the add-on method, meaning your UIM benefits are added on top of the at-fault driver's liability coverage. South Carolina uses the offset (difference) method, meaning your UIM coverage pays only the difference between the at-fault driver's limits and your UIM limits.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need consent from my insurer before settling with the at-fault driver?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, yes — you should notify your UIM carrier and obtain consent before accepting the at-fault driver's policy limits. Failing to do so can forfeit your UIM claim. South Carolina has similar notification requirements.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a UM/UIM claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations is 2 years from the date of injury under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. In South Carolina, you have 3 years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. These deadlines apply to UM/UIM claims just as they do to standard personal injury claims.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage protects you when the at-fault driver has no insurance or insufficient limits. Georgia requires UM/UIM on all auto policies unless rejected in writing (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11) and uses the add-on method for UIM. South Carolina mandates UM coverage under S.C. Code § 38-77-150 but uses the offset method. Both states allow stacking across multiple vehicles. Georgia imposes a 2-year filing deadline (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33); South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

/blog/value-of-pain-and-suffering/.title: The Value of Pain and Suffering in Georgia and South Carolina Personal Injury Claims

_roden_faqs.question: What is pain and suffering in a personal injury case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Pain and suffering refers to the physical pain and emotional distress you experience as a result of an injury caused by someone else's negligence. It is a category of non-economic damages that compensates for losses like chronic pain, anxiety, depression, loss of enjoyment of life, and loss of consortium — things that do not have a specific dollar amount attached to them.

_roden_faqs.question: How is the value of pain and suffering calculated?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no set formula. The two most common methods are the multiplier method, which multiplies your economic damages by a factor of 1.5 to 5 based on severity, and the per diem method, which assigns a daily dollar amount multiplied by the number of days you are affected. If a case goes to trial, the jury has broad discretion to award what it considers fair.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on pain and suffering damages in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Georgia does not cap pain and suffering damages in any personal injury case. A previous cap on non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases was struck down as unconstitutional by the Georgia Supreme Court in Atlanta Oculoplastic Surgery, P.C. v. Nestlehutt (2010).

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on pain and suffering damages in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In most personal injury cases, no. However, South Carolina does cap non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases at $350,000 per defendant and $1.05 million total regardless of the number of defendants (S.C. Code § 15-32-220).

_roden_faqs.question: How does comparative fault affect my pain and suffering award?
_roden_faqs.answer: Both Georgia and South Carolina follow modified comparative fault rules. In Georgia, your award is reduced by your percentage of fault and you recover nothing if you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). In South Carolina, you recover nothing if you are 51% or more at fault. This reduction applies to all damages, including pain and suffering.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence do I need to prove pain and suffering?
_roden_faqs.answer: Strong evidence includes medical records documenting your injuries and treatment, mental health records such as therapy notes or psychiatric evaluations, a pain journal tracking your daily symptoms and limitations, photographs of your injuries, testimony from family and friends about changes in your life, and expert testimony from medical professionals about the severity and expected duration of your suffering.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Pain and suffering damages compensate injury victims for physical discomfort, emotional distress, anxiety, and diminished quality of life beyond economic losses. Insurers use multiplier or per diem methods to calculate these non-economic damages. Georgia does not cap pain and suffering in most personal injury cases, and South Carolina likewise imposes no general cap. Comparative fault reduces awards proportionally in both states, barring recovery at 50% fault in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and 51% in South Carolina.

/blog/what-happens-if-i-resign-while-on-.title: What Happens If You Resign While on Workers' Compensation in Georgia or South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: Will I lose my workers' comp benefits if I resign?
_roden_faqs.answer: Not automatically. Workers' compensation benefits are tied to your work-related injury, not your employment status. Medical benefits continue regardless of resignation. Wage replacement benefits (TTD and TPD) may continue if your wage loss is due to the injury rather than your choice to leave, but the insurer will likely argue your income loss is voluntary.

_roden_faqs.question: Do medical benefits continue after I resign from my job?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-15-60), the employer's workers' comp insurer must continue covering all reasonable and necessary medical treatment for the work injury regardless of your employment status. This includes doctor visits, surgery, physical therapy, and prescriptions.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the 'voluntary limitation of income' defense?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-240), the insurer can argue that you are voluntarily limiting your income by resigning from a job you were capable of performing. If the workers' comp board agrees, your wage replacement benefits can be suspended. The burden is on the insurer to prove suitable work was available within your restrictions.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I resigned because my employer was retaliating against me for filing a claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: This may qualify as constructive discharge, which is treated as involuntary termination — preserving your wage benefits. Both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-17) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 41-1-80) prohibit employer retaliation for filing workers' comp claims. Document all incidents of retaliation before resigning.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I take a new job while receiving workers' comp benefits?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, but it affects your payments. If the new job pays equal to or more than your pre-injury wage, TTD benefits end. If it pays less, you may receive TPD benefits for the difference. Medical benefits continue regardless. You must report new employment to the insurer — failing to disclose income can result in fraud allegations.

_roden_faqs.question: What happens if I refuse a light-duty job offer and resign instead?
_roden_faqs.answer: This is one of the highest-risk scenarios. The insurer can argue you refused suitable employment, triggering benefit suspension under Georgia's O.C.G.A. § 34-9-240 or South Carolina's S.C. Code § 42-9-60. Before refusing, have an attorney evaluate whether the job is genuinely within your restrictions and offered in good faith.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Resigning while on workers' comp does not automatically end your benefits, but it creates risks. Medical benefits continue regardless of employment status in both Georgia and South Carolina. Wage replacement benefits are vulnerable — insurers will invoke the voluntary limitation of income defense (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-240) or unjustified refusal (S.C. Code § 42-9-60). Constructive discharge preserves benefits. Before resigning, consult an attorney, get your doctor's restrictions documented, and consider waiting until after your impairment rating.

/blog/what-if-i-suspect-medical-malpract.title: What to Do If You Suspect Medical Malpractice in Georgia or South Carolina

_roden_faqs.question: What is the first thing I should do if I suspect medical malpractice?
_roden_faqs.answer: Seek follow-up care from a different healthcare provider immediately. An independent doctor can evaluate your condition, identify what went wrong, provide corrective treatment, and create medical records documenting the complications — all of which serve as critical evidence if you pursue a claim.

_roden_faqs.question: How do I know if what happened to me qualifies as medical malpractice?
_roden_faqs.answer: Medical malpractice occurs when a healthcare provider deviates from the accepted standard of care — doing something a competent provider would not have done, or failing to do something they should have — and that deviation causes harm. A bad outcome alone is not malpractice. A medical malpractice attorney can review your records and consult with medical experts to determine whether your case qualifies.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice lawsuit in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia imposes a two-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71) from the date of the negligent act, with a discovery rule that can extend this to two years from when the injury was or should have been discovered. An absolute five-year statute of repose applies. Georgia also requires an expert affidavit at the time of filing (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1).

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice lawsuit in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina allows three years from the date of the negligent act or from discovery (S.C. Code § 15-3-545), with a six-year statute of repose. You must also serve a Notice of Intent to File Suit at least 90 days before filing the complaint (S.C. Code § 15-79-125), and mandatory mediation is required before trial.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I talk to my doctor or the hospital about the suspected malpractice?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Do not confront the provider, give a recorded statement to their malpractice insurer, or sign any documents without having an attorney review them first. Anything you say can be documented and used against you. Once you hire an attorney, all communications go through your legal team.

_roden_faqs.question: How much does it cost to hire a medical malpractice attorney?
_roden_faqs.answer: Most medical malpractice attorneys work on a contingency fee basis, meaning you pay nothing upfront and owe nothing unless your case results in compensation. The attorney advances all costs of investigation, expert review, and litigation. This makes experienced legal representation accessible regardless of your financial situation.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: If you suspect medical malpractice, act quickly: get independent medical care, request your complete records, document everything, and avoid discussing the situation with the provider or their insurer. Georgia requires a two-year filing and expert affidavit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71, § 9-11-9.1); South Carolina allows three years but requires 90-day pre-suit notice and mandatory mediation (S.C. Code § 15-3-545, § 15-79-125). Both states have strict statutes of repose — five years in Georgia, six in South Carolina.

/blog/what-is-the-role-of-a-personal-inj.title: What Does a Personal Injury Lawyer Do?

_roden_faqs.question: What does a personal injury lawyer do for my case?
_roden_faqs.answer: A personal injury lawyer investigates your accident, gathers evidence, identifies liable parties, handles all communication with insurance companies, calculates your full damages including future costs, negotiates a fair settlement, and takes your case to trial if necessary. They manage every aspect of the legal process on your behalf.

_roden_faqs.question: How much does a personal injury lawyer cost?
_roden_faqs.answer: Most personal injury lawyers work on a contingency fee basis, meaning you pay nothing upfront and no hourly fees. The attorney only gets paid a percentage of the recovery if they win your case. The firm also advances case expenses like expert witness fees and filing costs, which are reimbursed from the settlement or verdict.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations for most personal injury claims is two years from the date of injury under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. In South Carolina, you have three years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. Missing these deadlines means losing your right to sue, so consult an attorney promptly after any injury.

_roden_faqs.question: When should I hire a personal injury lawyer after an accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: You should consult an attorney as soon as possible after your accident. Early involvement allows your lawyer to preserve critical evidence, protect you from making harmful statements to insurance adjusters, begin building your claim while facts are fresh, and ensure all filing deadlines are met.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the comparative fault rule in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Both states use modified comparative fault systems. In Georgia, you can recover damages if you are less than 50% at fault under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33. In South Carolina, the threshold is 51%. In both states, your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault.

_roden_faqs.question: What types of cases do personal injury lawyers handle?
_roden_faqs.answer: Personal injury lawyers handle car accidents, truck accidents, motorcycle crashes, slip and fall injuries, medical malpractice, workers compensation claims, dog bites, brain injuries, wrongful death, pedestrian and bicycle accidents, boating accidents, and many other cases where negligence caused injury.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do first if my workers'  compensation claim is denied?
_roden_faqs.answer: Read the denial letter carefully to understand the specific reasons for rejection. Then continue your medical treatment, gather supporting documentation including medical records and witness statements, and consult an experienced workers' compensation attorney who can evaluate your case and guide your appeal.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to appeal a denied workers' comp claim in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must file your initial workers' compensation claim within one year of the injury or last authorized medical treatment under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82. Appeal deadlines after a hearing decision are strict, so consult an attorney immediately after receiving a denial.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to appeal a denied workers' comp claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In South Carolina, you have two years from the date of injury or last payment of compensation to file a claim under S.C. Code § 42-15-40. Appeals from a Commissioner's decision must be filed within 14 days. An attorney ensures all deadlines are met.

_roden_faqs.question: Can my employer fire me for filing a workers' compensation claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-17) and South Carolina have anti-retaliation protections for workers who file compensation claims. If your employer retaliates against you for filing a claim, you may have additional legal remedies available.

_roden_faqs.question: What types of benefits can I receive through workers' compensation?
_roden_faqs.answer: Workers' compensation covers medical benefits for all reasonable treatment, temporary total disability (wage replacement while unable to work), temporary partial disability, permanent partial disability, permanent total disability, vocational rehabilitation, and death benefits for dependents in fatal workplace accidents.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer to appeal a denied workers' compensation claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: While you can technically appeal on your own, the process involves hearings before administrative judges, strict procedural rules, and evidence requirements. An experienced workers' compensation attorney significantly improves your chances of a successful appeal and ensures all deadlines and legal requirements are met.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: A denied workers' compensation claim is not final — injured workers in Georgia and South Carolina have the right to appeal. /blog/what-to-do-when-you-are-in-a-car-a.title: Car Accident Checklist: What to Do After a Wreck in Georgia and South Carolina

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do immediately after a car accident in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Check yourself and others for injuries and call 911 immediately. Move to a safe location if possible, exchange information with the other driver (name, insurance, license plate, driver's license number), and document the scene with photos and video. Get the responding officer's name and badge number so you can obtain a copy of the police report. Do not admit fault or apologize — let the investigation determine responsibility. See a doctor within 24-48 hours even if you feel fine, as many injuries like concussions, whiplash, and internal bleeding do not produce immediate symptoms.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a car accident lawsuit in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations for personal injury claims is 2 years from the date of the accident under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. In South Carolina, you have 3 years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. Missing these deadlines permanently bars your right to file a lawsuit and recover compensation. However, you should not wait — evidence deteriorates, witnesses become harder to locate, and the insurance company's advantage grows with time. Contact an attorney as soon as possible after your accident.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. You have no legal obligation to provide a recorded statement to the at-fault driver's insurance company in either Georgia or South Carolina. Insurance adjusters are trained to ask questions designed to elicit responses that can be used to reduce or deny your claim. Even innocent statements can be taken out of context. Politely decline the recorded statement and refer them to your attorney. You should cooperate with your own insurance company as required by your policy, but consult an attorney before providing detailed statements.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I was partially at fault for the car accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Both Georgia and South Carolina follow modified comparative fault rules, meaning you can still recover compensation even if you were partially responsible. In Georgia, under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, you can recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault — at 50% or more, you recover nothing. In South Carolina, you can recover as long as you are not more than 50% at fault (less than 51%). In both states, your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are 20% at fault and your damages are $100,000, you would receive $80,000.

_roden_faqs.question: How much is my car accident case worth in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: The value of a car accident claim depends on several factors, including the severity of your injuries, total medical expenses (past and future), lost wages and reduced earning capacity, property damage, pain and suffering, and the impact on your quality of life. Cases involving serious injuries such as traumatic brain injuries, spinal cord injuries, or injuries requiring surgery typically have higher values. Insurance companies routinely undervalue claims in early settlement offers. An experienced car accident attorney can calculate the full value of your case and negotiate for maximum compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer after a car accident in Georgia or South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: While not legally required, hiring a car accident lawyer significantly increases your chances of receiving full and fair compensation. You should strongly consider an attorney if you suffered injuries requiring medical treatment, missed work, the other driver was uninsured, liability is disputed, a commercial truck or motorcycle was involved, or the insurance company is delaying or lowballing your claim. At Roden Law, we handle all car accident cases on a contingency fee basis — you pay nothing unless we win. We have recovered over $300 million for clients across Georgia and South Carolina.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do temporary total disability (TTD) benefits last?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, TTD benefits can last up to 400 weeks (approximately 7.7 years) from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261). In South Carolina, the maximum is 500 weeks (approximately 9.6 years) (S.C. Code § 42-9-10). Benefits end earlier if you return to work, your doctor releases you, or you reach maximum medical improvement (MMI).

_roden_faqs.question: Do workers' comp medical benefits ever expire?
_roden_faqs.answer: In both Georgia and South Carolina, medical benefits have no specific time limit. The employer's insurer must continue providing reasonable and necessary medical treatment for the work-related condition even after disability (wage replacement) benefits have ended. This includes surgery, physical therapy, prescriptions, and medical devices.

_roden_faqs.question: What is maximum medical improvement (MMI) and how does it affect my benefits?
_roden_faqs.answer: MMI is the point when your doctor determines your condition has stabilized and is unlikely to improve significantly with further treatment. Reaching MMI typically ends TTD benefits and triggers a transition to permanent disability benefits (PPD or PTD) based on your impairment rating. Insurers often pressure doctors to declare MMI early to cut off benefits.

_roden_faqs.question: Can workers' comp benefits last for life?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, catastrophic injuries — spinal cord injuries causing paralysis, amputation of major limbs, severe brain injury, severe burns, or total blindness — qualify for lifetime benefits (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1). In South Carolina, certain catastrophic injuries may qualify for benefits beyond the standard 500-week maximum. Medical benefits have no time limit in either state.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if my workers' comp benefits are cut off?
_roden_faqs.answer: Get a written explanation from the insurer, continue all medical treatment, and contact a workers' compensation attorney immediately. Your attorney can file a hearing request — a WC-14 form in Georgia or a Form 50 in South Carolina — to have an administrative law judge review the termination and potentially reinstate your benefits.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a waiting period before workers' comp benefits begin?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. In both states, there is a 7-day waiting period before disability benefits begin. In Georgia, the first 7 days are paid retroactively if you miss more than 21 consecutive days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-220). In South Carolina, the retroactive threshold is 14 days (S.C. Code § 42-9-200).

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Workers' compensation benefit duration depends on the type of disability and your state. Georgia caps TTD at 400 weeks (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261); South Carolina allows 500 weeks (S.C. Code § 42-9-10). Georgia provides lifetime benefits for catastrophic injuries (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1). Medical benefits have no time limit in either state. Benefits typically end when you return to work, reach MMI, or hit the statutory maximum — but wrongful terminations can be challenged through a hearing.

/blog/when-is-the-right-time-to-hire-a-p.title: When Is the Right Time to Hire a Personal Injury Lawyer After an Accident in Georgia or South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: How soon after an accident should I hire a personal injury lawyer?
_roden_faqs.answer: As soon as possible — ideally within the first few days. Critical evidence can disappear quickly (surveillance footage is overwritten, witnesses forget details, vehicle damage is repaired). Early involvement also prevents you from making statements to insurance adjusters that could damage your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a deadline for hiring a lawyer after an accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: The statute of limitations sets the absolute deadline: 2 years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and 3 years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). However, waiting until near the deadline makes it much harder to build a strong case. Most experienced attorneys prefer to get involved early.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I hire a lawyer before talking to the insurance company?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Insurance adjusters contact accident victims quickly — often within days — to take recorded statements and make lowball settlement offers. Once you hire an attorney, all communication goes through your lawyer, protecting you from making damaging statements or accepting an inadequate offer.

_roden_faqs.question: What if my injuries seem minor — should I still hire a lawyer?
_roden_faqs.answer: Consider a free consultation even for seemingly minor injuries. Many injuries — whiplash, concussions, soft tissue damage, herniated discs — do not show their full severity for days or weeks. A quick consultation costs nothing and helps you understand whether your injuries may be more serious than they initially appear.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I hire a lawyer weeks or months after the accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, as long as you are within the statute of limitations. However, the longer you wait, the more evidence may be lost and the more the insurance company may use the delay against you. If you have already given a recorded statement or accepted a partial payment, an attorney can still help — but early involvement is always better.

_roden_faqs.question: What triggers should prompt me to hire a lawyer immediately?
_roden_faqs.answer: Hire immediately if: you suffered serious injuries requiring surgery or hospitalization, the other party disputes fault, multiple vehicles or parties are involved, a commercial truck or government vehicle was involved, the insurance company denied your claim or made a lowball offer, or anyone involved in the accident died.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Hire a personal injury lawyer as soon as possible after an accident — ideally within days. Evidence deteriorates quickly, and insurance adjusters move fast to secure recorded statements and lowball settlements. Georgia allows 2 years to file (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33); South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Immediate triggers include serious injuries, disputed liability, commercial vehicles, claim denials, and fatalities. Free consultations cost nothing and protect your rights.

/blog/why-wont-a-personal-lawyer-take-my.title: Why a Personal Injury Lawyer Might Not Take Your Case in Georgia or South Carolina

_roden_faqs.question: Why would a personal injury lawyer refuse to take my case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Common reasons include: no clear liability (cannot prove the other party was at fault), the statute of limitations has expired (2 years in Georgia, 3 years in South Carolina), insufficient damages (injuries too minor to justify litigation costs), significant comparative fault on your part, or no available insurance coverage to pay a judgment.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still file a claim if one lawyer turned me down?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Different attorneys evaluate cases differently. One lawyer may decline a case that another would accept. If you are turned down, ask the attorney to explain why and whether they think another lawyer might see it differently. Get at least 2-3 consultations before concluding you do not have a viable claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Does the statute of limitations matter when finding a lawyer?
_roden_faqs.answer: Absolutely. Georgia allows only 2 years from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). As the deadline approaches, fewer attorneys will take the case because there is less time to investigate and prepare. Contact a lawyer as early as possible.

_roden_faqs.question: Will a lawyer reject my case if I have pre-existing injuries?
_roden_faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Both Georgia and South Carolina follow the eggshell plaintiff doctrine — a defendant takes the victim as they find them. If the accident aggravated a pre-existing condition, you can recover for the worsening. However, proving the aggravation requires strong medical documentation, which some attorneys may view as too difficult.

_roden_faqs.question: What if no lawyer will take my case?
_roden_faqs.answer: If multiple attorneys decline, options include: filing a claim yourself in small claims court (for smaller amounts), contacting your state bar association for a referral, trying legal aid organizations, or filing an insurance claim directly without an attorney. Understanding why lawyers declined helps you assess your realistic options.

_roden_faqs.question: Do lawyers only take cases they think they can win?
_roden_faqs.answer: Because personal injury lawyers work on contingency (they only get paid if you win), they must evaluate whether a case is likely to produce a recovery that justifies the time and expense invested. This does not mean your case has no merit — it means the lawyer assessed the risk-reward balance and decided it was not the right fit for their practice.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Personal injury lawyers may decline cases due to unclear liability, expired statutes of limitations (2 years GA, 3 years SC), insufficient damages, significant comparative fault, or lack of insurance coverage. Getting turned down by one lawyer does not mean your case has no merit — seek multiple consultations. Pre-existing conditions do not automatically bar recovery under the eggshell plaintiff doctrine. The closer you are to the filing deadline, the harder it becomes to find representation.

/blog/workers-comp-for-carpal-tunnel-syn.title: Can You Get Workers' Comp for Carpal Tunnel in Georgia and South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: Can I get workers' comp for carpal tunnel syndrome?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Both Georgia and South Carolina cover carpal tunnel syndrome as an occupational disease under their workers' compensation systems when the condition arises out of and in the course of employment. You must establish a causal connection between your work duties and the development of CTS.

_roden_faqs.question: How do I prove my carpal tunnel is work-related?
_roden_faqs.answer: You need medical evidence from a doctor linking your CTS to your work duties, documentation of the repetitive hand and wrist movements your job requires, nerve conduction studies confirming the diagnosis, and a timeline showing your symptoms developed during the period of repetitive work.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the deadline to report carpal tunnel to my employer?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must report within 30 days under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80, typically starting from when you knew or should have known the condition was work-related. In South Carolina, the reporting deadline is 90 days under S.C. Code § 42-15-20.

_roden_faqs.question: What benefits can I receive for work-related carpal tunnel?
_roden_faqs.answer: Benefits include full medical treatment (doctor visits, therapy, surgery), temporary total or partial disability wage replacement (typically two-thirds of your average weekly wage), permanent partial disability compensation if you have lasting impairment, and vocational rehabilitation if you cannot return to your former job.

_roden_faqs.question: Can my employer deny my carpal tunnel claim because I have a pre-existing condition?
_roden_faqs.answer: Having a pre-existing condition does not automatically disqualify your claim. If your work duties aggravated, accelerated, or worsened a pre-existing carpal tunnel condition, you are still entitled to workers' compensation benefits in both Georgia and South Carolina.

_roden_faqs.question: How long is recovery from carpal tunnel release surgery?
_roden_faqs.answer: Recovery from carpal tunnel surgery typically takes several weeks to several months. Most workers cannot return to full duty for 4-6 weeks after surgery, and those with physically demanding jobs requiring repetitive hand work may need even longer. Workers' compensation covers all medical expenses and provides disability benefits during recovery.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Carpal tunnel syndrome qualifies for workers' compensation in both Georgia and South Carolina as an occupational disease. Code § 42-15-20) and two years for filing (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). Workers' comp is no-fault — pre-existing conditions and employee actions do not bar claims.

/blog/workers-comp-medical-coverage/.title: Types of Medical Care Covered by Workers' Compensation in Georgia and South Carolina

_roden_faqs.question: What medical expenses does workers' compensation cover?
_roden_faqs.answer: Workers' compensation covers emergency room treatment, surgery, hospitalization, prescription medications, physical therapy, specialist visits, diagnostic testing, medical equipment, prosthetics, home health care, and travel expenses to medical appointments. All treatment must be reasonable and necessary to treat your work-related injury.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I choose my own doctor for a workers' comp claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, your employer must provide a panel of at least six physicians, and you choose from that panel. In South Carolina, the employer initially selects the treating physician, but you can petition the Workers' Compensation Commission for a change of doctor if you are dissatisfied with your care.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if my workers' comp medical treatment is denied?
_roden_faqs.answer: Get the denial in writing, ask your doctor to document why the treatment is medically necessary, file a formal dispute with the State Board of Workers' Compensation (Georgia) or Workers' Compensation Commission (South Carolina), and contact an attorney who can file motions to compel treatment.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to pay out-of-pocket for workers' comp medical treatment?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Workers' compensation has no deductibles, copays, or out-of-pocket maximums. The employer's insurer pays your medical providers directly. If you do pay out of pocket for covered treatment, you are entitled to reimbursement including travel costs.

_roden_faqs.question: Does workers' comp cover mental health treatment?
_roden_faqs.answer: Workers' compensation may cover mental health treatment including psychiatric care, counseling for PTSD, and treatment for depression related to workplace injuries. However, mental health claims are among the most frequently denied or limited by insurance companies.

_roden_faqs.question: How long does workers' comp medical coverage last?
_roden_faqs.answer: Workers' compensation medical benefits generally continue for as long as treatment is authorized and medically necessary. There is no fixed time limit, but insurers may periodically challenge ongoing treatment through utilization review or independent medical examinations.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Workers' compensation in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-15-60) covers all reasonable and necessary medical treatment for work injuries, including emergency care, surgery, prescriptions, physical therapy, specialist visits, and medical equipment with no out-of-pocket costs to the employee. Georgia requires employers to provide a physician panel while South Carolina gives employers initial doctor selection.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the legal BAC limit for boating in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Both states set the legal limit at 0.08% BAC for boaters 21 and older, the same threshold as driving. Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 52-7-12) and South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 50-21-112) criminalize operating any vessel at or above this level.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I get punitive damages if a drunk boater injured me?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Both Georgia and South Carolina allow punitive damages in BUI cases. Georgia caps most punitive awards at $250,000 with exceptions for impaired operation cases. South Carolina has no statutory cap but requires clear and convincing evidence of reckless conduct.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a marina bar that served the drunk boater?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potentially. Under Georgia's dram shop law (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-40) and South Carolina's statute (S.C. Code § 61-4-580), establishments that serve visibly intoxicated persons who then cause injuries may be held liable.

_roden_faqs.question: Is BUI a criminal offense in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia BUI (O.C.G.A. § 52-7-12) is a misdemeanor with penalties including fines up to $1,000, up to 12 months in jail, and mandatory completion of a boater safety course. Repeat offenses carry enhanced penalties.

_roden_faqs.question: How does a criminal BUI case affect my civil injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: The criminal case and civil case are separate proceedings. A BUI conviction provides strong evidence of negligence in your civil claim, but you can pursue civil damages regardless of the criminal outcome, using a lower burden of proof.

_roden_faqs.question: Does maritime law or state law apply to my commercial vessel accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: It depends on the location of the accident, the type of vessel, and whether you were a crew member or passenger. Accidents on navigable waters are often governed by federal maritime law, which may provide different remedies than state law. An experienced maritime attorney can determine which laws apply.

_roden_faqs.question: What is a Jones Act claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: The Jones Act (46 U.S.C. § 30104) allows seamen injured during employment to sue their employer for negligence. Unlike workers' compensation, Jones Act claims allow recovery for pain and suffering and are tried before a jury.

_roden_faqs.question: Can passengers sue charter boat operators for injuries?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Charter boat operators owe passengers a duty of reasonable care. If the operator was negligent — through reckless operation, failure to maintain the vessel, inadequate safety equipment, or BUI — passengers can pursue injury claims.

_roden_faqs.question: What is maintenance and cure in maritime law?
_roden_faqs.answer: Maintenance and cure is a maritime remedy requiring vessel owners to pay injured seamen's living expenses (maintenance) and medical costs (cure) during recovery, regardless of fault. This obligation continues until the seaman reaches maximum medical improvement.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a maritime injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: The statute of limitations varies by claim type. Jones Act claims must be filed within 3 years. General maritime negligence claims have a 3-year deadline. LHWCA claims must be filed within 1 year. State law claims follow the 2-year (Georgia) or 3-year (South Carolina) deadlines.

_roden_faqs.question: Who is liable if I slip and fall on a wet dock?
_roden_faqs.answer: The marina or dock owner may be liable if they failed to maintain non-slip surfaces, provide adequate drainage, post warning signs, or take reasonable steps to keep walkways safe. Premises liability law requires property owners to exercise ordinary care for invitees.

_roden_faqs.question: What is electric shock drowning?
_roden_faqs.answer: Electric shock drowning occurs when faulty electrical systems at docks or marinas leak alternating current into the surrounding water. Swimmers can be paralyzed by the current and drown. Marina operators have a duty to maintain properly grounded electrical systems and install ground fault protection.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a dock injury claim?

_roden_faqs.question: What is the minimum age to operate a jet ski in Georgia and South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue for a jet ski accident caused by a mechanical defect?

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a boating accident claim in Georgia and South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to wear a life jacket on a jet ski?

_roden_faqs.question: Is a kayak tour company liable if I get hurt during a guided trip?

Signed waivers do not always bar claims, especially involving gross negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to wear a life jacket in a kayak in Georgia?

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after a kayak or canoe accident?

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a kayak accident claim?

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue for a boom strike injury on a sailboat?

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do immediately after a powerboat collision?
_roden_faqs.answer: Ensure everyone's safety, call 911 and the local marine patrol, render aid to injured persons, document the scene with photos, exchange information with other boat operators, and report the accident to the appropriate state agency. Seek medical attention promptly.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the boat owner if someone else was driving?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Boat owners can be held vicariously liable for accidents caused by operators they permitted to use their vessel. This is particularly important when the at-fault operator lacks adequate insurance coverage.

_roden_faqs.question: Is excessive speed on the water illegal in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 52-7-17) requires operators to maintain a reasonable and prudent speed. Operating at excessive speed for conditions — even if there is no posted speed limit — constitutes negligence and may violate the Boat Safety Act.

_roden_faqs.question: How is fault determined in a boating collision?
_roden_faqs.answer: Fault is determined by examining navigation rules, operator conduct, witness statements, Coast Guard reports, and physical evidence. Both states use modified comparative fault, reducing your damages by your percentage of responsibility.

_roden_faqs.question: What damages can I recover after a speedboat accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may recover medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, disability, emotional distress, and property damage. In cases involving reckless or intoxicated operation, punitive damages may also be available.

/brain-injury-lawyers/anoxic-hypoxic-bra.title: Anoxic and Hypoxic Brain Injury Lawyers
/brain-injury-lawyers/anoxic-hypoxic-bra.excerpt: Suffered an anoxic or hypoxic brain injury from oxygen deprivation in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys pursue negligence claims for brain damage caused by near-drowning, medical errors, and toxic exposure.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between anoxic and hypoxic brain injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: An anoxic brain injury involves a complete loss of oxygen to the brain. A hypoxic brain injury involves a partial reduction in oxygen supply. Both can cause permanent brain damage, with anoxic injuries typically being more severe.

_roden_faqs.question: How quickly does oxygen deprivation cause brain damage?
_roden_faqs.answer: Irreversible brain damage can begin within four to six minutes of oxygen deprivation. The longer the brain goes without oxygen, the more severe and widespread the damage. Even brief episodes of hypoxia can cause lasting cognitive deficits.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue for carbon monoxide poisoning that caused brain damage?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Carbon monoxide poisoning causing anoxic brain injury may give rise to claims against landlords who failed to maintain heating systems, manufacturers of defective appliances, employers who failed to ensure adequate ventilation, and property managers who ignored CO detector requirements.

_roden_faqs.question: Is anoxic brain injury from medical malpractice actionable?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Anesthesia errors, surgical complications, failure to monitor oxygen levels, and delayed emergency response that result in oxygen deprivation brain injury may constitute medical malpractice. Georgia requires an expert affidavit (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1) when filing malpractice claims.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for an anoxic brain injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: For general negligence claims: 2 years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and 3 years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Medical malpractice claims have separate deadlines: 2 years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71) and 3 years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-545).

/brain-injury-lawyers/birth-related-brai.title: Birth-Related Brain Injury Lawyers
/brain-injury-lawyers/birth-related-brai.excerpt: Did your child suffer a brain injury during birth due to medical negligence in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys pursue birth injury malpractice claims for cerebral palsy, HIE, and other birth-related brain damage.

_roden_faqs.question: What causes cerebral palsy at birth?
_roden_faqs.answer: Many cases of cerebral palsy are caused by oxygen deprivation (hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy) during labor and delivery. When medical teams fail to monitor fetal distress, delay emergency C-sections, or mismanage complications, the resulting oxygen deprivation can cause permanent brain damage leading to cerebral palsy.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a birth injury claim in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia's medical malpractice statute of limitations is 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71), but for birth injuries to minors, the deadline is extended to the child's 7th birthday (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-73). However, filing as early as possible preserves evidence and witnesses.

_roden_faqs.question: What is hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE)?
_roden_faqs.answer: HIE is brain damage caused by reduced oxygen and blood flow to a baby's brain during labor or delivery. It is the most common cause of birth-related brain injury and can result in cerebral palsy, seizure disorders, developmental delays, and cognitive impairment.

_roden_faqs.question: How much are birth injury brain damage cases worth?
_roden_faqs.answer: Birth injury cases involving permanent brain damage are among the highest-value medical malpractice claims, frequently resulting in settlements or verdicts worth millions of dollars. The value depends on the severity of the injury and the cost of lifetime care and lost earning capacity.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need a medical expert to file a birth injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia requires an expert affidavit from a qualified medical professional at the time of filing (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1). South Carolina requires expert testimony to establish the standard of care and how it was breached. Our attorneys work with leading medical experts.
