/brain-injury-lawyers/closed-head-injury.title: Closed Head Injury Lawyers
/brain-injury-lawyers/closed-head-injury.excerpt: Suffered a closed head injury in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys fight for full compensation for brain injuries caused by blunt force impact without skull fracture or penetration.

_roden_faqs.question: What is a closed head injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: A closed head injury is brain damage caused by a blow or jolt to the head without the skull being fractured or penetrated. The brain is injured by striking the inside of the skull, by rotational forces tearing nerve fibers, or by bleeding within the intact skull.

_roden_faqs.question: How is a closed head injury different from an open head injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: In a closed head injury, the skull remains intact. In an open or penetrating head injury, the skull is fractured or penetrated by an object. Both can cause severe brain damage, but closed head injuries are more common and can be harder to diagnose because there is no visible skull damage.

_roden_faqs.question: Can a closed head injury be detected on a CT scan?
_roden_faqs.answer: Standard CT scans detect bleeding and large contusions but may miss subtle closed head injuries, particularly diffuse axonal injury. Advanced imaging including MRI, DTI, and fMRI may be needed to reveal the full extent of the damage.

_roden_faqs.question: What is diffuse axonal injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is widespread damage to the brain's nerve fibers (axons) caused by rotational forces. It is one of the most serious forms of closed head injury and a common cause of prolonged unconsciousness, coma, and permanent disability after TBI.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a closed head injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations is 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, it is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Because closed head injury symptoms may develop or worsen over time, it is important to consult an attorney as early as possible.

/brain-injury-lawyers/concussion-mild-tb.excerpt: Suffered a concussion or mild traumatic brain injury in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys fight for fair compensation even when insurance companies downplay so-called "mild" brain injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: Is a concussion considered a traumatic brain injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. A concussion is classified as a mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Despite the "mild" label, concussions can cause significant and lasting cognitive, physical, and emotional symptoms that substantially impact quality of life.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I get compensation for a concussion even without losing consciousness?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Loss of consciousness is not required for a concussion diagnosis. Any alteration in mental state — feeling dazed, confused, or disoriented — after a head impact can indicate a concussion. Medical evidence and neuropsychological testing can prove the injury.

_roden_faqs.question: What is post-concussion syndrome?
_roden_faqs.answer: Post-concussion syndrome (PCS) is a condition where concussion symptoms — headaches, dizziness, cognitive difficulties, mood changes — persist for weeks, months, or years after the initial injury. PCS significantly increases the value of a concussion claim.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a concussion injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations is 2 years from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, it is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). However, concussion symptoms may develop over time, so early medical documentation is critical.

_roden_faqs.question: Why do insurance companies undervalue concussion claims?
_roden_faqs.answer: Insurance companies exploit the "mild" TBI label and the fact that concussions often do not appear on standard CT or MRI scans. An experienced attorney uses advanced neuroimaging, neuropsychological testing, and expert testimony to demonstrate the true severity of the injury.

/brain-injury-lawyers/penetrating-brain-.excerpt: Suffered a penetrating brain injury in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys pursue maximum compensation for catastrophic open head injuries caused by objects penetrating the skull.

_roden_faqs.question: What is a penetrating brain injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: A penetrating brain injury occurs when an object fractures the skull and enters the brain tissue. This is also called an open head injury. Common causes include flying debris from vehicle accidents, workplace projectiles, and falls onto sharp objects.

_roden_faqs.question: How does a penetrating brain injury differ from a closed head injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: In a penetrating injury, the skull is breached and an object enters the brain. In a closed head injury, the skull remains intact. Penetrating injuries have higher mortality rates and typically cause more localized but severe damage along the projectile's path.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the long-term prognosis for penetrating brain injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: Prognosis varies by severity and location, but most survivors of significant penetrating brain injuries face permanent neurological deficits, including cognitive impairment, physical disability, personality changes, and seizure disorders. Many require lifelong assisted care.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I file a product liability claim for a penetrating brain injury caused by a defective tool?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. If a defective power tool, safety shield, or industrial equipment failed and caused a penetrating brain injury, you may have a product liability claim against the manufacturer, distributor, and retailer under both Georgia and South Carolina law.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a penetrating brain injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has a 2-year deadline (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina has a 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). For incapacitated victims, these deadlines may be tolled until a guardian is appointed to act on the victim's behalf.

/brain-injury-lawyers/second-impact-synd.title: Second Impact Syndrome Lawyers
/brain-injury-lawyers/second-impact-synd.excerpt: Suffered catastrophic brain damage from second impact syndrome in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys hold coaches, schools, and medical providers accountable for allowing premature return to activity after a concussion.

_roden_faqs.question: What is second impact syndrome?
_roden_faqs.answer: Second impact syndrome (SIS) occurs when a person suffers a second concussion before fully recovering from a first. The second impact triggers rapid, catastrophic brain swelling that can cause permanent brain damage or death — even if the second impact appears minor.

_roden_faqs.question: How common is second impact syndrome?
_roden_faqs.answer: SIS is rare but devastating, with a mortality rate of approximately 50%. It most commonly affects young athletes aged 15-25 who are returned to play before their initial concussion has fully resolved. Strict adherence to return-to-play protocols can prevent SIS.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a coach for returning my child to play after a concussion?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia's Return to Play Act (O.C.G.A. § 20-2-324.1) and South Carolina's Youth Athletic Concussion Prevention Act (S.C. Code § 59-63-75) require immediate removal from play and medical clearance. A coach who violates these laws is negligent.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a second impact syndrome claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has a 2-year deadline (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina has 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). For minors, the limitations period is tolled until the child turns 18 in both states, but filing promptly preserves critical evidence.

_roden_faqs.question: Are punitive damages available in second impact syndrome cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. When coaches or organizations knowingly violate concussion protocols or pressure injured athletes to return to play, their conduct may rise to the level of reckless disregard warranting punitive damages under both Georgia and South Carolina law.

/brain-injury-lawyers/severe-traumatic-b.title: Severe Traumatic Brain Injury Lawyers
/brain-injury-lawyers/severe-traumatic-b.excerpt: Suffered a severe traumatic brain injury in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys pursue maximum compensation for catastrophic TBI causing permanent cognitive impairment, disability, and loss of independence.

_roden_faqs.question: What qualifies as a severe traumatic brain injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: A severe TBI involves loss of consciousness exceeding 24 hours, post-traumatic amnesia lasting more than 7 days, a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3-8, visible structural damage on brain imaging, or the need for neurosurgical intervention.

_roden_faqs.question: How much is a severe TBI case worth?
_roden_faqs.answer: Severe TBI cases are among the highest-value personal injury cases, often worth millions of dollars. The value depends on the severity of cognitive and physical impairment, the victim's age and pre-injury earnings, the cost of lifetime care, and the defendant's degree of fault.

_roden_faqs.question: Can a severe TBI victim file their own lawsuit?
_roden_faqs.answer: If the TBI victim is incapacitated, a legal guardian, conservator, or next friend can file the lawsuit on their behalf. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 29-4-1 et seq.) and South Carolina provide procedures for appointing guardians for incapacitated adults.

_roden_faqs.question: What is a life care plan in a TBI case?
_roden_faqs.answer: A life care plan is a comprehensive document prepared by a certified life care planner projecting all future medical, rehabilitation, and personal care needs for the remainder of the victim's life. It forms the basis for calculating future damages in severe TBI cases.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a severe TBI claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has a 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina has a 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). For incapacitated victims, tolling provisions may pause these deadlines until a guardian is appointed.

/brain-injury-lawyers/sports-related-bra.title: Sports-Related Brain Injury Lawyers
/brain-injury-lawyers/sports-related-bra.excerpt: Suffered a brain injury from sports or recreational activities in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys hold negligent coaches, facilities, and organizations accountable for preventable sports-related TBIs.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a coach or school for my child's sports concussion?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, if the coach or school was negligent — for example, by returning a concussed athlete to play without medical clearance, violating Georgia's Return to Play Act (O.C.G.A. § 20-2-324.1) or South Carolina's Youth Athletic Concussion Prevention Act (S.C. Code § 59-63-75).

_roden_faqs.question: Does the assumption of risk defense bar all sports injury claims?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Assumption of risk applies to the inherent risks of a sport, not to negligent conduct by coaches, facilities, or organizations. Returning a concussed athlete to play, providing defective equipment, or maintaining unsafe facilities are actionable even in athletic settings.

_roden_faqs.question: What is Georgia's Return to Play Act?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia's Return to Play Act (O.C.G.A. § 20-2-324.1) requires youth sports organizations to educate athletes and parents about concussions, remove athletes suspected of having a concussion, and require medical clearance before return to play. Violations support negligence claims.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a helmet manufacturer if the helmet failed to prevent a brain injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. If the helmet was defectively designed, manufactured, or marketed with misleading safety claims, you may have a product liability claim against the manufacturer. Equipment must meet applicable safety standards for the sport.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a sports brain injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has a 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina has 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). For minors, the limitations period is tolled until the child turns 18, but filing promptly preserves evidence and strengthens the case.

_roden_faqs.question: Who is liable — the manufacturer or the store that sold it?

Having multiple liable parties can increase available insurance coverage for your recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: What is an arc flash injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: An arc flash is an explosive release of electrical energy through the air, producing intense heat (up to 35,000°F), blinding light, pressure waves, and shrapnel. Arc flash injuries can cause severe burns, hearing loss, and blast trauma even without direct electrical contact.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a power company for an electrical burn from a downed power line?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Power companies have a duty to maintain their lines and promptly respond to outages and downed lines. If a power company's negligence — such as deferred maintenance, failure to clear vegetation, or delayed response — caused your electrical burn, they can be held liable.

_roden_faqs.question: What OSHA standards apply to electrical safety?
_roden_faqs.answer: OSHA's electrical safety standards (29 CFR 1910 Subpart S for general industry; 29 CFR 1926 Subpart K for construction) require lockout/tagout procedures, safe clearance distances, GFCI protection, insulated tools, and arc-flash rated PPE. Violations are strong evidence of negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: Are electrical burns covered by workers' compensation?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. On-the-job electrical burns are covered by workers' comp in both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1) and South Carolina. Third-party claims against contractors, equipment manufacturers, or power companies may also be available for additional damages.

_roden_faqs.question: How serious are internal injuries from electrocution?
_roden_faqs.answer: Very serious. Electrical current damages internal tissues that cannot be seen externally. Victims may suffer muscle destruction, organ damage, cardiac complications, nerve damage, and kidney failure from muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis). Delayed complications like cataracts can appear months later.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a restaurant for a hot coffee or soup burn?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, if the restaurant served beverages or food at unreasonably dangerous temperatures without adequate warnings, used defective containers, or if employees negligently spilled hot liquids on you. Restaurants have a duty to serve products safely.

_roden_faqs.question: Is my landlord liable if the tap water scalded my child?
_roden_faqs.answer: A landlord may be liable if the water heater was set above safe temperatures (the recommended maximum is 120°F) or if anti-scald devices were required but not installed. Georgia and South Carolina landlords must maintain safe conditions for tenants.

_roden_faqs.question: How hot does water have to be to cause a scald burn?
_roden_faqs.answer: Water at 140°F causes a third-degree burn in just 5 seconds. At 150°F, a severe burn occurs in 2 seconds. At 160°F, it takes less than 1 second. The CPSC recommends setting water heaters to no higher than 120°F.

_roden_faqs.question: What damages can I recover for a scalding injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may recover medical expenses, surgery costs, pain and suffering, permanent scarring and disfigurement, emotional distress, lost wages, and future medical care. In cases involving reckless conduct, punitive damages may also be available.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a scalding burn lawsuit?

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a car manufacturer if my vehicle caught fire after a crash?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. If a design or manufacturing defect — such as an inadequately protected fuel tank, faulty wiring, or defective fuel lines — caused or worsened the fire, the manufacturer can be held strictly liable under product liability law.

_roden_faqs.question: What if my vehicle was subject to a fire-related recall?

_roden_faqs.question: Can an auto mechanic be liable for a vehicle fire?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. If negligent repairs — such as improper fuel system work, faulty electrical connections, or failure to address oil leaks — caused or contributed to the fire, the mechanic or repair shop can be held liable for resulting burn injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: Are electric vehicle battery fires handled differently?

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a vehicle fire burn claim?

_roden_faqs.question: What workers' compensation benefits are available for burn injuries in Georgia?

_roden_faqs.question: Can OSHA violations help my burn injury case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. OSHA violations can serve as strong evidence of negligence in a third-party claim. Common violations in burn cases include failure to provide PPE, inadequate hazard communication, and improper lockout/tagout procedures.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after suffering a burn at work?
_roden_faqs.answer: Seek immediate medical attention, report the injury to your employer, document the hazardous condition with photos, preserve any defective equipment, file a workers' compensation claim, and consult an attorney to evaluate potential third-party claims.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a workers' compensation claim for a burn injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must report the injury to your employer within 30 days and file a claim within one year (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). In South Carolina, the notice period is 90 days and the filing deadline is two years. Missing these deadlines can bar your claim.

/car-accident-lawyers/bus-accident/.title: Bus Accident Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/bus-accident/.excerpt: Injured in a bus accident in Georgia or South Carolina? Our lawyers handle claims involving private buses, charter buses, shuttle services, and hotel courtesy vehicles.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the common carrier duty of care in bus accident cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: Commercial bus operators are classified as common carriers under Georgia and South Carolina law, meaning they owe passengers the highest duty of care — extraordinary diligence for passenger safety. This is a stricter standard than the reasonable care required of ordinary drivers.

_roden_faqs.question: How much insurance do bus companies carry?
_roden_faqs.answer: FMCSA requires commercial bus operators carrying 16 or more passengers to maintain minimum insurance of $5 million. Smaller operators must carry at least $1.5 million. Many bus companies carry additional umbrella coverage.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a hotel for an accident in their shuttle bus?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Hotels that operate courtesy shuttles are responsible for the safe operation of those vehicles. If the shuttle driver was negligent or the vehicle was poorly maintained, the hotel or resort may be liable for your injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I was a passenger on the bus that crashed?
_roden_faqs.answer: As a bus passenger, you benefit from the common carrier heightened duty of care. Bus companies must exercise extraordinary diligence for passenger safety. You can pursue a claim against the bus company, the driver, and any other parties whose negligence contributed to the crash.

_roden_faqs.question: Are charter bus companies regulated by the federal government?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Charter bus companies operating across state lines or for hire must register with FMCSA, comply with passenger carrier safety regulations, maintain CDL-qualified drivers, follow hours-of-service rules, and carry minimum insurance of $5 million for buses with 16+ passengers.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a bus accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations is 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, you have 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). If the bus was operated by a government entity, shorter notice deadlines may apply.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the bus accident was caused by a fatigued driver?
_roden_faqs.answer: FMCSA hours-of-service regulations limit how long commercial bus drivers can operate without rest. If the driver exceeded these limits, it is strong evidence of negligence by both the driver and the bus company that allowed or required the violations.

/car-accident-lawyers/commercial-vehicle.title: Commercial Vehicle Accident Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/commercial-vehicle.excerpt: Injured in a crash with a commercial vehicle? Our attorneys handle claims involving delivery trucks, company cars, fleet vehicles, and employer liability.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the employer if their employee caused my accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under the doctrine of respondeat superior, employers are vicariously liable for accidents caused by employees acting within the scope of their employment. The employer's commercial insurance policy typically provides substantially higher coverage limits.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between a commercial vehicle and a semi-truck case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Semi-truck cases involve tractor-trailers exceeding 10,001 pounds and subject to extensive FMCSA regulations. Commercial vehicle cases cover a broader category including delivery vans, company cars, and service vehicles that may not fall under federal motor carrier regulations.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the commercial driver was an independent contractor, not an employee?
_roden_faqs.answer: Even when companies classify drivers as independent contractors, courts examine the actual level of control the company exercises. If the company controls the manner of work (routes, schedules, equipment), the driver may be deemed an employee for liability purposes.

_roden_faqs.question: How much insurance do commercial vehicles carry?
_roden_faqs.answer: Commercial vehicles often carry substantially higher insurance limits than personal vehicles. Federally regulated carriers must maintain $750,000 to $5 million in coverage depending on cargo type. Many commercial policies carry $1 million or more.

_roden_faqs.question: What if a government vehicle caused my accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may file a claim against the government entity, but strict notice requirements and shorter filing deadlines apply. In Georgia, you must provide ante litem notice before suing. South Carolina has its own tort claims act with specific procedures.

_roden_faqs.question: Does my claim change if the driver was using a personal vehicle for work?
_roden_faqs.answer: The employer can still be liable if the driver was performing work duties. Both the driver's personal insurance and the employer's coverage may apply. This is common with employees using personal vehicles for deliveries, sales calls, or work errands.

/car-accident-lawyers/company-car-accide.title: Company Car Accident Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/company-car-accide.excerpt: Injured in a company car crash in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys pursue claims against negligent employees and their employers to secure full compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the employer if their employee hit me while driving a company car?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under respondeat superior, employers are vicariously liable for accidents caused by employees driving company vehicles within the scope of employment. The employer's commercial insurance typically provides significantly higher coverage limits.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the employee was running a personal errand in the company car?
_roden_faqs.answer: Liability depends on the circumstances. If the employer permits personal use of the company car, or if the errand was incidental to work duties (such as stopping for lunch during a work trip), the employer may still be liable. Georgia and South Carolina courts examine the specific facts.

_roden_faqs.question: Does the employer have to check driving records before giving an employee a company car?
_roden_faqs.answer: While not always legally required, failure to screen driving records before assigning company vehicles can establish a negligent hiring or negligent entrustment claim if the employee has a poor driving history and causes an accident.

_roden_faqs.question: What insurance applies in a company car accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: The employer's commercial auto insurance is typically primary when the employee is driving a company-owned vehicle. Businesses often carry $1 million or more in coverage plus umbrella policies. Both the driver's and employer's policies may apply.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a company car accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations is 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, you have 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). However, evidence of employer negligence — such as training records and internal communications — should be preserved quickly.

_roden_faqs.question: What is negligent entrustment in a company car case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Negligent entrustment occurs when an employer provides a company vehicle to a driver the employer knew or should have known was unfit — such as a driver with multiple DUI convictions, a suspended license, or a history of at-fault accidents.

/car-accident-lawyers/construction-vehic.title: Construction Vehicle Accident Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/construction-vehic.excerpt: Hurt in a construction vehicle crash on Georgia or South Carolina roads? Our lawyers hold construction companies accountable for unsafe equipment operation and work zone negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: Who is liable if a construction dump truck hit my car?
_roden_faqs.answer: Multiple parties may be liable: the driver, the construction company that employed the driver, the general contractor overseeing the project, and potentially the vehicle or equipment owner. Our attorneys identify all responsible parties to maximize your recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I was hit in a construction work zone?
_roden_faqs.answer: Construction companies must comply with MUTCD work zone traffic control standards, including proper signage, flaggers, and barriers. If inadequate work zone setup contributed to your accident, the construction company and potentially the government entity overseeing the project may be liable.

_roden_faqs.question: Are construction companies required to carry commercial insurance?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Construction companies operating commercial vehicles must carry commercial auto insurance. Federal regulations require minimum coverage of $750,000 to $5 million for large vehicles. Construction companies typically carry substantial commercial policies plus umbrella coverage.

_roden_faqs.question: What OSHA regulations apply to construction vehicles on public roads?
_roden_faqs.answer: OSHA construction standards (29 CFR 1926) require operator training, vehicle maintenance, traffic control plans, and safety procedures for work near public roads. Violations of these standards are evidence of negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a construction vehicle accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations is 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, you have 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). If a government entity is involved, shorter notice deadlines may apply.

_roden_faqs.question: What if debris from a construction vehicle caused my accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Construction companies are responsible for properly securing loads on their vehicles. FMCSA cargo securement rules and DOT regulations establish loading standards. When debris falls from a construction vehicle and causes an accident, the company is liable for failing to secure its load.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I was partially at fault for my car accident in Darien?

However, your compensation will be reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are found 20% at fault and your total damages are $100,000, you would receive $80,000. However, if you are found 50% or more at fault, you cannot recover any compensation at all. Insurance companies frequently attempt to shift blame to injury victims to reduce or deny payouts. Our Darien car accident attorneys know how to counter these tactics and build a strong case that accurately reflects the other party's negligence. Call (912) 303-5850 for a free case review.

_roden_faqs.question: How much is my car accident case worth in Darien?

There is no fixed formula for calculating what a case is worth — it depends entirely on the facts and circumstances involved. Insurance companies often make lowball initial offers hoping you will accept less than your case is truly worth. At Roden Law, we have recovered over $300 million for our clients across Georgia and South Carolina and can provide an honest, thorough evaluation of your case. Contact our Darien office at (912) 303-5850 for a free, no-obligation consultation.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after a car accident in Darien?
_roden_faqs.answer: Call 911 and get medical attention immediately, even if you feel fine — some injuries like whiplash and concussions take hours or days to show symptoms. Document the scene with photos and video, exchange insurance information with the other driver, and get contact details from any witnesses. File a police report and keep all medical records and receipts. Most importantly, speak with an experienced car accident lawyer before giving any recorded statements to insurance companies, as adjusters may use your words against you. /car-accident-lawyers/delivery-vehicle-a.title: Delivery Vehicle Accident Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/delivery-vehicle-a.excerpt: Injured in a delivery vehicle crash in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys hold delivery companies and their drivers accountable for accidents caused by tight schedules and reckless driving.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue Amazon if an Amazon delivery driver hit me?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potentially, yes. While Amazon often uses Delivery Service Partners (DSPs) — third-party companies that hire their own drivers — courts examine the actual control Amazon exercises over the delivery process. If Amazon controls routes, delivery windows, and operational standards, it may share liability.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the delivery driver was an independent contractor?
_roden_faqs.answer: Even if a company classifies a driver as an independent contractor, courts look at the actual working relationship. If the company controls routes, schedules, vehicle requirements, or uniforms, the driver may be deemed an employee for liability purposes.

_roden_faqs.question: Are delivery companies required to carry commercial insurance?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Companies operating delivery vehicles for business purposes must carry commercial auto insurance. Federal regulations require carriers operating vehicles over 10,001 pounds to maintain minimum coverage of $750,000 to $5 million depending on cargo.

_roden_faqs.question: What if a delivery vehicle hit me while I was walking in my neighborhood?
_roden_faqs.answer: Pedestrians struck by delivery vehicles have strong claims. Delivery drivers have a heightened duty of care in residential areas. Both the driver and the delivery company can be held liable for your injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a delivery vehicle accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations is 2 years from the date of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Contact an attorney promptly to preserve critical evidence.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence is important in a delivery vehicle accident case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Key evidence includes the driver's delivery route data, GPS and telematics records, the company's safety and training policies, the driver's employment records and driving history, and any dashcam or surveillance footage from the area.

/car-accident-lawyers/distracted-driving.title: Distracted Driving Accident Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/distracted-driving.excerpt: Injured by a distracted driver in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys prove phone use and other distractions to hold negligent drivers fully accountable.

_roden_faqs.question: How do you prove the other driver was distracted?
_roden_faqs.answer: We subpoena cell phone records, obtain vehicle infotainment data, review surveillance and dashcam footage, take witness statements, and analyze police reports. Modern smartphones and vehicles generate extensive digital evidence that can prove distraction.

_roden_faqs.question: Is holding a phone while driving illegal in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia's Hands-Free Act (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-241.2) prohibits drivers from holding or physically touching a phone while operating a vehicle. Hands-free devices (Bluetooth, dash mounts) are permitted.

_roden_faqs.question: What about South Carolina's distracted driving law?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 56-5-3890) prohibits texting while driving but still allows drivers to hold their phone for calls. The law is narrower than Georgia's hands-free law.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I recover punitive damages from a distracted driver?
_roden_faqs.answer: Possibly. If the driver's conduct was particularly egregious — such as watching a video or actively texting at high speed — a court may award punitive damages to punish the reckless behavior.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the distracted driver was using a work phone or driving for their employer?
_roden_faqs.answer: If the driver was distracted while performing work duties, their employer may also be liable under respondeat superior. This can significantly increase the available insurance coverage and compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: How common are distracted driving accidents?
_roden_faqs.answer: NHTSA reports that approximately 424,000 people are injured and over 3,000 are killed annually in distracted driving crashes. The CDC identifies texting as the most dangerous form of distraction.

/car-accident-lawyers/drunk-driver-accid.title: Drunk Driver Accident Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/drunk-driver-accid.excerpt: Injured by a drunk driver in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys pursue maximum compensation from impaired drivers and establishments that over-served them.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a bar or restaurant that served the drunk driver?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under Georgia's dram shop law (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-40) and South Carolina's statute (S.C. Code § 61-4-580), establishments that knowingly serve alcohol to visibly intoxicated patrons can be held liable for injuries caused by those patrons.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the drunk driver was not convicted of DUI?
_roden_faqs.answer: A criminal conviction is not required to file a civil injury claim. Civil cases use a lower burden of proof (preponderance of evidence vs. beyond a reasonable doubt), so you may still recover damages even if criminal charges are dismissed.

_roden_faqs.question: Are punitive damages available in drunk driving cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Both Georgia and South Carolina allow punitive damages in drunk driving cases to punish especially reckless behavior. Georgia generally caps punitive damages at $250,000, with exceptions for DUI cases. South Carolina caps them at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530) and requires clear and convincing evidence.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a drunk driving accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

_roden_faqs.question: What compensation can I recover after a drunk driving accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may recover medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, emotional distress, property damage, and potentially punitive damages. Wrongful death claims may also be available if a loved one was killed by an impaired driver.

_roden_faqs.question: How does a criminal DUI case affect my civil claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: The two cases are separate proceedings. A DUI conviction can serve as strong evidence of negligence in your civil case, but the civil case proceeds independently regardless of the criminal outcome.

/car-accident-lawyers/government-vehicle.title: Government Vehicle Accident Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/government-vehicle.excerpt: Injured in an accident caused by a government vehicle in Georgia or South Carolina? Our lawyers navigate sovereign immunity rules and strict notice deadlines to pursue your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the government if a government vehicle hit me?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. Georgia's Tort Claims Act and South Carolina's Tort Claims Act waive sovereign immunity for negligent vehicle operation by government employees. Federal vehicle claims proceed under the Federal Tort Claims Act. Strict notice and filing requirements apply.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the ante litem notice requirement in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Under O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5, you must provide written notice to a municipal governing authority within 6 months of the accident before you can file a lawsuit. A claim against a county is different — it must be presented within 12 months under O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1. The notice must describe the time, place, and extent of your injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: Are there damage caps in government vehicle accident cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina caps recovery at $300,000 per claimant and $600,000 per occurrence against a single government entity. Federal claims under the FTCA do not have a statutory cap but do not allow punitive damages or jury trials. Georgia's Tort Claims Act has specific caps depending on the entity.

_roden_faqs.question: What if a police car caused my accident during a high-speed chase?
_roden_faqs.answer: Emergency vehicle immunity is not absolute. When officers drive with reckless disregard for public safety — such as pursuing suspects at excessive speeds through residential areas without adequate warning — the government entity may be liable.

_roden_faqs.question: How do I file a claim against a federal vehicle like a USPS truck?
_roden_faqs.answer: You must file an administrative claim with the responsible federal agency (such as USPS) within 2 years of the accident under the Federal Tort Claims Act. The agency has 6 months to respond before you can file suit in federal court.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a government vehicle accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Deadlines vary by entity: Georgia municipal claims require ante litem notice within 6 months; state claims must be filed within 12 months with DOAS; federal claims must be filed within 2 years under the FTCA. The standard personal injury statute of limitations also applies.

_roden_faqs.question: What if a military vehicle caused my accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Claims against the U.S. military proceed under the Federal Tort Claims Act. You must file an administrative claim with the appropriate military branch within 2 years. An experienced attorney can guide you through the federal claims process.

/car-accident-lawyers/hit-and-run-accide.title: Hit & Run Accident Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/hit-and-run-accide.excerpt: Victim of a hit and run in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys help you recover compensation through uninsured motorist coverage and investigative resources.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I recover compensation if the hit and run driver is never found?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. If you carry uninsured motorist (UM) coverage on your auto insurance policy, you can file a UM claim to cover your medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering — even if the at-fault driver is never identified.

_roden_faqs.question: Is uninsured motorist coverage required in Georgia and South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia requires insurers to offer UM coverage, and it is included unless you explicitly reject it. South Carolina includes UM coverage by default — you must sign a written rejection to opt out.

_roden_faqs.question: What are the criminal penalties for a hit and run in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-270, leaving the scene of an accident with injuries is a felony in Georgia, punishable by 1 to 5 years in prison. If the accident results in death, penalties increase to 3 to 15 years.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I only got a partial license plate number?
_roden_faqs.answer: Even partial information can be valuable. Our attorneys work with law enforcement and investigators to cross-reference partial plates, vehicle descriptions, surveillance footage, and debris evidence to identify hit and run drivers.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a hit and run accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: The personal injury statute of limitations is 2 years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and 3 years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). However, you should report the incident to police and your insurance company immediately.

_roden_faqs.question: Will my insurance rates go up if I file a UM claim after a hit and run?
_roden_faqs.answer: Because you are not at fault in a hit and run, filing a UM claim should not increase your premiums. UM coverage exists specifically for situations like these. Your attorney can help you navigate the claims process.

/car-accident-lawyers/multi-vehicle-pile.title: Multi-Vehicle Pileup Lawyers
/car-accident-lawyers/multi-vehicle-pile.excerpt: Injured in a multi-vehicle pileup on a Georgia or South Carolina highway? Our attorneys untangle complex liability and pursue every available source of compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: How is fault determined in a multi-vehicle pileup?
_roden_faqs.answer: Accident reconstruction experts analyze vehicle damage patterns, event data recorders, skid marks, and witness statements to establish the sequence of impacts and each driver's degree of fault. Multiple drivers often share liability.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I recover damages if I am partially at fault in a pileup?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia allows recovery if you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina allows recovery if less than 51% at fault. Your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault.

_roden_faqs.question: What if multiple drivers caused the pileup?
_roden_faqs.answer: You can pursue claims against all at-fault drivers simultaneously. Multiple insurance policies may apply, which can increase the total compensation available for your injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: Can the government be liable for a pileup caused by road conditions?

_roden_faqs.question: What is a T-bone accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: A T-bone accident, also called a side-impact or broadside collision, occurs when the front of one vehicle strikes the side of another at a roughly perpendicular angle, forming a T-shape. These crashes most commonly occur at intersections when one driver runs a red light, stop sign, or fails to yield the right of way.

_roden_faqs.question: Why are T-bone accidents so dangerous?
_roden_faqs.answer: T-bone crashes are especially dangerous because vehicle doors provide far less structural protection than the front or rear of a car. Occupants on the struck side sit just inches from the point of impact, even with side airbags deployed. The IIHS reports that side-impact crashes account for about 23% of all passenger vehicle occupant deaths.

_roden_faqs.question: How is fault determined in a T-bone collision?
_roden_faqs.answer: Fault typically depends on which driver had the right of way. Evidence like traffic camera footage, witness statements, police reports, and vehicle black box data help establish who violated a traffic signal or failed to yield. Georgia and South Carolina both use modified comparative fault rules.

_roden_faqs.question: What compensation can I recover after a T-bone accident?

/construction-accident-lawyers/crane-hea.excerpt: Injured in a crane or heavy equipment accident on a construction site in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys hold contractors, equipment owners, and manufacturers accountable for equipment-related injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: Who is liable for a crane collapse on a construction site?
_roden_faqs.answer: Multiple parties may be liable: the general contractor for site safety, the crane operator for operational errors, the crane owner/rental company for maintenance failures, and the manufacturer for equipment defects. OSHA investigation findings help establish responsibility.

_roden_faqs.question: Does OSHA require crane operators to be licensed?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. OSHA's crane standard (29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC) requires crane operators in construction to be certified by an accredited testing organization. Employers must also ensure operators are qualified for the specific type of crane being used.

_roden_faqs.question: Can a bystander injured by a crane collapse sue?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Unlike employees who are generally limited to workers' compensation, bystanders and members of the public can file full personal injury lawsuits against all responsible parties, recovering complete damages including pain and suffering.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the heavy equipment was rented?
_roden_faqs.answer: Equipment rental companies may be liable if they rented defective equipment, failed to conduct proper inspections, or rented to unqualified operators. The rental agreement does not necessarily shield the rental company from liability for injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a crane accident claim?

/construction-accident-lawyers/defective.excerpt: Injured by defective construction equipment in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys hold equipment manufacturers, distributors, and rental companies strictly liable for injuries caused by dangerous tools and machinery.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need to prove the manufacturer was negligent?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Under strict product liability law in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11) and South Carolina, you only need to prove the equipment was defective and the defect caused your injury. You do not need to prove how or why the defect occurred.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue an equipment rental company for a defect?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Rental companies have a duty to inspect and maintain equipment. If they rented defective equipment or failed to perform required maintenance, they can be held liable for resulting injuries alongside the manufacturer.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if defective equipment injures me at work?
_roden_faqs.answer: Seek medical attention, report the injury to your employer, do NOT return the defective equipment to the rental company or discard it, take photos of the equipment and the defect, file a workers' compensation claim, and consult an attorney about potential product liability claims.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I file a product liability claim in addition to workers' compensation?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Workers' comp covers medical bills and wage replacement, but product liability claims against third-party manufacturers allow you to recover additional damages including pain and suffering, disfigurement, and potentially punitive damages.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a defective equipment claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia's personal injury statute of limitations is 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), with a 10-year statute of repose for products (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11). South Carolina allows 3 years for personal injury (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Evidence preservation is critical — consult an attorney immediately.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the most common cause of construction site electrocutions?
_roden_faqs.answer: Contact with overhead power lines is the leading cause of construction electrocution deaths. OSHA requires minimum clearance distances of at least 10 feet from power lines under 50kV, with greater distances for higher-voltage lines.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a power company for a construction site electrocution?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Power companies may be liable if they failed to de-energize lines upon request, failed to relocate lines near construction activity, or failed to install protective covers. They have a duty to respond to safety requests from contractors working near their lines.

_roden_faqs.question: What is OSHA's lockout/tagout requirement?
_roden_faqs.answer: Lockout/tagout (29 CFR 1910.147) requires that electrical systems be completely de-energized, locked out, and tagged before any worker performs maintenance or construction work on them. Failure to follow LOTO procedures is a leading cause of electrocution.

_roden_faqs.question: Are electrocution injuries covered by workers' compensation?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. On-the-job electrocution injuries are covered by workers' comp in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1) and South Carolina. Third-party claims against general contractors, power companies, and equipment manufacturers may also provide additional compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: What if my family member was killed by electrocution on a construction site?
_roden_faqs.answer: Surviving family members may file wrongful death claims against responsible third parties and receive workers' compensation death benefits. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1) and South Carolina both allow wrongful death actions for fatal electrocutions.

/construction-accident-lawyers/falling-o.title: Falling Object Injury Lawyers

_roden_faqs.question: Is my employer liable if I was hit by a falling tool on a construction site?
_roden_faqs.answer: Your employer is covered by workers' compensation, which provides medical and wage benefits regardless of fault. Third-party claims against general contractors, subcontractors doing the overhead work, or tool manufacturers may provide additional compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: What OSHA standards protect workers from falling objects?
_roden_faqs.answer: OSHA requires hard hats (29 CFR 1926.100), toeboards on scaffolds (29 CFR 1926.451), overhead protection such as debris nets, barricading areas below overhead work, and proper material handling procedures. Violations are evidence of negligence.

_roden_faqs.question: Can a pedestrian sue for a falling object from a construction site?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Pedestrians and members of the public injured by falling construction debris can file personal injury lawsuits against the general contractor, subcontractors, and property owner. They are not limited to workers' compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I was wearing a hard hat but still got injured?
_roden_faqs.answer: Hard hats protect against some falling objects but have limitations. If you were injured despite wearing a hard hat, you still have valid claims. The fact that you wore safety equipment demonstrates you were following safety rules.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a falling object injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Workers' comp deadlines are 1 year in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82) and 2 years in South Carolina. Personal injury claims allow 2 years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and 3 years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

_roden_faqs.question: Is roofing really one of the most dangerous jobs?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. The Bureau of Labor Statistics consistently ranks roofing among the occupations with the highest fatal injury rates. Falls from roofs are the primary cause, but roofers also face burns, electrocution, and heat illness risks.

_roden_faqs.question: What fall protection does OSHA require for roofing work?
_roden_faqs.answer: OSHA (29 CFR 1926 Subpart M) requires fall protection for all roofing workers more than 6 feet above ground. On low-slope roofs, guardrails, safety nets, fall arrest systems, or warning line/safety monitor systems are required. Steep-slope roofs require guardrails, nets, or fall arrest systems.

_roden_faqs.question: Can a homeowner be liable for a roofer's injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potentially. Homeowners who hire unlicensed or uninsured roofing contractors, fail to disclose known roof hazards, or maintain dangerous conditions on their property may share liability for roofing injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: What if my roofing employer did not provide fall protection?
_roden_faqs.answer: Your employer's failure to provide required fall protection is an OSHA violation that supports your workers' compensation claim and may support third-party claims. Document the lack of safety equipment and report the violation to OSHA.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a roofing accident claim?

/construction-accident-lawyers/scaffold-.excerpt: Fell from a scaffold or ladder on a construction site in Georgia or South Carolina? Our attorneys pursue workers' compensation and third-party negligence claims for fall injuries caused by unsafe equipment and OSHA violations.

_roden_faqs.question: What are OSHA's requirements for scaffold safety?
_roden_faqs.answer: OSHA (29 CFR 1926.451) requires guardrails on scaffolds 10+ feet high, competent person inspections before each shift, proper scaffold construction and load ratings, safe access via ladders or stairways, and fall protection for all workers on scaffolds.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue my employer for a scaffold fall?
_roden_faqs.answer: Generally, workers' compensation is your exclusive remedy against your employer. However, you can file third-party claims against general contractors, scaffold manufacturers, property owners, and other parties whose negligence caused your fall.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the scaffold was improperly assembled?
_roden_faqs.answer: If the scaffold was improperly erected — missing guardrails, unstable foundation, improper bracing — the general contractor, scaffold erector, and scaffold supplier may all face liability. OSHA requires a "competent person" to supervise scaffold assembly.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a construction fall injury claim?

_roden_faqs.question: Who is responsible for trench safety on a construction site?

_roden_faqs.answer: Call 911 immediately. Do not enter the trench — secondary collapses are common and can bury rescuers. Keep others away from the trench edges. Professional rescue teams with specialized equipment are needed for safe extraction.

_roden_faqs.answer: After an electric scooter accident in Savannah: seek medical attention immediately, even for seemingly minor injuries; call 911 and file a police report; photograph the scooter (including the ID number), the accident scene, road conditions, and your injuries; save the scooter rental app data showing your trip details and rental agreement; get contact information from any witnesses; do not admit fault or give a recorded statement to any insurance company; and contact an attorney before accepting any settlement. Electric scooter accident evidence can disappear quickly — rental companies may repair or redistribute the scooter, and app data may be deleted. Our Savannah attorneys can send a preservation letter to protect this critical evidence. Call (912) 303-5850 today.

_roden_faqs.answer: Your health insurance will typically cover treatment for electric scooter accident injuries, but it may assert a subrogation lien (a right to be reimbursed from any settlement or verdict you receive). Auto insurance may also apply — if you have uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage and a vehicle was involved, your auto policy may cover your scooter accident injuries. The scooter rental company's commercial insurance policy may also provide coverage. Navigating multiple insurance sources is one of the most complex aspects of e-scooter accident claims. _roden_faqs.question: How much is my electric scooter accident case worth in Savannah?

Common e-scooter injuries include traumatic brain injuries (many riders don't wear helmets), broken bones, facial injuries, dental damage, and road rash. Severe cases involving permanent disability or disfigurement are worth significantly more. /electric-scooter-accident-lawyers/scoot.excerpt: Injured due to a defective electric scooter in Georgia or South Carolina? Our product liability attorneys hold manufacturers and rental companies accountable for dangerous e-scooter defects.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the e-scooter manufacturer if the scooter malfunctioned?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Under Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11) and South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 15-73-10), manufacturers are strictly liable for injuries caused by defective products. You can pursue claims for manufacturing defects, design defects, or failure to warn.

_roden_faqs.question: Is Lime or Bird liable if their rental scooter was defective?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Rental scooter companies have a duty to maintain their fleets and remove defective scooters from circulation. If they deploy a scooter with known brake, battery, or steering issues, they can be held liable for resulting injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if my e-scooter malfunctioned and caused a crash?
_roden_faqs.answer: Do not return the scooter. Photograph it from multiple angles, note the scooter ID number, seek medical attention, and contact an attorney immediately. Preserving the scooter and its electronic data is critical to proving a defect claim.

_roden_faqs.question: What types of compensation are available in an e-scooter defect case?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may recover medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, and property damage. In cases involving grossly defective products or corporate cover-ups, punitive damages may also be available to punish the manufacturer.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file an e-scooter product liability claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia has a 2-year statute of limitations for personal injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and a 10-year statute of repose for product liability. South Carolina allows 3 years for personal injury (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Contact an attorney promptly to preserve your rights.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Puedo demandar al conductor que me atropelló mientras andaba en bicicleta?
_roden_faqs.answer: Sí. En Georgia el ciclista tiene los mismos derechos sobre la vía que el conductor de un automóvil. Si el conductor iba distraído, no cedió el paso, abrió su puerta frente a usted o se pasó una luz roja, usted puede presentar un reclamo por lesiones personales. Georgia aplica una regla de negligencia comparativa modificada: usted puede recuperar daños siempre que su responsabilidad sea menor al 50% (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). Aunque el conductor diga que usted tuvo parte de la culpa, un abogado con experiencia puede demostrar el alcance real de la negligencia de él.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Qué pasa si el conductor se dio a la fuga después de atropellarme?
_roden_faqs.answer: Todavía puede recuperar una compensación. Si usted tiene cobertura contra conductores sin seguro (UM) en su póliza de auto, esa cobertura muchas veces se aplica aunque iba en bicicleta y no manejando. Reporte el atropello y fuga a la policía de Savannah de inmediato, anote todo lo que recuerde del vehículo (color, marca, modelo, placa y dirección en que huyó) y revise si hay cámaras de seguridad cerca. _roden_faqs.question: ¿Qué compensación puedo recibir por un accidente de bicicleta en Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: Las víctimas de un accidente de bicicleta en Savannah pueden reclamar gastos médicos (atención de emergencia, cirugía, rehabilitación y tratamiento futuro), salarios perdidos y la reducción de su capacidad para ganarse la vida, dolor y sufrimiento, el daño a su bicicleta y su equipo, cicatrices y desfiguración, y la pérdida del disfrute de la vida. Como el ciclista no tiene una carrocería que lo proteja, las lesiones suelen ser graves: lesiones cerebrales traumáticas, huesos rotos, lesiones de columna y raspones profundos son muy comunes. El valor de su caso depende de la gravedad de sus lesiones, del impacto en su vida diaria y de la fuerza de la evidencia. En Roden Law peleamos por el valor completo de su reclamo, no por la oferta baja de la aseguradora. Llame al (912) 303-5850 para una consulta gratis; atendemos en español.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Qué debo hacer después de un accidente de auto en Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: Llame al 911 y busque atención médica de inmediato, aunque se sienta bien: lesiones como el latigazo cervical y las concusiones pueden tardar horas o días en dar síntomas. Documente la escena con fotos y video, intercambie la información del seguro con el otro conductor y pida los datos de contacto de cualquier testigo. Presente un reporte policial y guarde todos sus expedientes médicos y recibos. Lo más importante: hable con un abogado de accidentes con experiencia antes de dar cualquier declaración grabada a las aseguradoras, porque los ajustadores pueden usar sus palabras en su contra. Un abogado de nuestra oficina de Savannah puede encargarse de toda la comunicación con las aseguradoras, reunir y preservar la evidencia clave, consultar con expertos y construir un caso sólido de su parte para que usted se concentre en recuperarse. _roden_faqs.question: ¿Cuánto vale mi caso de accidente de auto en Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: Cada caso de accidente de auto es distinto y su valor depende de varios factores propios de su situación: la gravedad de sus lesiones, el total de gastos médicos pasados y futuros, los salarios perdidos y la capacidad de ganar dinero que quedó reducida, los daños a su vehículo, el dolor y el sufrimiento, y el impacto a largo plazo en su calidad de vida. No hay una fórmula fija para calcular cuánto vale un caso; depende por completo de los hechos y las circunstancias. Las aseguradoras suelen hacer ofertas muy bajas al principio con la esperanza de que usted acepte menos de lo que su caso realmente vale. En Roden Law hemos recuperado más de $300 millones para nuestros clientes en Georgia y Carolina del Sur, y podemos darle una evaluación honesta y completa de su caso. Comuníquese con nuestra oficina de Savannah al (912) 303-5850 para una consulta gratis y sin ningún compromiso.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Debo dar una declaración grabada a la aseguradora después de un accidente en Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: No; usted no debe dar una declaración grabada a la aseguradora del otro conductor sin consultar primero con un abogado. Por lo general sí tiene que cooperar con su propia aseguradora según los términos de su póliza, pero la compañía del conductor culpable no tiene ningún derecho legal a exigirle una declaración grabada. Los ajustadores están entrenados para hacer preguntas diseñadas para sacar respuestas que sirvan para reducir o negar su reclamo, y hasta frases inocentes como “me siento bien” o “no lo vi venir” pueden sacarse de contexto y usarse en su contra más adelante. En Georgia usted no tiene obligación legal de darle una declaración grabada a la aseguradora de la otra parte: decline con cortesía y remítalos a su abogado. En Roden Law manejamos toda la comunicación con las aseguradoras por usted, protegiendo sus derechos mientras construimos el caso más fuerte posible. Llame a nuestra oficina de Savannah al (912) 303-5850 para una consulta gratis antes de hablar con cualquier ajustador.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Cuánto tarda en resolverse un acuerdo por accidente de auto en Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: El tiempo varía bastante según lo complejo que sea su caso, pero la mayoría se resuelve entre 6 y 18 meses. Influyen varios factores: la gravedad de sus lesiones y cuánto tarde usted en llegar a la mejoría médica máxima (MMI), qué tan clara esté la culpa y si la responsabilidad se disputa, cuántas partes y aseguradoras estén involucradas, si la compañía negocia de buena fe y si se vuelve necesario un pleito. Los casos sencillos, con responsabilidad clara y lesiones menores, pueden cerrarse en pocos meses; los casos complejos con lesiones graves, culpa disputada o varios demandados pueden tomar un año o más. Es importante no apurar un acuerdo: aceptar una oferta baja antes de entender el alcance real de sus lesiones puede dejarlo pagando de su bolsillo la atención médica futura. Nuestros abogados de accidentes en Savannah no lo van a presionar para que acepte menos de lo que vale su caso; buscamos la máxima recuperación aunque tome más tiempo. Llame al (912) 303-5850 para una evaluación gratuita de su caso.

La ley del estado permite acumular (stacking) su propia cobertura contra conductores sin seguro o con seguro insuficiente (UM/UIM) entre varias pólizas, y con frecuencia esa es la mayor fuente de recuperación. Nosotros identificamos y reclamamos todas las pólizas disponibles, no solo la del otro conductor.

_roden_faqs.answer: En Georgia el plazo es de 2 años contados desde la fecha del accidente (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Si deja pasar ese plazo, lo normal es que pierda para siempre el derecho a reclamar. Dos años parecen mucho, pero las pruebas de un choque de moto desaparecen rápido: la motocicleta se repara, los videos se borran y los testigos olvidan detalles. Llame a nuestra oficina de Savannah al (912) 303-5850 para una consulta gratuita.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Puedo reclamar si yo también tuve parte de la culpa?
_roden_faqs.answer: Sí, siempre que su responsabilidad sea menor al 50%. Georgia aplica una regla de negligencia comparativa modificada (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33): su compensación se reduce según su porcentaje de culpa, así que si le asignan un 20% y sus daños son de $100,000, recibiría $80,000. Con 50% o más, ya no recupera nada. Por eso las aseguradoras intentan echarle la culpa al motociclista desde el primer día, y por eso conviene hablar con un abogado antes de dar cualquier declaración.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Qué debo hacer después de un accidente de motocicleta en Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: Llame al 911 y acepte la atención médica aunque crea que puede caminar; en moto no hay carrocería que lo proteja y las lesiones serias pueden sentirse horas después. Si puede, tome fotos y video de la motocicleta, del otro vehículo, de la señalización y del pavimento, y pida nombre y teléfono de los testigos. No admita culpa ni dé declaraciones grabadas a la aseguradora del otro conductor. Los heridos graves se atienden en el Memorial Health University Medical Center; pida copia del reporte policial en cuanto pueda.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Mi estatus migratorio afecta mi reclamo por el accidente?
_roden_faqs.answer: No le preguntamos por su estatus migratorio y no es lo que decide su reclamo. Lo que importa es que otro conductor causó el accidente y que usted resultó lesionado. Su estatus no le impide reclamar una compensación en Georgia. Lo atendemos en español de principio a fin y la consulta es confidencial y sin compromiso.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Cuánto cuesta un abogado de accidentes de motocicleta en Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: Nada por adelantado. Roden Law trabaja por honorarios de contingencia: nuestros honorarios salen de un porcentaje de lo que recuperemos para usted y, si no ganamos, usted no paga honorarios. No hay cuotas por consulta ni cobros por hora. Roden Law ha recuperado más de $300 millones para clientes lesionados en Georgia y Carolina del Sur. Llame al (912) 303-5850 para una revisión gratuita de su caso.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Cuánto tiempo tengo para presentar un reclamo por un accidente de peatón en Charleston?
_roden_faqs.answer: El plazo general en Carolina del Sur es de 3 años desde la fecha de la lesión (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Las lesiones de peatón suelen ser graves, así que conviene revisar el caso cuanto antes, mientras los videos y los testigos todavía existen.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿El conductor siempre tiene la preferencia sobre el peatón en Carolina del Sur?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. La ley de Carolina del Sur (S.C. Code §§ 56-5-3110 a 56-5-3230) da al peatón la preferencia en cruces marcados y no marcados, y exige a los conductores un alto grado de cuidado con las personas a pie. Un conductor que no cede el paso normalmente es negligente.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Puedo recuperar compensación si crucé fuera del paso peatonal?
_roden_faqs.answer: Con frecuencia sí. Carolina del Sur aplica la regla de negligencia comparativa modificada del 51%: usted recupera mientras no haya tenido más del 50% de la culpa. Cruzar a mitad de cuadra puede reducir el monto, pero rara vez elimina el reclamo, y el conductor pudo haber fallado en mantener la debida vigilancia.

_roden_faqs.question: ¿Qué pasa si el conductor huyó o no tenía seguro?
_roden_faqs.answer: Los atropellos con fuga y con conductores sin seguro son comunes en Charleston. En esos casos su propia cobertura de motorista sin seguro o con seguro insuficiente (UM/UIM) suele ser la fuente de recuperación, y Carolina del Sur permite apilar esa cobertura. Roden Law identifica todas las pólizas que puedan aplicar.
