/resources/south-carolina-comparative-ne.title: South Carolina Comparative Negligence — the 51% Bar Explained
/resources/south-carolina-comparative-ne.excerpt: South Carolina is a modified comparative negligence state with a 51% bar: you can recover if you are less than 51% at fault, but your award drops by your fault share.

_roden_faqs.question: Is South Carolina a comparative negligence state?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina follows modified comparative negligence with a 51% bar, adopted in Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (1991). You can recover compensation as long as you are less than 51% at fault, but your award is reduced by your percentage of fault. At 51% or more fault, you recover nothing.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the 51% bar in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: The 51% bar is the cutoff for recovery. If you are 50% or less at fault, you can recover damages, reduced by your fault percentage. If you are 51% or more at fault, you are barred from recovering anything. That one-percentage-point line can be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, which is why fault is heavily contested.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still recover if the accident was partly my fault in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, as long as your share of fault is less than 51%. Many injured people wrongly assume any mistake bars their claim, but South Carolina only reduces your award in proportion to your fault. For example, on a $200,000 case where you are 25% at fault, you would recover $150,000.

_roden_faqs.question: How do insurance companies use comparative fault against me?
_roden_faqs.answer: Insurers try to inflate your percentage of fault because every point reduces what they owe, and pushing you to 51% erases the claim entirely. They request early recorded statements, argue you were distracted or speeding, and make fast lowball offers. An attorney counters with evidence to keep your fault percentage as low as the facts support.

_roden_faqs.question: What happens to my settlement if I am found 30% at fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: Your recovery is reduced by your fault percentage. If you are 30% at fault on a case worth $300,000, you recover $210,000 — that is the full value minus your 30% share. As long as you stay below 51% at fault, you still recover; the award is simply reduced proportionally.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: South Carolina follows modified comparative negligence with a 51% bar. You can recover compensation as long as you are less than 51% at fault for your own injuries, but your award is reduced by your percentage of fault. If you are 51% or more at fault, you recover nothing. For example, on a $300,000 case, being 20% at fault leaves you $240,000, while 51% fault leaves you $0. Insurance companies routinely try to inflate your fault percentage to cut or eliminate your payout, which is why how fault is assigned has a direct dollar impact on your case.
meta._roden_meta_description: South Carolina is a modified comparative negligence state with a 51% bar: you can recover if you are less than 51% at fault, but your award drops by your fault share.

/resources/south-carolina-liquor-liabili.title: What South Carolina's 2026 Liquor Liability Law Changed
/resources/south-carolina-liquor-liabili.excerpt: South Carolina rewrote its liquor liability law effective 1 January 2026. What Act 42 changed about a bar's exposure in a drunk-driving case, what it left alone, and why the date of your accident decides which version applies.

_roden_faqs.question: I was hit by a drunk driver in South Carolina. Does Act 42 apply to my case?
_roden_faqs.answer: It depends on when your cause of action arose or accrued, not on when you read this. Section 11 of the Act applies it only to causes of action arising or accruing after 1 January 2026. The South Carolina Code publishes both versions of § 15-38-15 for exactly this reason. If your accident is anywhere near that date, establishing which version governs is the first thing to settle, not something to assume.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still sue the bar that over-served the driver?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Act 42 did not abolish dram-shop liability, and that is the most common thing said wrongly about it. What the Act changed is how a licensed establishment's share is calculated. Under § 61-2-147, where a verdict is rendered against both the establishment and a driver charged under § 56-5-2930, § 56-5-2933 or § 56-5-2945, the establishment is jointly and severally liable for fifty percent of the plaintiff's actual damages.

_roden_faqs.question: Did Act 42 change South Carolina's comparative negligence rule?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. The rule barring recovery for a plaintiff more than half at fault is untouched, and so is the fifty-percent threshold in § 15-38-15(A) that decides when a defendant faces joint and several liability. This is worth stating plainly because the equivalent claim circulated widely and wrongly about Georgia's 2025 tort reform, and the same error is likely to attach to this Act.

_roden_faqs.question: Is the change good or bad for injured people?
_roden_faqs.answer: Neither, cleanly. Removing alcohol from the exception in § 15-38-15(F) closed one route to holding a defendant liable for all the damages. Section 61-2-147 opened a narrower, more specific one aimed squarely at licensed establishments in DUI cases. Which matters more depends on the facts of a particular case — who the defendants are, what each is found to have done, and when it happened.

_roden_faqs.question: What does the word “knowingly” change in § 61-6-2220?
_roden_faqs.answer: That section prohibits a licensed establishment from selling alcohol to a person in an intoxicated condition, and Act 42 added that the sale must be made knowingly. It is a single word in an eleven-section act and easy to miss, but that prohibition is the statutory hook a dram-shop claim is built on, so the addition of a knowledge element is not a drafting nicety.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: South Carolina's 2025 Act No. 42 (H.3430) took effect 1 January 2026 and applies only to causes of action arising or accruing after that date, so the South Carolina Code now publishes two versions of S.C. Code § 15-38-15 side by side. The fifty-percent threshold in § 15-38-15(A) did not change. What changed is subsection (F): conduct involving alcohol, and gross negligence, no longer fall outside the limit on joint and several liability. In their place the Act created § 61-2-147, under which a drunk driver charged under § 56-5-2930, § 56-5-2933 or § 56-5-2945 is placed on the jury verdict form, and where a verdict is rendered against both that driver and a licensed establishment, the establishment is jointly and severally liable for fifty percent of the plaintiff's actual damages. The Act also inserted one word into § 61-6-2220: an establishment may not knowingly sell alcohol to a person in an intoxicated condition. Licensee insurance under § 61-2-145 is now stated as an annual aggregate with a per-occurrence floor of half that amount, and a new Chapter 3 of Title 61 requires certified alcohol server training. Act 42 did not abolish dram-shop liability and did not change South Carolina's comparative negligence rule.

/resources/south-carolina-motorcycle-acc.title: How Much Is a SC Motorcycle Accident Case Worth?
/resources/south-carolina-motorcycle-acc.excerpt: South Carolina motorcycle accident settlements range widely with injury severity. There is no cap on your compensatory damages — and the punitive cap can disappear entirely.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the average motorcycle accident settlement in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no reliable single average, because South Carolina motorcycle accident settlements range from tens of thousands of dollars for moderate injuries to several million for catastrophic ones. Value depends on injury severity, medical bills, lost income, fault, and available insurance. South Carolina places no cap on your compensatory damages. Every case is unique and no result is guaranteed.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on damages in a South Carolina motorcycle accident case?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. South Carolina places no cap on compensatory damages — economic or non-economic — in an ordinary motorcycle injury case. The non-economic cap applies only to medical-malpractice claims. Punitive damages are generally capped under S.C. Code § 15-32-530, but that cap is removed entirely if the at-fault driver was under the influence.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I recover more if a drunk driver hit my motorcycle in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potentially yes. Under S.C. Code § 15-32-530(C), the usual punitive-damage cap is removed entirely when the defendant was driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, was convicted of a felony from the conduct, or acted with intent to harm. That can allow a larger punitive award on top of your compensatory damages in a drunk-driving crash.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a motorcycle accident claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In South Carolina, you generally have 3 years from the date of the crash to file a motorcycle accident lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. If you miss this deadline, you usually lose the right to recover compensation entirely. Acting early also helps preserve evidence such as the crash report, vehicle data, and witness accounts.

_roden_faqs.question: Will not wearing a helmet reduce my South Carolina motorcycle settlement?
_roden_faqs.answer: It can. South Carolina uses modified comparative negligence, so insurers may argue that not wearing a helmet increased your injuries and try to shift fault to you. Your award is reduced by your fault percentage and barred at 51% or more. Whether a helmet affects value depends on the injuries and the facts, and an attorney can push back on inflated fault claims.

_roden_faqs.question: Are punitive damages available in South Carolina motorcycle accident cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: Sometimes. Punitive damages may be available when a driver acted recklessly or willfully, such as drunk driving or extreme speeding. They are generally capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or an inflation-adjusted minimum (about $739,000 as of 2026, adjusted annually), but that cap is removed entirely for DUI, felony conduct, or intent to harm. They are not guaranteed.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: South Carolina motorcycle accident settlements range from tens of thousands of dollars for moderate injuries to several million for catastrophic ones, and South Carolina places no cap on your compensatory damages (economic or non-economic). If a drunk driver caused your crash, the punitive-damage cap can be removed entirely under S.C. Code § 15-32-530(C). Your award is reduced by your share of fault and barred at 51%. You generally have 3 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Every case is unique and no result is guaranteed.
meta._roden_meta_description: South Carolina motorcycle accident settlements range widely with injury severity. There is no cap on your compensatory damages — and the punitive cap can disappear entirely.

/resources/south-carolina-personal-injur.title: South Carolina Personal Injury FAQ
/resources/south-carolina-personal-injur.excerpt: Answers to the most common South Carolina personal injury questions: deadlines, fault, settlement value, medical bills, and whether you need a lawyer.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In South Carolina, you generally have 3 years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. Claims against government entities have a shorter deadline, and medical malpractice has special discovery and repose rules. Because missing the deadline usually bars your claim entirely, it is best to confirm your specific deadline with an attorney early. See our guide at /resources/south-carolina-statute-of-limitations/.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a car accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: A South Carolina car accident claim must generally be filed within 3 years of the crash (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). If a city, county, or state vehicle was involved, a shorter government-claims deadline may apply. Acting early also helps preserve evidence like vehicle data and witness statements.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the deadline to sue the government in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Claims against government entities fall under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act and generally must be filed within 2 years. That window extends to 3 years only if you file an optional verified claim with the agency within 1 year of the injury. Because the government deadline is shorter than the ordinary 3-year rule, contact an attorney immediately if a city, county, or state entity may be responsible.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the government if a public vehicle or road caused my injury in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, but claims against government entities fall under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, which has a shorter deadline and special rules compared with ordinary claims. In general you have 2 years to file, extended to 3 years only if you file an optional verified claim with the agency within 1 year. If any government body may be responsible, contact an attorney immediately so you do not miss the shorter window.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for medical malpractice in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: A South Carolina medical malpractice claim generally must be filed within 3 years of the date you discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the injury (S.C. Code § 15-3-545). An outer limit called the statute of repose bars most claims more than 6 years after the malpractice, regardless of when it was discovered. Special notice and expert-affidavit requirements also apply, so consult a lawyer early.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the deadline for a wrongful death claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: A South Carolina wrongful death claim generally must be filed within 3 years of the date of death and must be brought by the personal representative of the deceased person's estate (S.C. Code § 15-51-20). Because the rules around who can file and how damages are distributed are specific, families should consult an attorney promptly.

_roden_faqs.question: What happens if I miss the statute of limitations in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: If you file after the deadline passes, the court will almost always dismiss your case and you lose the right to recover, no matter how strong the facts are. A few narrow exceptions can pause the clock, such as claims involving minors or a defendant who left the state, but you should never rely on an exception. The safest course is to speak with an attorney well before the 3-year mark.

_roden_faqs.question: Does the filing deadline change if the injured person is a minor in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Often, yes. In many South Carolina injury cases involving a child, the statute of limitations is paused until the child turns 18, giving them time to file as a young adult. The rules have limits and exceptions, especially for claims against the government, so a parent should still consult an attorney early rather than assuming the deadline is far off.

_roden_faqs.question: How soon should I contact a lawyer after an accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: As soon as possible. Early involvement lets an attorney preserve evidence, identify all liable parties, deal with insurers before they pressure you, and protect your deadline. Waiting can let evidence disappear and deadlines approach. The consultation is free, and there are no fees unless we win.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still recover if the accident was partly my fault in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina uses modified comparative negligence with a 51% bar. You can recover as long as you are 50% or less at fault, but your award is reduced by your fault percentage. For example, on a $200,000 case where you are 25% at fault, you recover $150,000. At 51% or more fault, you recover nothing. See /resources/south-carolina-comparative-negligence/.

_roden_faqs.question: How does comparative fault affect my settlement in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault, and you are barred entirely if you are 51% or more at fault. On a $300,000 case, 20% fault leaves you $240,000, while 51% fault leaves you nothing. Insurers try to inflate your fault to cut your payout, which is why how fault is assigned has a direct dollar impact.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the 51% bar rule in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: The 51% bar means you can recover damages only if your share of fault is 50% or less; at 51% or more, you are barred from recovering anything. This is South Carolina's modified comparative negligence rule, established in case law (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.) rather than by statute. If you are allowed to recover, your award is still reduced in proportion to your fault.

_roden_faqs.question: How is fault decided when several drivers are involved in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: When more than one defendant is at fault, your fault is compared against the defendants' combined fault, not each one separately. So if you are 40% at fault and two defendants share the other 60%, you are under the 51% bar and can still recover. This combined-comparison rule can make the difference between recovering and being barred, so how fault is apportioned matters a great deal.

_roden_faqs.question: Who decides how much fault I share in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: If your case settles, fault is negotiated between your attorney and the insurer based on the police report, physical evidence, and witness accounts. If the case goes to trial, the jury assigns each party a percentage of fault. Because insurers push to raise your percentage and cut your payout, strong evidence and legal advocacy directly affect the final number.

_roden_faqs.question: Does South Carolina reduce my recovery if I wasn't wearing a seatbelt?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Under S.C. Code § 56-5-6540(C), a seatbelt violation is not negligence per se or contributory negligence and is not admissible as evidence in a civil action. Your recovery is not reduced for failing to wear a seatbelt, and the focus stays on who caused the crash. If an adjuster raises seatbelt use, that is not a basis South Carolina law recognizes — but tell your attorney, because how it is raised can still matter to how the claim is handled.

_roden_faqs.question: The insurance company says I'm mostly at fault. Can I fight that in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. An insurer's fault assessment is a negotiating position, not a final ruling. Police reports, photos, black-box or event-data-recorder data, and witness statements can all shift the fault picture in your favor. Because being pushed over the 51% line ends your claim entirely, it is worth having an attorney challenge an unfair fault finding.

_roden_faqs.question: How much is my personal injury case worth in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no fixed average. Your case value depends on the severity of your injuries, your total medical bills and lost income, the impact on your life, your share of fault, and the available insurance coverage. Cases range from a few thousand dollars for minor injuries to seven figures for catastrophic ones. An attorney can give you an honest estimate after reviewing the facts.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the average car accident settlement in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no reliable single average, because settlements span a wide range based on injury severity, fault, and insurance limits. Minor soft-tissue cases may settle for a few thousand dollars, while serious-injury cases reach six or seven figures. Be skeptical of any average figure; your case is valued on its own specific facts.

_roden_faqs.question: What types of compensation can I recover in a South Carolina injury case?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may recover economic damages (medical bills, lost wages, lost earning capacity, property damage) and non-economic damages (pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life, disfigurement). In cases of egregious conduct, punitive damages may also be available. The total depends on the severity of your injuries and the strength of the evidence.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on damages in South Carolina personal injury cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: In ordinary injury cases such as car and truck crashes, there is no cap on compensatory damages, meaning both your economic and non-economic damages are uncapped. South Carolina caps punitive damages and caps non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases specifically, but that malpractice cap does not apply to ordinary negligence claims. Most accident victims pursuing standard claims are not limited by a non-economic cap.

_roden_faqs.question: How are pain and suffering damages calculated in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina has no fixed formula for pain and suffering. These non-economic damages account for physical pain, emotional distress, and reduced quality of life, and their value depends on the severity and permanence of your injuries, the length of your recovery, and how your daily life has changed. Because they are subjective, strong medical records and testimony are key to supporting a full amount.

_roden_faqs.question: Are punitive damages available in South Carolina, and are they capped?
_roden_faqs.answer: Punitive damages may be available when a defendant's conduct was reckless, willful, or malicious, and they are meant to punish rather than compensate. South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times your compensatory damages or an inflation-adjusted floor of roughly $739,000 as of 2026, updated annually. That cap is removed entirely when the harm was caused by driving under the influence, a felony, or an intent to harm (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).

_roden_faqs.question: Are my injury settlement proceeds taxable in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Generally, compensation for physical injuries and related medical expenses is not treated as taxable income, while portions like punitive damages or certain interest can be taxable. Tax treatment depends on how your settlement is structured and your individual situation. Because this is a tax question rather than a legal-claim question, confirm the details with a tax professional.

_roden_faqs.question: Does a pre-existing condition lower my case value in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Not automatically. Under the eggshell-plaintiff principle, a defendant takes you as they find you, so you can still recover for the extent an accident aggravated or worsened a pre-existing condition. The key is separating your prior baseline from the new harm, which makes clear medical documentation especially important. Insurers often blame old injuries to cut value, so this is worth pushing back on.

_roden_faqs.question: How much is a rear-end collision case worth in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no set figure. Rear-end cases range widely because a low-speed bump with no lasting injury is very different from a high-speed impact causing herniated discs or a concussion. Value turns on your medical treatment, lasting symptoms, lost income, and the available insurance. An attorney can give you a realistic range after reviewing your records.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I was injured by an uninsured driver in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: You may still recover through your own uninsured motorist (UM) coverage, which South Carolina requires on every auto policy. UM coverage steps in to pay for your injuries when the at-fault driver has no insurance. Reviewing every applicable policy is often the difference between a capped payout and full compensation, so have an attorney check your coverage. See /resources/south-carolina-um-uim-stacking/.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between UM and UIM coverage in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage pays when the at-fault driver has no insurance at all, and it is required on every South Carolina auto policy. Underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage is optional and pays when the at-fault driver has some insurance but not enough to cover your losses. Both protect you rather than the other driver, and together they can be the primary source of recovery in serious crashes.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I stack UM/UIM coverage in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Often, yes. South Carolina allows class-one insureds, meaning the named insured, their spouse, and resident relatives, to stack UM and UIM limits across multiple vehicles or policies in many situations. Whether stacking applies depends on which vehicles and policies were involved (S.C. Code §§ 38-77-150 and 38-77-160). Passengers and permissive users are class-two insureds and generally cannot stack, so an attorney's review of every policy matters. See /resources/south-carolina-um-uim-stacking/.

_roden_faqs.question: What are the minimum car insurance limits in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina requires minimum liability limits of $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for bodily injury, plus $25,000 for property damage (often written 25/50/25), and matching UM coverage (S.C. Code § 38-77-140). These minimums are low relative to the cost of serious injuries, which is why UM/UIM stacking and every available policy matter. An attorney can identify all coverage that might apply to your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I accept the insurance company's first offer in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Usually not. First offers are typically far below the full value of a claim and are made before you fully understand your injuries and future costs. Once you accept and sign a release, you cannot reopen the claim. It is wise to have an attorney evaluate any offer before you accept it.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I give a recorded statement to the insurance company in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: You should speak with an attorney first. Adjusters use recorded statements to lock you into early words that can later be used to minimize your injuries or shift fault onto you. You are generally not required to give the at-fault driver's insurer a recorded statement. Let your lawyer handle communications so an offhand remark does not reduce your recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: Who pays my medical bills after an accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In the short term, your own health insurance, MedPay coverage, or out-of-pocket payments typically cover treatment. Ultimately, if another party was at fault, their liability insurance should reimburse your medical expenses as part of your injury claim. An attorney can help coordinate these sources and pursue full reimbursement from the at-fault party.

_roden_faqs.question: The at-fault driver didn't have enough insurance in South Carolina. What now?
_roden_faqs.answer: When the at-fault driver's liability limits are too low to cover your losses, your own underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage can make up part of the gap, and stacking may increase what is available. There may also be other responsible parties or policies, such as an employer's coverage if the driver was working. An attorney's job is to find every source of recovery so you are not left short.

_roden_faqs.question: Will my own insurance rates go up if I use my UM/UIM coverage in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Using UM or UIM coverage after a crash you did not cause should not, on its own, be treated as an at-fault claim, though insurer practices vary. The point of the coverage you paid for is to protect you when another driver cannot. If you have a concern about a rate change, an attorney can help you understand your rights before you decide how to proceed.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to pay my medical bills while my South Carolina case is pending?
_roden_faqs.answer: The bills remain your responsibility as they come due, but there are ways to manage them while your claim proceeds. Health insurance, MedPay, and in some cases treatment on a medical lien can bridge the gap until your case resolves. An attorney can help coordinate these options and, at settlement, negotiate what must be repaid so more of the recovery stays with you.

_roden_faqs.question: What is MedPay and how does it work in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: MedPay, or medical payments coverage, is an optional add-on to your auto policy that pays for accident-related medical bills regardless of who caused the crash, up to your coverage limit. It can cover early expenses like the emergency room and follow-up visits while your liability claim is still pending. Because it pays quickly and without a fault determination, it is worth checking whether you carry it.

_roden_faqs.question: What is a medical lien in a South Carolina injury case?
_roden_faqs.answer: A medical lien is a claim that a provider or health insurer has to be repaid from your settlement for the accident-related care they covered. It lets you get treatment now and pay from the recovery later. Liens can significantly reduce your net payout, but they are often negotiable, and an attorney routinely works to lower them so you keep more of your settlement.

_roden_faqs.question: Why is it important to get medical treatment right after an accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Prompt treatment protects both your health and your claim. Some serious injuries, like concussions or internal damage, are not obvious at first, and a delay can let them worsen. Gaps in treatment also give insurers a reason to argue your injuries were minor or unrelated to the crash, so following your doctor's plan consistently supports both your recovery and your case.

_roden_faqs.question: What happens if I have a gap in my medical treatment in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Gaps in care do not automatically defeat your claim, but insurers use them to argue you were not really hurt or that something else caused your injuries. If you had to pause treatment for financial or scheduling reasons, that context matters and can be explained. The best approach is to follow your provider's recommendations and document the reasons for any interruption.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I choose my own doctor after a car accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. After a car accident, you are free to treat with your own physicians and specialists. This is different from a workers' compensation claim, where the employer or its insurer generally directs which authorized doctor you see. Keeping thorough records of every provider and visit strengthens your injury claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Will I have to repay my health insurer from my settlement in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Often, yes. If your health insurer paid for accident-related care, it may assert a right of reimbursement or subrogation to be paid back out of your recovery. The amount is frequently negotiable, and the rules depend on the type of plan you have. An attorney can work to reduce these claims so more of the settlement reaches you.

_roden_faqs.question: Is South Carolina a no-fault state for car accidents?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. South Carolina is an at-fault, or tort, state, not a no-fault state. The driver who caused the crash, and their insurance, is responsible for the resulting injuries and damages. This is different from no-fault states where you turn first to your own insurer regardless of who caused the crash.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do at the scene of a car accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: If you can, move to safety, call 911, and get a police report started. Photograph the vehicles, the scene, and any visible injuries, and collect the other driver's insurance information and the names of witnesses. Seek medical care promptly even if you feel okay, and avoid admitting fault or giving a recorded statement before speaking with an attorney.

_roden_faqs.question: Why are truck accident claims different from car accident claims in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Truck cases involve federal safety regulations, professional drivers, and often multiple responsible parties such as the driver, the trucking company, and maintenance contractors. The injuries tend to be more severe and the available insurance larger, which means insurers and defense teams fight harder. Critical evidence like driver logs and onboard data can also disappear quickly, so early legal action matters.

_roden_faqs.question: How long does a trucking company keep the driver's logs and black-box data in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Under federal rules, carriers are only required to keep hours-of-service logs for about 6 months and driver vehicle inspection reports for about 3 months, and there is no required retention period for the truck's electronic control module or black-box data. That evidence can be overwritten or destroyed unless it is preserved. Sending a legal preservation letter quickly is one of the most important early steps in a truck case.

_roden_faqs.question: What if evidence in my truck accident case gets destroyed in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina does not have a separate lawsuit for spoliation of evidence, but a court can instruct the jury that it may assume destroyed evidence would have been unfavorable to the party that lost or discarded it. That potential jury instruction is a strong reason for trucking companies to preserve records. A prompt preservation letter from your attorney helps protect key data before it disappears.

_roden_faqs.question: Who can be held responsible in a South Carolina truck accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Depending on the facts, responsibility may extend beyond the driver to the trucking company, the owner of the trailer, a maintenance provider, a cargo loader, or a parts manufacturer. Identifying every liable party matters because it can open additional insurance coverage for serious injuries. An attorney investigates the ownership, employment, and maintenance chain to find all sources of recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: Are the car seat laws in South Carolina part of a car accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina's child restraint law (S.C. Code § 56-5-6410) requires children to be rear-facing until at least age 2, in a forward-facing harness after that, in a booster starting at age 4, and in an adult seat belt only at age 8 or 57 inches with a proper belt fit. While the law is about safety and citations, restraint use can come up in a claim involving a child. See /resources/south-carolina-car-seat-laws/.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the other driver in my South Carolina crash was working at the time?
_roden_faqs.answer: If the at-fault driver was on the job, their employer may also be legally responsible, which can open a larger commercial insurance policy. This applies to delivery drivers, rideshare and commercial vehicles, and company cars. Because employer liability can substantially increase available coverage, it is worth investigating the driver's status early in the case.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to wear a helmet to recover after a motorcycle accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina requires helmets only for riders and passengers under 21 (S.C. Code § 56-5-3660). There is no statute that automatically bars or reduces a claim simply because an adult rider was not wearing a helmet. Any argument about helmet use would run through ordinary comparative fault, so not wearing one does not by itself defeat your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still recover if I wasn't wearing a helmet in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, if you were 21 or older, since the law does not require a helmet for adult riders. A defendant might try to argue that not wearing a helmet contributed to head injuries, but that is a comparative-fault argument, not an automatic bar. Whether it reduces your recovery at all depends on the facts and the type of injury involved.

_roden_faqs.question: Are motorcycle accident injuries treated differently in South Carolina claims?
_roden_faqs.answer: The legal rules are the same as other vehicle claims, including the 3-year deadline and the 51% comparative-fault bar, but motorcycle crashes tend to cause more severe injuries because riders lack the protection of a car. That severity can raise case value but also draws harder pushback from insurers, who sometimes rely on bias against riders. Strong evidence of the other driver's fault is especially important.

_roden_faqs.question: Does bias against motorcyclists affect my claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: It can. Some insurers and jurors assume riders are reckless, and adjusters may lean on that assumption to shift fault onto you. Because being pushed to 51% fault would bar your recovery entirely, countering that bias with clear evidence, such as the police report, witness accounts, and scene photos, is critical. An attorney experienced with motorcycle cases knows how to confront these assumptions.

_roden_faqs.question: Does my car insurance cover me on a motorcycle in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Motorcycles typically require their own policy, and coverage like UM and UIM may depend on the specific vehicles and policies involved. After a serious crash, it is important to review every policy in your household to identify all coverage that might apply. An attorney can sort out which policies respond and whether stacking is available.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after a motorcycle accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Get medical attention right away, because motorcycle injuries are often serious even when adrenaline masks the pain, and call the police to document the crash. Photograph the scene, your bike, and your injuries, and gather witness information. Avoid discussing fault at the scene, and contact an attorney early so evidence can be preserved and your deadline protected.

_roden_faqs.question: How much is a motorcycle accident case worth in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no set average. Because motorcycle crashes often cause serious injuries such as fractures, road rash, and brain or spinal injuries, case values can be higher, but the amount still depends on your specific injuries, lost income, fault, and available insurance. An attorney can give you a realistic range after reviewing your medical records and the coverage involved.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to prove my employer was at fault to get workers' comp in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. South Carolina workers' compensation is a no-fault system, so you generally can receive benefits for a work-related injury regardless of who was at fault. In exchange, benefits are limited to things like medical care and wage replacement rather than pain and suffering. You do need to show the injury arose out of and in the course of your employment.

_roden_faqs.question: How soon must I report a work injury in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: You should report a work injury to your employer as soon as possible, and no later than 90 days from the accident (S.C. Code § 42-15-20). Reporting late can jeopardize your benefits. You then generally have 2 years from the injury to file a formal claim with the Workers' Compensation Commission (S.C. Code § 42-15-40).

_roden_faqs.question: How much does workers' comp pay in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: For total disability, South Carolina pays two-thirds (66 2/3%) of your average weekly wage, subject to a state maximum that is set each year, which is $1,189.94 per week for 2026, and a minimum of $75. There is a 7-day waiting period before benefits start, and those first days are paid retroactively if your disability lasts more than 14 days (S.C. Code § 42-9-200). See /resources/how-much-does-south-carolina-workers-comp-pay/.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I pick my own doctor in a South Carolina workers' comp case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Usually not. In South Carolina workers' compensation, the employer or its insurance carrier generally directs your care and chooses the authorized treating physician. Seeing an unauthorized doctor on your own may mean those bills are not covered. If you believe the authorized care is inadequate, an attorney can help you seek a change or a second opinion through the proper channels.

_roden_faqs.question: How are body-part injuries valued in South Carolina workers' comp?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina uses a scheduled-loss system that assigns a set number of weeks of benefits to each body part (S.C. Code § 42-9-30), for example roughly 220 weeks for an arm, 195 for a leg, 185 for a hand, and 300 for the back. Your permanent partial disability award is generally your impairment rating percentage multiplied by the scheduled weeks and by two-thirds of your average weekly wage. See /resources/south-carolina-workers-comp-body-part-values/.

_roden_faqs.question: What does MMI mean in South Carolina workers' compensation?
_roden_faqs.answer: MMI, or maximum medical improvement, is the point at which your condition has stabilized and is not expected to improve further with treatment. At MMI, a doctor assigns an impairment rating, which is used to calculate any permanent disability benefits. Reaching MMI is a key milestone, because it shifts the case from ongoing treatment toward valuing the permanent effects of your injury.

_roden_faqs.question: What can I do if my workers' comp claim is denied in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: A denial is not the end of your claim. You can request a hearing before a single Commissioner, and if needed appeal to the Appellate Panel within 14 days using Form 30, then to the South Carolina Court of Appeals within 30 days, and ultimately the Supreme Court. Because the appeal ladder has strict deadlines, it is wise to involve an attorney quickly after a denial. See /resources/south-carolina-workers-comp-claim-denied/.

_roden_faqs.question: How long can I receive workers' comp benefits in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Most South Carolina workers' compensation benefits are capped at 500 weeks of compensation. Certain catastrophic injuries, specifically paraplegia, quadriplegia, or physical brain damage, can qualify for lifetime benefits. Because the value and duration of benefits depend on how your injury is classified, an attorney can help make sure your case is evaluated correctly.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I get reimbursed for travel to medical appointments in South Carolina workers' comp?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina workers' compensation reimburses mileage for travel to authorized medical care when the round trip is more than 5 miles one way, at a rate set each year, which is 72.5 cents per mile as of 2026. Keep a log of your appointments and mileage so you can submit it for reimbursement. An attorney can help ensure you receive everything you are owed.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue if I slipped and fell on someone's property in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Possibly. In South Carolina, a property owner or business can be liable if it knew or should have known about a dangerous condition and failed to fix it or warn you, and that hazard caused your injury. You generally have 3 years to file, and your recovery is reduced by your share of fault under the 51% bar. An attorney can assess whether the owner's negligence is provable.

_roden_faqs.question: What do I have to prove in a South Carolina slip-and-fall case?
_roden_faqs.answer: You generally must show that a dangerous condition existed, that the property owner knew or reasonably should have known about it, that they failed to fix it or warn you, and that this caused your injury. A central issue is often whether the hazard was present long enough that the owner should have discovered it. Evidence like surveillance video, incident reports, and photos is critical.

_roden_faqs.question: How long does a hazard have to be present for the store to be liable in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no fixed number of minutes. The question is whether the dangerous condition existed long enough that a reasonably careful business should have discovered and addressed it, which the law calls constructive notice. A spill that just happened may not create liability, while one left for a long time likely does. Evidence such as timestamps and video helps establish how long the hazard was there.

_roden_faqs.question: Does my status as a visitor affect a premises case in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina considers whether you were an invitee, such as a customer, a licensee, or a trespasser, and a property owner owes the greatest duty of care to invitees. As a business customer, you are generally owed a duty to keep the premises reasonably safe and to warn of known hazards. Your specific status shapes what the owner had to do to protect you.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I recover if I wasn't watching where I was going in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Possibly, because South Carolina's comparative-fault rule lets you recover as long as you are 50% or less at fault, though your award is reduced by your share. Property owners and their insurers often argue the hazard was open and obvious to shift blame onto you. Whether that argument succeeds depends on the facts, so it is worth having an attorney evaluate the fault picture before you assume you have no case.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do after a slip and fall in a South Carolina store?
_roden_faqs.answer: Report the fall to a manager and ask that an incident report be made, then photograph the hazard and the area before it is cleaned up. Get the names of any witnesses and seek medical care promptly. Ask whether there is surveillance footage, and contact an attorney quickly so a preservation request can be sent before video is overwritten.

_roden_faqs.question: Are landlords liable for injuries on rental property in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: They can be, depending on the circumstances. A landlord may be responsible for injuries caused by dangerous conditions in areas they control or are required to maintain, such as common stairways or walkways, especially when they knew about a hazard and failed to repair it. Liability turns on who had control over the dangerous condition. An attorney can help identify the responsible party.

_roden_faqs.question: Who can file a wrongful death claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: A South Carolina wrongful death action must be brought by the personal representative of the deceased person's estate, not directly by individual family members (S.C. Code § 15-51-20). The recovery is then distributed to statutory beneficiaries in order: the spouse and children first, then parents, then other heirs. If no personal representative has been appointed, the court can appoint one so the case can proceed.

_roden_faqs.question: What damages can be recovered in a South Carolina wrongful death case?
_roden_faqs.answer: A South Carolina wrongful death claim can recover for the beneficiaries' losses, including lost financial support, lost companionship and guidance, and their grief and mental anguish, along with funeral and burial expenses. A separate survival action may recover for the losses the deceased personally suffered before death, such as their own pain and suffering. Together these address both the family's and the deceased's losses.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between a wrongful death and a survival action in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: A wrongful death action compensates the surviving family for their losses, such as lost support, companionship, and grief. A survival action (S.C. Code § 15-5-90) belongs to the estate and recovers for what the deceased personally endured before death, including their pre-death pain, suffering, and expenses. The two claims are often pursued together and cover different harms.

_roden_faqs.question: How is a wrongful death settlement distributed in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Wrongful death proceeds pass to statutory beneficiaries in order set by law: first the spouse and children, then the parents, then other heirs. The personal representative brings the case, but the recovery belongs to the beneficiaries rather than the estate's general creditors. Because distribution and any required court approval can be complex, families benefit from legal guidance.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do we have to file a wrongful death claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: A South Carolina wrongful death claim generally must be filed within 3 years of the date of death. If a government entity is responsible, a shorter Tort Claims Act deadline may apply. Because appointing a personal representative and investigating the death takes time, families should speak with an attorney well before the deadline approaches.

_roden_faqs.question: Can we recover if our loved one was partly at fault in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Possibly. South Carolina's 51% comparative-fault rule applies to wrongful death claims, so beneficiaries can recover as long as the deceased was 50% or less at fault, with the award reduced by that percentage. If the deceased was 51% or more at fault, recovery is barred. How fault is apportioned can therefore be decisive, which makes a thorough investigation important.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on wrongful death damages in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In an ordinary wrongful death case against a private defendant, there is no cap on compensatory damages. Punitive damages are subject to South Carolina's statutory limits, and claims against government entities are capped under the Tort Claims Act at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence with no punitive damages. Which rules apply depends on who is responsible for the death.

_roden_faqs.question: How much does a personal injury lawyer cost in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Roden Law handles personal injury cases on a contingency fee basis: you pay no attorney fees upfront and owe nothing unless we win. Our fee is a percentage of the recovery. If we do not win, you do not pay attorney fees. This lets anyone access experienced representation regardless of their finances.

_roden_faqs.question: What does contingency fee mean in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: A contingency fee means your attorney's fee is a percentage of the money recovered, and you pay nothing in attorney fees unless the case is won. There are no upfront costs to start your case, and the fee comes out of the settlement or verdict at the end. This arrangement lets injured people hire experienced counsel without paying by the hour.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer for a personal injury claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: You are not legally required to hire a lawyer, but represented claimants typically recover significantly more, even after fees. Insurers have adjusters and lawyers working to minimize your payout. An attorney investigates, values your claim accurately, handles the insurers, and litigates if needed. Roden Law works on contingency, so you pay nothing unless we win.

_roden_faqs.question: How long does a personal injury case take in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: It varies widely. Straightforward claims may resolve in a few months, while serious-injury cases that require full medical treatment, investigation, or litigation can take a year or more. Settling too early, before your injuries are fully understood, often leaves money on the table, so timing should follow your recovery and the strength of the evidence.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to go to court for my South Carolina personal injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Most personal injury claims settle without a trial. However, if the insurer refuses to offer fair compensation, your attorney may file suit and take the case toward trial. Having a firm that is willing and able to go to court often improves settlement offers, because insurers know the claim can be tried if necessary.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I bring to my free consultation with a South Carolina injury lawyer?
_roden_faqs.answer: Bring anything you have that documents the incident and your injuries: the police or incident report, photos, insurance information for everyone involved, medical records and bills, and any correspondence from insurers. Notes about how the injury has affected your work and daily life are also helpful. Even if you do not have everything, an attorney can still evaluate your case and help gather the rest.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I already gave a statement or signed something after my accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: It is still worth talking to an attorney. Early statements or documents can complicate a claim, but they do not always end it, and a lawyer can assess the impact and advise on next steps. What matters most is that you stop giving further statements and get legal advice before doing anything else. The consultation is free, and there are no fees unless we win.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I switch lawyers if I'm unhappy with my current one in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Generally, yes. You have the right to change attorneys, and doing so usually does not increase your total fee, because fee questions between the old and new lawyer are typically worked out from the single contingency fee. If you feel your case is not getting the attention it deserves, it is reasonable to seek a second opinion. Roden Law can review where your case stands at no cost.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do immediately after an accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Seek medical attention right away, even if you feel fine, because some serious injuries are not obvious at first. Call the police and get a report, document the scene with photos, collect witness contact information, and preserve evidence. Do not give a recorded statement to any insurer before speaking with an attorney, and contact a lawyer early so an investigation can begin while evidence is fresh.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I go to the doctor even if I feel fine after a South Carolina accident?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Adrenaline can mask pain, and injuries like concussions, whiplash, and internal damage may not show symptoms for hours or days. A prompt medical evaluation protects your health and creates a record linking your injuries to the crash. Delaying care can worsen an injury and give insurers an opening to argue you were not really hurt.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence should I collect after an accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: If you are able, take photos of the vehicles, the scene, road conditions, and your injuries, and collect the names and contact information of any witnesses. Save the police or incident report number, insurance details, and any receipts or records related to the accident. Preserving this evidence early, before it disappears, strengthens your claim significantly.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I post about my accident on social media in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: No. Insurers and defense lawyers routinely search claimants' social media, and even innocent posts or photos can be taken out of context to dispute your injuries or your version of events. It is safest to avoid posting about the accident, your injuries, or your activities while your claim is pending. When in doubt, ask your attorney first.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I not do after an accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Avoid admitting fault at the scene, giving a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer, or accepting a quick settlement before you understand your injuries. Do not skip or delay medical treatment, and do not post about the accident on social media. Each of these can be used to reduce or deny your claim, so it is wise to talk to an attorney first.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I have to report my accident to the police in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: You should call the police for any crash involving injuries or significant property damage, and South Carolina requires reporting accidents that meet certain injury or damage thresholds. A police report creates an official, neutral record of the crash that can be valuable evidence later. Even when a report is not strictly required, having one usually helps your claim.

_roden_faqs.question: How do I get a copy of my accident report in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: South Carolina crash reports are generally available through the investigating law enforcement agency or the state, and there is typically a small fee. It can take a few days after the crash for the report to be filed and available. If you have trouble obtaining it, your attorney can request the report and the underlying records as part of building your case.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still have a case if I didn't go to the hospital right away in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, delayed treatment does not automatically end your claim, though it can make things harder. Insurers use gaps in care to argue your injuries were minor or unrelated, so the sooner you are evaluated and the more consistently you treat, the stronger your case. If you waited for understandable reasons, that context can be explained, and an attorney can still assess your options.

/resources/south-carolina-premises-liabi.excerpt: South Carolina premises liability covers far more than falls — negligent security, assaults, and unsafe conditions. There is no cap on your compensatory damages in ordinary cases.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the average premises liability settlement in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no reliable single average. South Carolina premises liability settlements range from tens of thousands of dollars to several million, depending on the hazard, how badly you were hurt, whether the owner had notice, and your share of fault. Negligent-security and catastrophic-injury cases sit at the high end. Every case is unique and no result is guaranteed.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between premises liability and slip and fall in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Premises liability is the broad category covering any injury from an unsafe property — negligent security and assaults, inadequate maintenance, pool and stairwell hazards, and parking-lot dangers. A slip and fall is one common subset involving falls specifically. Both require proving the owner was negligent about a hazard they knew or should have known about.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue for an assault or shooting at a business in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Sometimes. A negligent-security claim can hold a property owner responsible when they failed to provide reasonable security — lighting, cameras, or guards — despite known crime risk, and that failure allowed an assault or shooting to occur. Evidence of prior crime on or near the property is often key to showing the harm was foreseeable and preventable.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on damages in a South Carolina premises liability case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Not in an ordinary case against a private owner — South Carolina places no cap on compensatory damages. But if the property is government-owned, the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-120) caps damages at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence and bars punitive damages against the government.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In South Carolina, you generally have 3 years from the date of injury to file a premises liability lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. If a government entity owns the property, notice deadlines can be much shorter. Acting early also helps preserve evidence like surveillance video and incident reports before they disappear.

_roden_faqs.question: Are punitive damages available in South Carolina premises liability cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: They can be, against a private owner who acted recklessly — for example, ignoring repeated warnings about violent crime or a known deadly hazard. Under S.C. Code § 15-32-530, punitive damages are generally capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or an inflation-adjusted minimum (about $739,000 as of 2026, adjusted annually). They are not available against a government defendant.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the average slip and fall settlement in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no reliable single average. Most South Carolina slip and fall settlements range from a few thousand dollars for minor falls to six or seven figures for serious ones. Value depends heavily on whether the property owner had notice of the hazard, how badly you were hurt, and your share of fault. Every case is unique and no result is guaranteed.

_roden_faqs.question: What do I have to prove to win a slip and fall case in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: You generally must prove the property owner was negligent about a dangerous condition — that they knew about the hazard (actual notice) or that it existed long enough that they should have known (constructive notice) and failed to fix it or warn you. Evidence like incident reports, cleaning logs, and surveillance video is often decisive.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on damages in a South Carolina slip and fall case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Not in an ordinary case against a private business or homeowner — South Carolina places no cap on compensatory damages. But if you fell on government property, the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-120) caps damages at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence and bars punitive damages.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In South Carolina, you generally have 3 years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. If a government entity owns the property, notice deadlines can be much shorter. Acting early also helps preserve evidence like surveillance video before it is overwritten.

_roden_faqs.question: Can my slip and fall settlement be reduced if I was partly at fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina uses modified comparative negligence, so your award is reduced by your fault percentage and barred if you are 51% or more at fault. Property owners often argue you ignored an obvious hazard or were not watching where you were going. An attorney can push back on inflated fault claims to protect your recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between a slip and fall case and a premises liability case?
_roden_faqs.answer: A slip and fall is one type of premises liability case — it involves falls specifically, from hazards like wet floors, uneven surfaces, stairs, or ice. Premises liability is the broader category that also covers negligent security, assaults on a property, pool and stairwell hazards, and other unsafe conditions. See our premises liability case value guide for the broader picture.

/resources/south-carolina-statute-of-lim.title: South Carolina Statute of Limitations for Personal Injury Claims
/resources/south-carolina-statute-of-lim.excerpt: In South Carolina you generally have 3 years to file a personal injury claim (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Some deadlines are shorter — here is how the clock works.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In South Carolina, you generally have 3 years from the date of your injury to file a personal injury lawsuit, under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. This covers most car, truck, motorcycle, pedestrian, slip-and-fall, and general negligence claims. Some claims — especially those against government entities — have shorter deadlines, so it is best to confirm your specific deadline with an attorney early.

_roden_faqs.question: What happens if I miss the statute of limitations in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: If you file after the deadline has passed, the court will almost always dismiss your case, no matter how strong it is. You typically lose the right to recover any compensation. Because the rule is so unforgiving, it is critical to act well before the deadline rather than waiting until it is nearly up.

_roden_faqs.question: Is the deadline different for medical malpractice in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. A South Carolina medical malpractice claim generally must be filed within 3 years of when you discovered, or should have discovered, the injury, but no later than an outside statute of repose measured from the date of the negligent act. Because the discovery and repose rules interact, malpractice deadlines are easy to miscalculate — have the timeline reviewed promptly if you suspect a medical error.

_roden_faqs.question: Does South Carolina have a shorter deadline for claims against the government?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Claims against a city, county, the state, a public hospital, or another government entity fall under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-10 et seq.) and must generally be filed within 2 years, rather than the usual 3. Filing an optional verified claim with the agency (within 1 year of the loss) can extend that deadline to 3 years. If any government body may be at fault, assume the deadline is short and contact an attorney immediately.

_roden_faqs.question: Can the South Carolina deadline ever be paused or extended?
_roden_faqs.answer: In limited situations, yes. The statute of limitations is generally tolled (paused) for injured minors, and the discovery rule can delay when the clock starts for injuries that are not immediately obvious. These exceptions are narrow and frequently disputed by insurers, so you should never assume one applies without legal advice.

/resources/south-carolina-truck-accident.title: How Much Is a SC Truck Accident Case Worth?
/resources/south-carolina-truck-accident.excerpt: Most SC truck accident settlements range from tens of thousands to several million dollars, depending on injury severity, fault, and the truck's insurance.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the average truck accident settlement in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: There is no reliable single average, because truck accident settlements in South Carolina range from tens of thousands of dollars for moderate injuries to several million for catastrophic ones. Value depends on injury severity, medical bills, lost income, fault, and the truck's commercial insurance limits. Every case is unique and no result is guaranteed.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a truck accident claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In South Carolina, you generally have 3 years from the date of the crash to file a truck accident lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. If you miss this deadline, you usually lose the right to recover compensation entirely. Acting early also helps preserve evidence like the truck's logbooks and black-box data.

_roden_faqs.question: Will my own fault reduce my South Carolina truck accident settlement?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina uses modified comparative negligence, so you can recover only if you are less than 51% at fault, and your award is reduced by your fault percentage. If your case is worth $200,000 and you are 25% at fault, you recover $150,000. At 51% or more fault, you recover nothing.

_roden_faqs.question: Why is a truck accident worth more than a car accident in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Truck accidents are often worth more because commercial trucks carry much higher insurance — frequently $750,000 to $1 million or more under federal FMCSA rules — and because multiple parties can be liable, including the carrier, driver, and broker. More coverage and more defendants mean more compensation is realistically available for serious injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: Are punitive damages available in South Carolina truck accident cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: Punitive damages may be available when a trucking company or driver acted recklessly or willfully, such as falsifying logs or violating fatigue rules. Under S.C. Code § 15-32-530, they are generally capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, with exceptions. They are never awarded in ordinary negligence cases and are not guaranteed.

Every case is unique and no result is guaranteed.

/resources/south-carolina-um-uim-stackin.title: Stacking UM and UIM Coverage in South Carolina
/resources/south-carolina-um-uim-stackin.excerpt: South Carolina lets drivers stack uninsured (UM) and underinsured (UIM) coverage across multiple vehicles or policies — potentially multiplying what you can recover.

_roden_faqs.question: Can you stack UM and UIM coverage in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina allows drivers to stack uninsured (UM) and underinsured (UIM) motorist coverage in many situations, meaning you may combine coverage limits from more than one vehicle or policy to increase what you can recover. Whether and how you can stack depends on your specific policies, so each policy must be reviewed carefully.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between UM and UIM coverage?
_roden_faqs.answer: Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage pays for your injuries when the at-fault driver has no liability insurance, or in hit-and-run cases where the driver cannot be identified. Underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage pays when the at-fault driver has insurance but not enough to cover the full extent of your injuries. Both protect you through your own policy.

_roden_faqs.question: How does stacking increase my recovery in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Stacking combines coverage limits from multiple vehicles or policies into a larger pool. For example, if you have $100,000 in UM coverage on each of two household vehicles, stacking may let you combine them toward your losses rather than being capped at a single limit. This can multiply the money available when the at-fault driver has little or no insurance.

_roden_faqs.question: How do I know if I can stack my coverage?
_roden_faqs.answer: It depends on your policy language, how the coverage was purchased, the number of vehicles and policies involved, and your relationship to the policyholders. Because the answer turns on details that are easy to misread, the safest approach is to have an attorney review every policy that might apply — people are often wrongly told that no additional coverage exists.

Stacking can dramatically raise the money available when the at-fault driver carries little or no insurance. /resources/south-carolina-workers-comp-b.title: South Carolina Workers' Comp Body Part Value Chart
/resources/south-carolina-workers-comp-b.excerpt: South Carolina's workers' comp body-part value chart under S.C. Code § 42-9-30: how many weeks of benefits each scheduled member (arm, hand, back, eye, more) is worth.

_roden_faqs.question: How many weeks of benefits is a body part worth in South Carolina workers' comp?
_roden_faqs.answer: S.C. Code § 42-9-30 sets a number of weeks for each body part, paid at two-thirds (66⅔%) of your average weekly wage. Key values include a hand at 185 weeks, an arm at 220 weeks, a leg at 195 weeks, a foot at 140 weeks, an eye at 140 weeks, and a shoulder at 300 weeks. The back is worth 300 weeks at 49% or less loss of use and 500 weeks at 50% or more.

_roden_faqs.question: How is the value of my injury calculated?
_roden_faqs.answer: Multiply three numbers: the scheduled weeks for the injured body part, your loss-of-use percentage (set at maximum medical improvement), and your compensation rate (66⅔% of your average weekly wage). For example, a 50% loss of use of a hand is 50% × 185 = 92.5 weeks, paid at your comp rate.

_roden_faqs.question: Why is a back injury worth more in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: The back is the one scheduled member with two tiers. A back injury with 49% or less loss of use is worth up to 300 weeks, while a back injury with 50% or more loss of use is worth up to 500 weeks. A back rated at 50% or more also triggers a rebuttable presumption of total and permanent disability, which is why the rating is heavily contested.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between a scheduled and unscheduled injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: A scheduled member is a body part on the § 42-9-30 list, such as an arm, hand, leg, or eye. An unscheduled or "whole person" injury is one not on the list and is compensated based on loss of earning capacity, up to 500 weeks. Disfigurement of a normally exposed area is a separate category worth up to 50 weeks.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I get more than the scheduled amount for my injury?
_roden_faqs.answer: Sometimes. The scheduled value is a floor, not a ceiling. Instead of the scheduled award, you may be able to pursue a loss of earning capacity (wage-loss) claim under S.C. Code § 42-9-20 or a total disability claim under § 42-9-10, either of which can pay more if the injury affects your ability to earn a living.

_roden_faqs.question: How does a partial loss of use affect my award?
_roden_faqs.answer: A partial loss of use is paid proportionally under § 42-9-30. For example, a 50% loss of use of a hand equals 50% × 185 = 92.5 weeks, and a 25% loss of use of a leg equals 25% × 195 = 48.75 weeks. The percentage comes from your loss-of-use rating, which is set once you reach maximum medical improvement.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: South Carolina's workers' compensation law assigns a set number of weeks of benefits to each body part under the "scheduled member" table in S.C. Code § 42-9-30. Each award is paid at two-thirds (66⅔%) of your average weekly wage for the listed number of weeks. For example, the loss of a hand is worth 185 weeks, an arm 220 weeks, and a leg 195 weeks. The back is the key exception: it is worth 300 weeks if you have 49% or less loss of use, but 500 weeks if you have 50% or more loss of use (and a 50%-or-more back injury triggers a rebuttable presumption of total and permanent disability). A partial loss of use is paid proportionally — for example, 50% loss of use of a hand equals 92.5 weeks. These week values are fixed by statute, but the dollar amount depends on your wages, which is why having your impairment rating and wage calculation done correctly matters.

/resources/south-carolina-workers-comp-c.title: What to Do If Your SC Workers' Comp Claim Is Denied
/resources/south-carolina-workers-comp-c.excerpt: A denied South Carolina workers' comp claim is not the end. Learn the appeal ladder, the deadlines (14 days, 30 days), and the forms you need to fight a denial.

_roden_faqs.question: What should I do if my South Carolina workers' comp claim is denied?
_roden_faqs.answer: A denial is not the end of your case. You request a hearing before a single Commissioner of the Workers' Compensation Commission using Form 50 (Form 52 for a death claim). If you lose, you can appeal up a defined ladder with short deadlines. Because the first appeal deadline is only 14 days, you should act quickly and consider getting an attorney involved.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to appeal a denied workers' comp claim in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: You have 14 days to appeal a single Commissioner's order to the Appellate Panel (full Commission) under § 42-17-50, using Form 30 with a $150 fee. From there you have 30 days to appeal to the South Carolina Court of Appeals under § 42-17-60. The final step, the South Carolina Supreme Court, is discretionary review.

_roden_faqs.question: Why do workers' comp claims get denied in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: Common reasons include disputes over whether the injury is work-related, claims that you missed the 90-day notice deadline or the 2-year filing deadline, pre-existing-condition arguments that blame a prior injury, and independent-contractor classification arguments that you were not a covered employee. Many of these defenses can be overcome with the right evidence.

_roden_faqs.question: What forms do I need to appeal a denial in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: You start by requesting a hearing with Form 50 (Form 52 for a death claim) before a single Commissioner. To appeal that Commissioner's order to the Appellate Panel, you file Form 30, the Request for Commission Review, within 14 days, along with a $150 fee.

_roden_faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer to appeal a denied workers' comp claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: It is strongly advisable. Once a claim is denied, the process is adversarial and deadline-driven. An attorney can gather the medical and employment evidence to overcome the denial, file the right forms on time, and present your case at the hearing and on appeal. South Carolina workers' comp attorneys work on contingency, with fees subject to Commission approval.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I appeal a South Carolina workers' comp denial to court?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. After the Appellate Panel (full Commission) rules, you can appeal to the South Carolina Court of Appeals within 30 days under § 42-17-60 — a direct route available for injuries on or after July 1, 2007. After that, you may seek discretionary review by the South Carolina Supreme Court.
