/wrongful-death-lawyers/defective-produc.excerpt: Lost a loved one due to a defective product in Georgia or South Carolina? Our wrongful death attorneys hold manufacturers, distributors, and retailers accountable for dangerous products that cause fatal injuries.

_roden_faqs.question: Who can be held liable for a death caused by a defective product?
_roden_faqs.answer: Any entity in the chain of distribution may be liable, including the product designer, manufacturer, component part suppliers, distributors, and retailers. Our attorneys investigate the entire chain to identify all responsible parties.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between a design defect and a manufacturing defect?
_roden_faqs.answer: A design defect means the product was inherently dangerous as designed — every unit is defective. A manufacturing defect means the design was adequate but a specific unit deviated from the design during production, making that particular product dangerous.

_roden_faqs.question: Should I keep the product that caused the death?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Preserving the product in its post-incident condition is critical for expert analysis. Do not repair, alter, or discard the product. Notify your attorney immediately so a preservation protocol can be established.

_roden_faqs.question: Does a product recall affect my wrongful death claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: A recall can actually strengthen your claim by demonstrating that the manufacturer knew the product was dangerous. However, recalls do not eliminate your right to file a claim — you may still pursue compensation for a death caused by a recalled product.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a defective product death claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, wrongful death claims must be filed within 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), with a 10-year product liability statute of repose. In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Deadlines may vary depending on the specific product and theory of liability.

/wrongful-death-lawyers/drowning-swimmin.title: Drowning and Swimming Pool Death Lawyers
/wrongful-death-lawyers/drowning-swimmin.excerpt: Lost a loved one in a drowning or swimming pool accident in Georgia or South Carolina? Our wrongful death attorneys hold negligent property owners, pool operators, and product manufacturers accountable.

_roden_faqs.question: Who is liable for a swimming pool drowning?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potentially liable parties include the pool owner, the property manager, the hotel or resort operator, the lifeguard or lifeguard company, and the manufacturer of defective pool equipment such as drain covers. Liability depends on who had the duty to maintain the pool and ensure safety.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the Virginia Graeme Baker Act?
_roden_faqs.answer: The Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act is a federal law requiring public pools and spas to have compliant drain covers to prevent suction entrapment. Violations of this law can serve as evidence of negligence in a drowning wrongful death case.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue an apartment complex if my child drowned in their pool?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Apartment complexes and HOAs that maintain pools have a duty to comply with safety regulations, including fencing, gate locks, and signage. The "attractive nuisance" doctrine may impose additional duties regarding child safety.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a drowning wrongful death claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, wrongful death claims must be filed within 2 years of the date of death (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

_roden_faqs.question: Do drowning victims suffer before death?
_roden_faqs.answer: Medical evidence indicates that drowning victims often experience a period of conscious terror and struggling before losing consciousness. This pre-death suffering is compensable through a survival action in addition to the wrongful death claim.

/wrongful-death-lawyers/fatal-car-accide.excerpt: Lost a loved one in a fatal car accident in Georgia or South Carolina? Our wrongful death attorneys pursue maximum compensation from negligent drivers and their insurers on behalf of surviving families.

_roden_faqs.question: Who can file a wrongful death claim for a fatal car accident in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the surviving spouse has the primary right to file. If there is no spouse, the children may file. If there are no children, the parents or estate administrator may bring the claim (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-2).

_roden_faqs.question: What damages are available in a fatal car accident wrongful death claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Damages include the full value of the deceased's life (future earnings and contributions), pre-death pain and suffering, medical expenses incurred before death, funeral and burial costs, and loss of companionship and support.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I file a wrongful death claim if the at-fault driver was uninsured?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. You may recover compensation through your loved one's uninsured motorist (UM) coverage. Additionally, other liable parties — such as employers, vehicle manufacturers, or establishments that served alcohol — may provide additional sources of recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: How is a wrongful death claim different from a criminal case?
_roden_faqs.answer: A wrongful death claim is a civil lawsuit seeking financial compensation, while a criminal case seeks punishment through the justice system. The two proceed independently — you can file a wrongful death claim regardless of whether criminal charges are filed or result in conviction.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a fatal car accident wrongful death claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the deadline is 2 years from the date of death (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, it is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Prompt action is critical to preserve evidence and identify all liable parties.

/wrongful-death-lawyers/fatal-truck-acci.title: Fatal Truck Accident Lawyers
/wrongful-death-lawyers/fatal-truck-acci.excerpt: Lost a loved one in a fatal truck accident in Georgia or South Carolina? Our wrongful death attorneys pursue claims against negligent trucking companies, drivers, and other liable parties for maximum compensation.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the trucking company in addition to the driver?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Trucking companies are often liable under respondeat superior (employer liability) and may also be directly liable for negligent hiring, inadequate training, failure to maintain vehicles, or pressuring drivers to violate hours-of-service rules.

_roden_faqs.question: What federal regulations apply to truck accident cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: The FMCSA establishes regulations for hours of service, driver qualifications, vehicle maintenance, drug testing, and cargo securement. Violations of these regulations serve as strong evidence of negligence in a wrongful death claim.

_roden_faqs.question: How much insurance do trucking companies carry?
_roden_faqs.answer: Federal law requires minimum insurance coverage of $750,000 for general freight carriers and up to $5 million for carriers transporting hazardous materials. Many large trucking companies carry policies well above the minimums.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence is important in a fatal truck accident case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Critical evidence includes electronic logging device (ELD) data, dashcam footage, GPS records, pre-trip inspection reports, driver qualification files, toxicology results, and the truck's maintenance history. A spoliation letter must be sent immediately to preserve this evidence.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a fatal truck accident claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, wrongful death claims must be filed within 2 years of the date of death (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

/wrongful-death-lawyers/medical-malpract.title: Medical Malpractice Death Lawyers
/wrongful-death-lawyers/medical-malpract.excerpt: Lost a loved one due to medical malpractice in Georgia or South Carolina? Our wrongful death attorneys pursue claims against negligent doctors, surgeons, hospitals, and healthcare providers.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the expert affidavit requirement in Georgia medical malpractice death cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: Under O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1, you must file an expert affidavit from a qualified medical professional simultaneously with your wrongful death complaint. The affidavit must identify at least one negligent act by each defendant. Failure to comply can result in dismissal.

_roden_faqs.question: Who can file a medical malpractice wrongful death claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the surviving spouse has the primary right to file (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-2). If there is no surviving spouse, children, parents, or the estate administrator may file. In South Carolina, the estate's personal representative files on behalf of statutory beneficiaries.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of repose for medical malpractice in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71, medical malpractice claims must generally be brought within 5 years of the negligent act, regardless of when the patient died. This absolute deadline applies even if the connection between the negligence and death was not discovered until later.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a hospital for a patient death?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Hospitals may be directly liable for systemic failures such as understaffing, inadequate infection control, or failure to enforce safety protocols. Hospitals may also be vicariously liable for the negligence of their employee physicians, nurses, and staff.

_roden_faqs.question: What damages are available in a medical malpractice death case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Damages include the full value of the deceased's life, loss of companionship, pre-death pain and suffering, medical expenses, and funeral costs. Georgia and South Carolina allow both wrongful death and survival actions to maximize the family's total recovery.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a wrongful death claim in South Carolina?

_roden_faqs.question: What is the difference between a wrongful death and a survival action?
_roden_faqs.answer: A wrongful death claim compensates the surviving family for their losses — lost support, companionship, grief, and funeral costs. A separate survival action (S.C. Code § 15-5-90) compensates the estate for what the deceased personally endured before death, including conscious pain and suffering and pre-death medical bills. The two are usually pursued together.

_roden_faqs.question: Is there a cap on wrongful death damages in South Carolina?
_roden_faqs.answer: In ordinary cases, no — South Carolina does not cap wrongful death damages. Two exceptions apply: claims against a government defendant are limited under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act ($300,000 per person / $600,000 per occurrence), and a death caused by medical malpractice is subject to the § 15-32-220 non-economic damages cap.

/wrongful-death-lawyers/nursing-home-wro.excerpt: Lost a loved one due to nursing home abuse or neglect in Georgia or South Carolina? Our wrongful death attorneys pursue claims against negligent nursing homes, assisted living facilities, and their corporate owners.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue a nursing home for a loved one's death?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. If your loved one died due to the nursing home's negligence, abuse, or understaffing, you can file a wrongful death claim against the facility and potentially its corporate owners and management company.

_roden_faqs.question: What evidence is important in a nursing home wrongful death case?
_roden_faqs.answer: Critical evidence includes the resident's medical records, staffing logs, CMS survey deficiency reports, incident reports, family complaints, photographs of the resident's condition, and Adult Protective Services investigation findings.

_roden_faqs.question: Are punitive damages available in nursing home wrongful death cases?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, in cases involving willful neglect, abuse, or reckless disregard for resident safety. Georgia generally caps punitive damages at $250,000 (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1) with exceptions, while South Carolina requires clear and convincing evidence of willful conduct.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I hold the nursing home's corporate owner liable?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. If the corporate entity controlled staffing levels, budgets, or care policies that contributed to the death, it may be held directly liable. Our attorneys investigate the corporate ownership structure to identify all responsible parties.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a nursing home wrongful death claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, wrongful death claims must be filed within 2 years of the date of death (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Evidence from nursing home records should be preserved as quickly as possible.

/wrongful-death-lawyers/pedestrian-cycli.title: Pedestrian and Cyclist Fatality Lawyers
/wrongful-death-lawyers/pedestrian-cycli.excerpt: Lost a loved one in a pedestrian or cyclist accident in Georgia or South Carolina? Our wrongful death attorneys pursue claims against negligent drivers, municipalities, and other responsible parties.

_roden_faqs.question: What if the driver who killed my loved one fled the scene?
_roden_faqs.answer: In hit-and-run fatalities, the deceased's uninsured motorist (UM) coverage may provide compensation. Additionally, if the driver is later identified, a wrongful death claim can be filed. Our attorneys work with law enforcement and private investigators to identify hit-and-run drivers.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I sue the city if poor road design contributed to the death?
_roden_faqs.answer: Potentially. If missing crosswalks, absent traffic signals, lack of bike lanes, or insufficient lighting contributed to the accident, the municipality or state DOT may bear partial liability. Claims against government entities have special procedures and shorter deadlines.

_roden_faqs.question: Does comparative fault apply if the pedestrian or cyclist was partially at fault?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia allows recovery if the deceased was less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina allows recovery if less than 51% at fault. Damages are reduced by the percentage of fault attributed to the deceased.

_roden_faqs.question: Why are pedestrian and cyclist fatalities increasing?
_roden_faqs.answer: Researchers attribute rising pedestrian and cyclist deaths to increased distracted driving (smartphone use), the growing popularity of larger vehicles (SUVs and trucks with bigger blind spots), higher speeds on roadways, and insufficient pedestrian and cycling infrastructure.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a pedestrian or cyclist fatality claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, the wrongful death statute of limitations is 2 years from the date of death (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, it is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Claims against government entities for unsafe road design may have shorter notice requirements.

_roden_faqs.question: What if I was partially at fault for my wrongful death in Savannah?
_roden_faqs.answer: Under Georgia's modified comparative fault under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, you can still recover damages as long as you are less than 50% responsible for the accident. However, your compensation will be reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are found 20% at fault and your total damages are $100,000, you would receive $80,000. However, if you are found 50% or more at fault, you cannot recover any compensation at all. Insurance companies frequently attempt to shift blame to injury victims to reduce or deny payouts. /wrongful-death-lawyers/workplace-fatali.title: Workplace Fatality Lawyers
/wrongful-death-lawyers/workplace-fatali.excerpt: Lost a loved one in a workplace accident in Georgia or South Carolina? Our wrongful death attorneys pursue claims beyond workers' compensation against negligent third parties, equipment manufacturers, and property owners.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I file a wrongful death claim if my loved one died at work?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, if a third party (someone other than the employer) contributed to the death. While workers' compensation is typically the exclusive remedy against the employer, you can file a separate wrongful death lawsuit against negligent third parties such as property owners, contractors, or equipment manufacturers.

_roden_faqs.question: What are workers' compensation death benefits?
_roden_faqs.answer: Workers' compensation death benefits provide a portion of the deceased worker's wages to the surviving spouse and dependents, plus funeral expenses. These benefits are limited and do not include pain and suffering or the full value of life available through a wrongful death claim.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I receive both workers' compensation and wrongful death damages?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, but the workers' compensation carrier may have a lien on your third-party wrongful death recovery. Our attorneys negotiate these liens to maximize the net amount your family receives.

_roden_faqs.question: What role does OSHA play in a workplace fatality case?
_roden_faqs.answer: OSHA investigates all workplace fatalities and may issue citations for safety violations. OSHA findings, while not binding in civil cases, provide valuable evidence of negligence that can strengthen a wrongful death claim.

_roden_faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a workplace fatality wrongful death claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: In Georgia, wrongful death claims must be filed within 2 years of the date of death (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Workers' compensation claims have separate, shorter reporting deadlines.
